11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a training paradigm where a model learns rich representations from UNLABELLED data by solving PRETEXT TASKS that the data itself provides supervision for — no human-annotated labels needed; the key insight is that the structure of natural data (images, text, audio) contains enough predictable patterns that a model forced to predict or reconstruct those patterns must learn semantically useful representations as a side effect.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: Labelled datasets are expensive and scarce, but unlabelled data is abundant — SSL lets models exploit the massive scale of unlabelled data (internet images, raw text, raw audio) to learn feature representations that TRANSFER well to downstream tasks with few or no labels; SSL became the dominant pretraining paradigm in NLP (BERT, GPT) and later vision (MAE, DINO) precisely because it decouples representation learning (cheap, scalable) from task-specific supervision (expensive, scarce).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: SSL designs a PRETEXT TASK that forces the model to extract meaningful structure: examples include CONTRASTIVE methods (pull different views of the same image together in embedding space, push different images apart — covered in this subtopic), MASKED methods (predict masked/missing patches or tokens from context — covered in Masked & Generative SSL), and PREDICTIVE methods (predict the representation of one view from another without negatives — BYOL, SimSiam); crucially, the PRETEXT TASK is discarded after pretraining — only the learned encoder is kept and fine-tuned or evaluated on downstream tasks; the quality of downstream transfer (measured via linear probe or few-shot accuracy) indicates how well the pretext task forced the model to learn SEMANTIC structure rather than shortcuts.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use SSL pretraining when you have ABUNDANT unlabelled data but few labels for your target task — the canonical scenario; also use as a starting point for transfer learning in domains where ImageNet-pretrained weights are a poor prior (medical imaging, satellite imagery, audio, molecular data) but domain-specific unlabelled data exists; SSL is especially valuable when the downstream task requires MULTIPLE different labelled tasks — one SSL-pretrained backbone can serve all of them.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid investing in custom SSL pretraining when a strong, publicly available pretrained model already exists for your domain/modality and fine-tuning it on your labelled data is sufficient — custom SSL training is expensive (often requiring multi-GPU setups for days/weeks) and only pays off when existing pretrained models genuinely underperform your domain's data distribution; avoid treating SSL as a substitute for ALL labelled data — evaluation (whether linear probe, few-shot, or fine-tuning) still requires some labelled examples to measure transfer quality.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: A common failure is REPRESENTATION COLLAPSE — the model learns to map all inputs to the same or similar representations, producing high 'similarity' between augmented views trivially (by making everything similar) without learning anything useful; different SSL methods handle this differently (contrastive methods use NEGATIVE pairs to prevent collapse, BYOL/SimSiam use asymmetric architectures or stop-gradient, masked methods use a reconstruction objective that resists collapse naturally); another failure is AUGMENTATION SENSITIVITY — if the augmentation strategy used during pretraining doesn't match the variation that matters for the downstream task, the model may learn features that are irrelevant to downstream performance.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: OpenAI's CLIP is a large-scale SSL approach (using image-text contrastive pairs from the internet) that produces image representations transferable to hundreds of classification tasks zero-shot — with no labels for those tasks at training time — simply because the contrastive objective forced the image encoder to align with text semantics; this illustrates SSL's core value: a single unlabelled-data pretraining run producing representations broadly useful across many downstream tasks that would each be expensive to annotate and train on individually.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: SimCLR (Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations, Chen et al. 2020) is a contrastive SSL method for vision that takes each image in a minibatch, applies TWO different random augmentations to produce a POSITIVE PAIR (two views of the same image), then trains an encoder+projection head to maximise similarity between the two views of the same image while minimising similarity between views of DIFFERENT images (the NEGATIVE pairs) using the NT-Xent (Normalized Temperature-scaled Cross Entropy) loss.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: SimCLR established that a surprisingly SIMPLE contrastive SSL pipeline — no special memory banks, no momentum encoders, no complex architectures — could match or exceed more complex predecessors (MoCo, CMC) when trained with LARGE BATCH SIZES (providing many negatives per sample), strong DATA AUGMENTATIONS, and a NON-LINEAR PROJECTION HEAD between the encoder and the loss; it clarified WHICH design choices mattered most for contrastive SSL (augmentation strength and batch size matter most; linear projection heads are suboptimal).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: For each image x in a minibatch of N images: apply two stochastic augmentations (t ~ T, t' ~ T) to get x_i = t(x) and x_j = t'(x) — the POSITIVE PAIR; encode both: h_i = f(x_i), h_j = f(x_j) (ResNet encoder); project to smaller space: z_i = g(h_i), z_j = g(h_j) (2-layer MLP projection head); compute NT-Xent loss over the 2N representations in the batch — for each view, it's a softmax where the positive (the other view of the same image) is the 'correct class' and the 2(N-1) other views are negatives; train to maximize this softmax probability; after training, DISCARD the projection head and use the encoder h for downstream tasks (h transfers better than z).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use SimCLR when you have access to LARGE GPU memory or can afford large batch sizes (256-8192) — SimCLR's performance scales strongly with batch size (more negatives per step); use it as a CLEAN, WELL-UNDERSTOOD baseline contrastive SSL method that's easy to implement and understand before trying more complex methods; use when you can afford the full-scale training with the recommended augmentation pipeline (random crop + color jitter + grayscale + Gaussian blur).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid SimCLR if GPU memory or batch-size constraints prevent running the large batches needed for good negative coverage — MoCo's memory bank design was specifically developed to provide many negatives WITHOUT requiring large batch sizes; avoid for domains where the standard augmentation pipeline (designed for natural images: crops, color jitter) is INAPPROPRIATE (medical imaging, spectral data, molecular graphs) — SimCLR's strong augmentation assumptions are more domain-specific than its architecture.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: SimCLR underperforms noticeably at SMALL batch sizes (< 256) because with few negatives per step, the loss can't distinguish positive pairs from the background distribution effectively — the method was designed around large-batch training and degrades more gracefully for MoCo-style methods at small batch; another practical issue is the PROJECTION HEAD: a common mistake is evaluating DOWNSTREAM performance using the projected representations z instead of the encoder representations h — z is optimized for the contrastive loss objective (not downstream tasks) and consistently underperforms h for linear evaluation; the projection head is for training only.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: The original SimCLR paper trained a ResNet-50 on ImageNet WITHOUT any labels and achieved 76.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with just a linear classifier on top of the frozen encoder — rivaling supervised ResNet-50 training (76.5%) at the time, demonstrating that the NT-Xent + large-batch contrastive pipeline can learn representations essentially as useful as supervised pretraining for standard transfer tasks, while requiring zero annotation.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: NT-Xent (Normalized Temperature-scaled Cross-Entropy) is the contrastive loss function used in SimCLR: given a minibatch of 2N views (N images × 2 augmentations each), for each view i the loss treats its paired view j as the POSITIVE and all other 2(N-1) views as NEGATIVES, computing a softmax-based cross-entropy loss that maximises the cosine similarity between the positive pair relative to all negatives — with a TEMPERATURE parameter τ controlling how peaked the distribution is.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: The NT-Xent loss operationalizes the contrastive SSL objective (pull same-image views together, push different-image views apart) in a differentiable, scalable way that works entirely within a standard minibatch — no separate memory bank, no special data structures; the TEMPERATURE parameter allows controlling the HARDNESS of the negatives (lower τ → loss focuses more on hard negatives close to the positive in embedding space; higher τ → softer, treats all negatives more equally) and the NORMALIZATION (L2 normalization before computing cosine similarity) prevents the embeddings from collapsing to arbitrarily large magnitudes.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: For views i and j (a positive pair): compute cosine similarity sim(z_i, z_j) = z_i · z_j / (||z_i|| ||z_j||); the NT-Xent loss for view i is: L_i = -log[ exp(sim(z_i, z_j) / τ) / Σ_{k≠i} exp(sim(z_i, z_k) / τ) ] where the denominator sums over all 2N-1 other views in the batch; the total loss averages over all 2N views; τ is a hyperparameter (SimCLR uses τ=0.07 as default); NORMALIZATION of embeddings before computing sim is critical — without it, the model can achieve low loss by making ||z|| large rather than learning meaningful directions.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use NT-Xent as the default contrastive loss when implementing SimCLR or any in-batch-negatives contrastive SSL method; the temperature τ is the primary hyperparameter to tune — start with τ ∈ [0.05, 0.1] for vision tasks; understand NT-Xent deeply if you're working with any contrastive learning framework (CLIP uses a very similar bidirectional version: both image→text and text→image softmax losses).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid NT-Xent with very small batch sizes where the number of in-batch negatives is too few for the loss to be meaningful (N < 64 makes for weak contrastive signal); also avoid when your data has many NEAR-DUPLICATE or SEMANTICALLY SIMILAR images in typical minibatches — these would appear as 'false negatives' (treated as repelled pairs even though they're semantically similar), a problem called FALSE NEGATIVE CONTAMINATION that degrades training and is harder to avoid in NT-Xent than in methods that use explicit negative mining or clustering.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: The most common practical issue is TEMPERATURE SENSITIVITY — NT-Xent is quite sensitive to τ; too-low τ makes the loss extremely focused on very hard negatives (can destabilize training if embeddings aren't well-initialized, causing early gradient explosions); too-high τ makes the loss too soft (model doesn't learn to distinguish similar negatives); the standard SimCLR τ=0.07 works for ImageNet-scale training but may need tuning for other domains or smaller datasets; another issue is FALSE NEGATIVES — in datasets with many images from the same class (e.g., faces, product photos), the negatives in a minibatch often INCLUDE other images of the same concept, and pushing them apart actively harms the representation quality for those semantically related images.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: CLIP's contrastive loss is essentially a bidirectional NT-Xent over image-text pairs: for a batch of N (image, caption) pairs, both image→text and text→image NT-Xent losses are computed and averaged; the images and texts of OTHER pairs in the batch are the negatives — at large batch sizes (N=32,768 in CLIP training), this provides rich contrastive signal from a diverse set of semantically distinct negatives, which is what makes the resulting shared embedding space useful for zero-shot classification (classify image by finding nearest text template in the shared space).

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: In contrastive SSL (SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, DINO), DATA AUGMENTATION is the mechanism that creates POSITIVE PAIRS: two 'views' of the same image that are different enough to be non-trivially similar yet similar enough to share the same semantic content — the model must learn to output similar representations for both despite their visual differences; the CHOICE OF AUGMENTATIONS defines what INVARIANCES the learned representation will have (a model trained with colour-jitter augmentation learns colour-invariant features; one trained with crops learns position-invariant features).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: Augmentation strategies are central to SSL because the REPRESENTATIONS LEARNED are determined by WHAT VARIES across views (which the model learns to be invariant to) and WHAT STAYS CONSTANT (which the model learns to preserve); SimCLR's ablation study showed that augmentation choice has a LARGER impact on representation quality than almost any other design choice (encoder architecture, loss function, projection head design) — making augmentation the most important hyperparameter for contrastive SSL practitioners to understand and tune.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: SimCLR's default augmentation pipeline (applied sequentially with randomness): RANDOM CROP (most important — crop to 20-100% of image area, then resize to fixed size; forces model to be position/scale invariant); RANDOM HORIZONTAL FLIP; COLOUR JITTER (randomly change brightness, contrast, saturation, hue — forces colour invariance, strength controlled by 's' parameter); RANDOM GRAYSCALE (with p=0.2 — further pushes colour invariance); GAUSSIAN BLUR (randomly apply blur — forces robustness to high-frequency details); the specific STRENGTHS of jitter and blur matter: SimCLR found strong colour jitter (s=1.0) was critical, and Gaussian blur helped for larger resolution inputs (224px); for domains other than natural images, these augmentations must be redesigned from first principles.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use the SimCLR/MoCo standard augmentation pipeline as-is for NATURAL IMAGE pretraining (photos, web images, ImageNet-like data); for TRANSFER to specialized domains, start by REMOVING augmentations that violate domain invariances (e.g., colour jitter should be very weak or absent for histopathology where stain colour carries diagnostic information; flipping may be inappropriate for text in images or medical scans with orientation convention); treat augmentation design as the FIRST thing to customize when adapting contrastive SSL to a new domain.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid applying SimCLR's augmentation pipeline blindly to non-natural-image domains — in medical imaging, satellite imagery, or audio spectrograms, the 'natural' augmentations may DESTROY the very features that distinguish classes (e.g., aggressive colour jitter in pathology images would corrupt tissue-type information encoded in staining colours); also avoid augmentations that create COLLAPSING INVARIANCES — if you apply an augmentation that makes ALL images look the same (e.g., converting all images to pure grayscale with p=1.0), the model trivially satisfies the contrastive objective without learning anything.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: A subtle but important failure is CROP OVERLAP BEING TOO SMALL — very aggressive crops (very small crop ratio, 5-10% of image area) can create views where the two crops DON'T share enough semantic content (the two views of 'a dog' might both show different background regions with no dog visible), making them false positives that confuse training; conversely, too-conservative crops (90-100% of image area) don't provide enough variation for the model to learn meaningful position invariance; the SimCLR crop range (20-100%) was tuned empirically and represents a practical sweet spot for natural images at ImageNet resolution.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: A research team adapting SimCLR to X-ray pretraining found that the standard color-jitter + grayscale augmentation from natural images was harmful (X-rays are already grayscale and their intensity values encode anatomical density — jittering intensity is semantically destructive), but that RANDOM CROP + RANDOM AFFINE + ELASTIC DEFORMATION were strong positives for X-ray SSL (reflecting the true invariances in radiology: the same anatomy from slightly different patient positions or breathing states should yield similar representations) — this required completely replacing the augmentation pipeline but the underlying NT-Xent/SimCLR training framework remained unchanged.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: MoCo (Momentum Contrast, He et al. 2020) is a contrastive SSL method designed to provide a LARGE, CONSISTENT set of negative representations without requiring a massive batch size — it solves SimCLR's batch-size dependency by maintaining a QUEUE (memory bank) of past encoded representations as negatives and using a MOMENTUM ENCODER (exponential moving average of the query encoder) to ensure the queue entries remain consistent with the current encoder state.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: SimCLR requires large batches (8192+) to have enough negatives for effective contrastive learning — this demands proportionally large GPU memory; MoCo decouples the NUMBER OF NEGATIVES from the BATCH SIZE by keeping a queue of K negatives (e.g., K=65,536) accumulated across many past minibatches, enabling effective contrastive training with standard batch sizes (256); the MOMENTUM encoder solves the consistency problem that arises when using a plain queue: old entries in the queue were encoded by an OLDER version of the network, making them inconsistent with current query representations — the momentum encoder (θ_k ← m·θ_k + (1-m)·θ_q with m=0.999) changes very slowly, keeping old queue entries approximately consistent.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: MoCo maintains: a QUERY ENCODER f_q (updated by backprop), a KEY ENCODER f_k (updated by EMA of f_q, NOT by backprop directly), and a QUEUE of K key representations; for each minibatch: encode query view with f_q to get q; encode key view with f_k to get k+; compute contrastive loss (InfoNCE): L = -log[ exp(q · k+ / τ) / (exp(q · k+ / τ) + Σ_{k- in queue} exp(q · k- / τ)) ]; update queue (enqueue new k+, dequeue oldest); update f_k by EMA: θ_k ← m·θ_k + (1-m)·θ_q; because f_k is NOT updated by gradients (only by EMA), the queue entries k- from previous iterations remain compatible with current query representations.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use MoCo when you have GPU memory constraints that make SimCLR's large-batch training impractical — MoCo achieves competitive performance with batch sizes of 256 by using the queue for negatives; use MoCo v2/v3 (improved versions) as a strong baseline for contrastive SSL that works well without massive compute infrastructure; MoCo's design pattern (momentum encoder + queue) has influenced many subsequent SSL methods beyond vision.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid using the original MoCo when more modern methods (MoCo v3, DINO, MAE) are available and your compute allows — MoCo v1's performance has been surpassed; avoid the queue approach for very RAPIDLY EVOLVING encoders (very high learning rates) where the momentum EMA may not maintain consistency well despite m=0.999; the queue/EMA mechanism adds implementation complexity compared to pure in-batch contrastive methods like SimCLR.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: The most common MoCo-specific pitfall is QUEUE STALENESS — if the learning rate is too high and the encoder changes rapidly, even with m=0.999 the older queue entries may become inconsistent with current encoder representations, manifesting as unstable training loss; another practical issue is QUEUE SIZE TUNING — too-small queues (K < 1024) don't provide enough negatives; too-large queues (K > 131072) can be fine but increase memory footprint without proportional benefit; in practice K=65536 is the standard starting point for ImageNet-scale training.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: MoCo's original ImageNet linear evaluation (top-1) achieved 60.6% (MoCo v1) and later 71.1% (MoCo v2 with projection head + cosine schedule from SimCLR), all with batch size 256 — demonstrating that the memory bank + momentum encoder design enables competitive contrastive SSL without the 8192-GPU-batch requirement of SimCLR, making it accessible on standard 8-GPU research setups; this practical accessibility drove MoCo's wide adoption in academic research settings with limited compute.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: MoCo v2 (Chen et al. 2020) and MoCo v3 (Chen & He 2021) are iterative improvements to the original MoCo contrastive SSL framework: MoCo v2 adopts design improvements shown effective in SimCLR (MLP projection head, stronger augmentations, cosine learning rate schedule) while retaining MoCo's momentum-encoder + queue architecture; MoCo v3 extends MoCo to Vision Transformers (ViT backbones) and replaces the queue with in-batch negatives (like SimCLR) at larger batch sizes, finding that a STOP-GRADIENT trick on the momentum branch is key to stable ViT training.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: MoCo v2 demonstrated that the performance gap between MoCo v1 (60.6% ImageNet linear probe) and SimCLR (69.3%) was largely explained by SimCLR's DESIGN CHOICES (projection head, stronger augmentation, cosine schedule) rather than SimCLR's in-batch-negatives approach — MoCo v2 borrowed those choices and reached 71.1% while keeping the smaller-batch-compatible momentum queue; MoCo v3 then addressed the INSTABILITY of ViT training under contrastive SSL objectives, finding that a patch-projection freeze + stop-gradient combination enables stable contrastive pretraining with ViT, enabling MoCo-style SSL to scale to modern architectures.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: MoCo v2 changes from v1: (1) adds a 2-layer MLP projection head (matching SimCLR's design), (2) adopts SimCLR's strong augmentation (color jitter, Gaussian blur), (3) uses cosine annealing learning rate schedule — these three changes account for most of the ~10% accuracy improvement over MoCo v1; MoCo v3 changes from v2: (1) moves to ViT backbone, (2) drops the queue (uses large in-batch negatives at batch 4096), (3) adds a PREDICTION HEAD (like BYOL — asymmetric architecture), (4) uses a STOP-GRADIENT on the momentum-encoder output (prevents instability from gradients flowing through both paths); the v3 paper found that a key instability source with ViTs was in the patch-projection layer, which was later patched by freezing it for the first few epochs.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use MoCo v2 if you want MoCo-style (small-batch-compatible) contrastive SSL with ResNet backbones but want stronger performance than v1; use MoCo v3 if you want to pretrain ViT backbones with contrastive SSL and need a well-studied recipe; in practice, for ViT pretraining, DINO/DINOv2 or MAE are often preferred over MoCo v3 for state-of-the-art transfer performance, but MoCo v3 is a valid baseline.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid selecting MoCo v1 for new projects — v2's improvements are trivial to adopt and substantially better; avoid MoCo v3 if you don't have the compute for large-batch ViT training (4096+ batch size) — at smaller ViT batch sizes, the in-batch-negative approach loses the momentum-queue advantage that made MoCo attractive for resource-constrained settings.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: The ViT training instability discovered in MoCo v3 (manifesting as sudden loss spikes during training, correlated with high gradient norm in the patch-projection layer) is a notable failure mode — the fix (freezing patch projection early) is a workaround that works but revealed that contrastive objectives interact with ViT architecture in non-obvious ways; this motivated later SSL methods (DINO, MAE) to use different objectives better-suited to ViT's inductive biases.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: MoCo v3 with ViT-B/16 backbone achieved 83.2% ImageNet linear probe accuracy — competitive with supervised ViT pretraining (81.8%), demonstrating that contrastive SSL can match supervised pretraining even for transformer architectures, not just CNNs; the critical insight enabling this (stop-gradient + frozen patch projection for stability) has since become standard knowledge for anyone implementing contrastive SSL with ViT backbones.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: BYOL (Bootstrap Your Own Latent, Grill et al. 2020) is a contrastive SSL method that achieves competitive representation learning WITHOUT any negative pairs — it only uses POSITIVE PAIRS (two augmented views of the same image), with an ASYMMETRIC architecture: an ONLINE network (with a predictor head) is trained to predict the output of a MOMENTUM TARGET network (EMA of the online network, NO predictor), preventing the trivial collapse solution that would occur if both networks had the same architecture.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: BYOL challenged the assumption that NEGATIVE PAIRS were necessary for contrastive SSL to prevent mode collapse — the prevailing wisdom was 'without negatives, the model collapses to constant representations'; BYOL showed that the ASYMMETRY between the online network (predictor + backprop) and the target network (EMA, no predictor, no gradient) is sufficient to prevent collapse, eliminating the large-batch / memory-bank requirements of SimCLR/MoCo and the associated false-negative problem.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: BYOL has two networks: ONLINE (θ): encoder f_θ → projector g_θ → predictor q_θ; TARGET (ξ): encoder f_ξ → projector g_ξ (NO predictor); training: for views v, v': online computes z = q_θ(g_θ(f_θ(v))); target computes z' = g_ξ(f_ξ(v')) (stop-gradient — target gets no gradients); loss: L = 2 - 2 · (z · z') / (||z|| · ||z'||) (MSE between L2-normalized representations, equivalent to cosine similarity maximization); total loss also adds the symmetric version (swap v and v'); target is updated ONLY by EMA: ξ ← τ·ξ + (1-τ)·θ (τ=0.996 initially, increased via cosine schedule); KEY: the predictor q_θ on the online side and its ABSENCE on the target side creates the asymmetry that prevents collapse.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use BYOL when negative-sample quality is a concern — in datasets with many semantically similar images (where in-batch negatives would be polluted with false negatives), BYOL's negative-free design avoids this problem; use when you want competitive SSL performance without tuning the number of negatives or batch size for negative diversity; BYOL's hyperparameters (EMA τ, augmentation strength) are more forgiving than SimCLR's batch-size requirements.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid BYOL if you don't have the infrastructure to carefully manage the EMA update schedule — τ should be annealed from 0.996 to 1.0 over training; with a constant or poorly-tuned τ, performance degrades significantly; avoid when debugging collapsed representations — if BYOL collapses (very rare with correct implementation), diagnosing the cause is harder than for contrastive methods because there's no obvious 'negative pushing' mechanism to check.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: BYOL's collapse prevention is subtle and was not fully understood theoretically for some time after its publication — empirically, collapse only occurs if BOTH networks are identical (same architecture, same weights, both trained by gradient); the predictor's absence in the target and the EMA (rather than gradient) update together prevent the optimization from finding collapse as a fixed point; a common implementation error is ACCIDENTALLY applying gradients to the target network (forgetting stop-gradient in the loss computation) or applying the predictor to BOTH branches — either causes collapse.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: BYOL's ablation study showed that removing the predictor from the online branch (making both branches symmetric) causes IMMEDIATE COLLAPSE to constant representations — confirming that the predictor asymmetry is not just a design choice but the critical mechanism preventing collapse; this empirical finding (combined with later theoretical analysis by researchers) established that ASYMMETRY, not negative pairs, is the true requirement for collapse prevention in SSL, inspiring subsequent methods like SimSiam and DINO that also eschew negatives.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: SimSiam (Exploring Simple Siamese Representation Learning, Chen & He 2021) is a minimal SSL method that learns representations with NO negative pairs, NO momentum encoder, and NO large batch sizes — using only a STOP-GRADIENT operation on one branch of a symmetric Siamese network with a predictor; SimSiam can be seen as finding the absolute minimum set of components needed for SSL to avoid collapse.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: BYOL showed negatives aren't needed but still requires a momentum encoder; SimSiam went further to show that EVEN THE MOMENTUM ENCODER is unnecessary — the stop-gradient alone prevents collapse when combined with a predictor; understanding SimSiam theoretically revealed that it can be interpreted as performing an EXPECTATION-MAXIMIZATION algorithm, where one branch is solving for optimal representations (E-step) and the other updates the network parameters (M-step), with the stop-gradient implementing the critical E-M separation.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: Architecture: one encoder f + one predictor h; both branches share the SAME WEIGHTS (true Siamese, unlike BYOL where weights diverge due to EMA); for views x1, x2: p1 = h(f(x1)), z2 = f(x2); loss: L = D(p1, stopgrad(z2)) / 2 + D(p2, stopgrad(z1)) / 2 where D is negative cosine similarity D(p,z) = -(p/||p||) · (z/||z||); the STOP-GRADIENT on z prevents the trivial solution (constant collapse): without it, the gradient flows through both z and p, and the optimizer can satisfy D(p,z)→-1 trivially by making all outputs the same constant; the predictor h learns to predict z from p, which requires the encoder to represent meaningful variation; NO MOMENTUM, NO QUEUE, NO LARGE BATCH needed.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use SimSiam when you want the SIMPLEST possible SSL baseline with minimal infrastructure (small batch, no special data structures, no EMA management); ideal for UNDERSTANDING SSL mechanics and ablating which components matter, since SimSiam strips SSL to its essential core; useful for SSL in low-compute settings where MoCo's queue or BYOL's EMA management is inconvenient.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid SimSiam in production SSL pretraining when state-of-the-art performance is required — SimSiam's performance, while impressive given its simplicity, is generally below MoCo v3, BYOL, DINO, and MAE at scale; avoid if your batch size is very small (< 64) — SimSiam's predictor convergence relies on receiving diverse pairs per update, and with tiny batches the predictor can oscillate; SimSiam is more of a research/understanding tool than a production SSL recipe.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: SimSiam can experience COLLAPSE in specific configurations — the original paper found that collapsing happens with batch normalization placed BEFORE the predictor (which affects the gradient flow in ways that remove the stop-gradient's protective effect) and with very low learning rates; the paper's recommended recipe (BN after the predictor, not before; SGD with lr=0.05 × batch/256; no weight decay on the predictor bias/BN) must be followed fairly carefully; departures from the recipe (especially BN placement) can cause silent collapse that's not immediately obvious from training loss curves alone.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: SimSiam's central contribution to SSL theory is that it provided a MINIMALIST 'control experiment' for understanding BYOL — by systematically removing MoCo's queue (no negatives), then BYOL's momentum encoder, and finding that only stop-gradient + predictor remain necessary, the SimSiam paper established that the STOP-GRADIENT is the essential invariance-breaking mechanism; this theoretical clarity influenced how researchers now understand the entire family of negative-free SSL methods and motivated the EM interpretation that unified these methods under a common theoretical framework.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: DINO (Self-DIstillation with NO labels, Caron et al. 2021) is a self-supervised method that trains a STUDENT network to match the output distribution of a TEACHER network (EMA of student) using a CROSS-ENTROPY loss between their softmax outputs over a set of 'prototype' dimensions — functioning as knowledge distillation from teacher to student where the teacher is itself bootstrapped from the student, all without any labels.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: DINO emerged from asking whether knowledge DISTILLATION (teacher→student softmax matching) could serve as a self-supervised signal, and discovering that it produces qualitatively better representations than prior methods in a notable way: DINO features exhibit EXPLICIT SEMANTIC SEGMENTATION properties — visualizing the self-attention maps of a DINO-trained ViT shows the model has spontaneously learned to segment objects in the scene without ever being trained to do so, a property not observed in supervised ViT training or other SSL methods at the time.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: Architecture: student network g_s and teacher network g_t (EMA of student, NO gradient); for each image, generate 2 GLOBAL crops (224×224) and 6-8 LOCAL crops (96×96); student sees ALL views; teacher sees ONLY the 2 global views (multi-crop strategy: student must match teacher on local crops by seeing global context); loss: H(P_t(x), P_s(x)) = -Σ P_t(x) log P_s(x) where P is softmax over K prototype dimensions (K=65536); CENTERING: subtract the running mean of teacher outputs to prevent collapse to a single prototype; SHARPENING: use low temperature τ_s=0.1 for student, higher τ_t=0.04 for teacher to produce sharp teacher targets; teacher updated by EMA: θ_t ← m·θ_t + (1-m)·θ_s (m from 0.996 → 1.0).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use DINO when working with ViT backbones where the semantic segmentation property of DINO attention maps is valuable downstream (e.g., weakly-supervised segmentation, visual grounding tasks that benefit from attention-based localization); use when the task requires FEATURES WITH SEMANTIC SPATIAL STRUCTURE rather than just global image embeddings; DINO features have shown strong performance on k-NN retrieval and dense prediction tasks without fine-tuning.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid DINO with CNN backbones if the attention-based properties are what you're after (CNNs don't have self-attention maps); avoid if the multi-crop strategy's computational cost is prohibitive (processing 8-10 crops per image at training time is 4-5× more compute than 2-crop methods); for pure classification transfer, MAE or DINOv2 often outperform DINO on standard benchmarks.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: The CENTERING mechanism is critical and easily overlooked in custom implementations — without centering, the teacher's softmax output can collapse to always predicting one dominant prototype (mode collapse), which the student then learns to match trivially; the TEMPERATURE for the teacher (τ_t) is also critical: too-high teacher temperature makes targets too uniform (weak training signal); too-low causes training instability (very sharp targets early in training when the teacher isn't yet meaningful); the recommended τ_t=0.04 works for ImageNet but may need adjustment for different datasets.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: A striking demonstration of DINO's emergent properties: a ViT-S/8 trained with DINO on ImageNet (no segmentation labels ever seen) produces self-attention maps where the 'CLS token' attention heads clearly highlight semantically meaningful object regions (the dog in a photo, the car in a street scene) — visualizing these as heatmaps produces near-perfect object segmentations competitive with supervised segmentation models trained WITH pixel labels; this emergent segmentation ability is interpreted as evidence that DINO's self-distillation objective encourages the ViT to use its attention mechanism to build truly semantic, spatially-aware representations rather than purely texture-based ones.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: DINOv2 (Oquab et al. 2023) is Meta AI's improved version of DINO that scales up SSL pretraining by combining the DINO objective with iBOT (masked-patch prediction, similar to MAE's objective) as a joint loss, training on a CURATED large-scale dataset (LVD-142M — 142 million images filtered from web data using a data curation pipeline), and producing ViT backbones that serve as strong GENERAL-PURPOSE VISION ENCODERS without any task-specific fine-tuning for many dense prediction tasks.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: DINO demonstrated good transfer properties but its performance was limited by TRAINING DATA SCALE and QUALITY — DINOv2 showed that combining DINO's self-distillation with an additional masked-prediction loss (iBOT) and training on a carefully curated, larger dataset dramatically improves the quality of resulting features for DENSE PREDICTION tasks (depth estimation, semantic segmentation) not just classification; DINOv2 features have become a widely-used starting point for vision foundation models because they generalize well without fine-tuning for dense prediction.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: DINOv2 combines two self-supervised objectives jointly: (1) DINO loss (as in the original — student/teacher cross-entropy on global/local crop CLS token outputs); (2) iBOT loss (student predicts masked patches from their unmasked context, while teacher provides the targets — a masked image modeling objective similar to BEiT/MAE but using the distillation framework); the two losses are weighted and summed; training uses larger ViT backbones (ViT-S/B/L/g, with ViT-g/14 being 1.1B parameters); DATA CURATION is a key contribution: raw web images are filtered using self-supervised retrieval to select a high-quality, diverse set of 142M images, removing near-duplicates, NSFW content, and low-quality images.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Use DINOv2 pretrained weights (available on HuggingFace) as a starting encoder for ANY vision task where you want strong out-of-the-box features without full fine-tuning — especially for dense prediction tasks (depth estimation, semantic segmentation, optical flow) where a linear head or lightweight decoder on top of frozen DINOv2 features achieves competitive performance; DINOv2 is a practical 'vision foundation model' for practitioners who want a general-purpose visual encoder.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid using DINOv2 if your task involves images very far from natural-image statistics (e.g., medical X-rays, satellite multispectral imagery) where domain-specific SSL pretraining on domain data produces better features — DINOv2 is trained on curated web photos and may not generalize well to radically different imaging modalities; also avoid if model size is a hard constraint (ViT-g/14 at 1.1B parameters is large for edge/mobile deployment).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: DINOv2's DATA CURATION approach (using SSL retrieval to select training data) is part of its quality advantage — reproducing DINOv2 training without the same curation quality on a different dataset will likely produce weaker features than the released model; practitioners who want to fine-tune DINOv2 pretrained weights sometimes find that the features are SO GOOD frozen that naive fine-tuning (updating all parameters) can OVERFIT on small labeled datasets and perform WORSE than a frozen DINOv2 + linear probe — using appropriate learning rates, layer-wise learning rate decay, and regularization is critical when fine-tuning large DINOv2 models.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: DINOv2's ViT-L/14 achieves 86.5% ImageNet top-1 with a LINEAR head on frozen features (no fine-tuning of the backbone) — surpassing the performance of many fully-supervised models and competitive with MAE fine-tuned on the full ImageNet; more impressively, a DINOv2-L backbone + simple linear head achieves competitive monocular depth estimation (RMSE within 5% of state-of-the-art specialized depth models that are fine-tuned end-to-end), demonstrating that DINOv2 features contain sufficient geometric/structural information for dense prediction without task-specific fine-tuning.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_it_is: In self-supervised representation learning, COLLAPSE refers to the failure mode where the encoder maps all inputs to the same (or very similar) representations regardless of input content — this trivially satisfies objectives like 'maximize similarity between augmented views' (all similarities are 1.0) but produces useless features; understanding why collapse happens and what mechanisms PREVENT it is foundational to understanding why different SSL methods are designed the way they are.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.why_it_exists: Every SSL method that aims to maximize similarity between positive pairs faces the collapse threat — the most direct gradient descent solution to 'maximize similarity' is constant output; the SSL literature can largely be read as a history of discovering DIFFERENT mechanisms that prevent collapse: contrastive negatives (SimCLR, MoCo), momentum encoder + stop-gradient asymmetry (BYOL, SimSiam), architectural constraints (BN, whitening), or reconstruction objectives (MAE, BEiT); understanding the collapse mechanism explains WHY each design choice in these methods is necessary and what happens when you remove it.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.how_it_works: Collapse can occur in TWO FORMS: (1) COMPLETE COLLAPSE — all outputs converge to a single constant vector; (2) DIMENSIONAL COLLAPSE — outputs use only a low-dimensional subspace (many embedding dimensions are constant or linearly dependent) while retaining some variation — dimensional collapse is subtler and common in practice even when complete collapse doesn't occur; MECHANISMS PREVENTING COLLAPSE: (A) NEGATIVE PAIRS (SimCLR, MoCo) — explicitly push different-image representations apart, making constant output increase the loss; (B) ASYMMETRY (BYOL, SimSiam) — the predictor must map online→target representations, which requires the encoder to preserve variation (a constant target makes the predictor's job trivial but doesn't help the online encoder's loss); (C) REDUNDANCY REDUCTION (Barlow Twins) — explicitly decorrelate embedding dimensions, directly preventing dimensional collapse; (D) RECONSTRUCTION (MAE, BEiT) — predicting pixel values requires encoding spatial detail that can't collapse; practical DETECTION: monitoring embedding variance, computing average cosine similarity within a batch (should be low), or checking that embedding singular values don't show a few dominant dimensions.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.use_when: Understand collapse mechanisms before DESIGNING or DEBUGGING any SSL method — if a new SSL experiment shows poor downstream performance despite low training loss, CHECKING FOR COLLAPSE is the first diagnostic step; this knowledge is also essential for INTERVIEWS on SSL (a common question is 'how does [BYOL/SimSiam/etc.] prevent collapse without negative pairs').
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.avoid_when: Avoid dismissing the collapse risk as theoretical — in practice, even production SSL implementations can silently partially collapse if architectural choices (e.g., BN placement in SimSiam) or hyperparameters (EMA τ, temperature) are wrong; the collapse doesn't always manifest as obviously wrong training loss curves, so proactive monitoring of embedding space statistics during training is valuable.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.what_goes_wrong: SILENT DIMENSIONAL COLLAPSE is the most practically important failure: the training loss looks fine (positive-pair similarity is high, negative repulsion is working), but downstream evaluation shows poor performance because the encoder uses only a low-rank subspace of its embedding space; this happens when regularization (weight decay, dropout) is absent or when the loss doesn't sufficiently cover all embedding dimensions; Barlow Twins and VICReg methods were specifically designed to address this by explicitly measuring and penalizing dimensional collapse through cross-correlation/covariance objectives.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Contras.real_example: A team reimplementing BYOL from scratch that accidentally applied gradients to BOTH the online and target branches (forgetting stop-gradient) would observe: training loss L→-1 rapidly (within 100 steps), but the encoder would output the same vector for all inputs — checking with torch.var(embeddings, dim=0).mean() ≈ 0 would confirm complete collapse; the fix (adding .detach() to the target branch output before computing loss) would restore normal training immediately, illustrating how a single-line implementation error leads to catastrophic but detectable collapse.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: MAE (Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners, He et al. 2022) is a self-supervised pretraining method for Vision Transformers (ViT) that randomly masks a HIGH FRACTION (75%) of image patches and trains the model to RECONSTRUCT the missing patches in pixel space — the high masking ratio makes the task non-trivial (can't just interpolate from neighbors) and forces the encoder to learn global semantic understanding.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: MAE brought masked-prediction SSL (the dominant NLP paradigm since BERT) to VISION in a way that actually works well — previous attempts (BEiT, etc.) required complex tokenizer pretraining; MAE showed that direct PIXEL RECONSTRUCTION with high masking is sufficient and scalable; crucially, MAE's ASYMMETRIC ARCHITECTURE (full encoder only on visible patches, lightweight decoder for reconstruction) makes training highly COMPUTE-EFFICIENT: processing only 25% of patches in the encoder dramatically speeds up training vs. feeding all patches to a full ViT.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: MAE: (1) randomly sample 25% of patches to keep (75% masked); (2) encode ONLY the visible patches with a full ViT encoder (this is key — masked tokens don't enter the encoder, saving ~3-4× compute); (3) add LEARNABLE MASK TOKENS for the masked positions; (4) decode ALL positions (visible + masked tokens) with a LIGHTWEIGHT separate decoder (fewer transformer blocks, smaller dimension) to predict masked patch pixel values; (5) compute MSE loss ONLY on the masked patches (not the visible ones — they're provided as input, predicting them would be trivial); (6) after pretraining, DISCARD the decoder and fine-tune only the encoder on downstream tasks.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Use MAE pretraining (or pretrained MAE weights from public releases) as the starting point for ViT fine-tuning on image classification, detection, or segmentation — MAE consistently outperforms supervised ImageNet pretraining as a ViT backbone initialization when fine-tuned on downstream tasks; MAE is the recommended SSL pretraining method when you have a ViT architecture and a large unlabelled dataset, particularly if you need strong FINE-TUNED performance rather than strong FROZEN FEATURES (where DINOv2 may be preferred).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid MAE when you need STRONG FROZEN FEATURES (linear probe or k-NN evaluation without fine-tuning) — MAE's features are not as good frozen as DINO/DINOv2 features, reflecting that MAE learns representations optimized for reconstruction (which requires low-level detail) rather than the semantic-level invariances useful for frozen transfer; avoid with CNN architectures (MAE requires ViT's patch tokenization); avoid on datasets too small for meaningful 75% masking to provide diverse reconstructions (tiny datasets may not benefit from pretraining vs. direct supervised training).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: A common misunderstanding is that MAE features should be as good FROZEN as they are FINE-TUNED — MAE features require fine-tuning to compete with DINO/DINOv2; applying a linear probe to frozen MAE features on ImageNet gives only ~68% (vs. 86%+ for DINOv2 frozen), which is NOT the recommended evaluation — MAE shines in the fine-tuning setting (87.8% with ViT-H fine-tuned); another issue is mask-ratio tuning: 75% is the sweet spot for ImageNet (lower ratios make the task too easy, higher ratios make it underconstrained); for other domains, the optimal mask ratio may differ.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: MAE with ViT-H/14 (600M parameters) fine-tuned on ImageNet achieves 87.8% top-1 accuracy — at the time surpassing all prior SSL methods and competitive with the best supervised pretraining; the key enabler was the asymmetric encoder/decoder design: encoding only 25% of patches makes ViT-H training on a standard 8-GPU server feasible in a few days, whereas encoding all 196 patches would be ~3-4× slower and memory-constrained; this computational efficiency made MAE the SSL method of choice for scaling ViT pretraining.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: The MAE DECODER is a small, narrow transformer used only during pretraining to reconstruct masked image patches from the encoder's output — it is DISCARDED after pretraining, and the encoder alone is used for downstream tasks; the decoder is intentionally LIGHTWEIGHT (shallow: 8 blocks vs. ViT-L's 24; narrow: 512 dimensions vs. ViT-L's 1024) because it only needs to solve the pretraining task, not be useful for downstream transfer.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: The decoder's separation from the encoder is what makes MAE's design elegant — since the decoder is only used during pretraining and discarded, it can be made VERY LIGHTWEIGHT without harming downstream performance; this design choice enables MAE to use large, powerful encoders (ViT-L, ViT-H) that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive to train with a masked objective applied to ALL tokens — by routing only the visible 25% of tokens through the expensive encoder and letting the cheap decoder reconstruct from them, training cost is dramatically reduced while the encoder learns rich representations.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: The decoder receives: (1) encoded visible patch representations (from encoder) + their positional embeddings, and (2) LEARNABLE MASK TOKENS (same learned vector for all masked positions) + their positional embeddings; it applies transformer blocks to ALL positions (visible + masked) so masked tokens can attend to visible encoded patches; the final linear projection maps from decoder dimension to PIXEL VALUES per patch (e.g., 16×16×3 = 768 pixel values per patch); loss: MSE between predicted and actual pixel values for masked patches only; after pretraining, the decoder is removed and the encoder is exposed to FULL input (all patches, no masking) for fine-tuning.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Understand the decoder's lightweight, pretraining-only role when implementing MAE or evaluating whether to invest in a heavier decoder — the paper's ablation showed that larger decoders (matching encoder size) don't improve FINE-TUNED encoder performance; only the encoder's quality matters for downstream transfer, and the decoder just needs to be 'good enough' to force the encoder to extract rich representations.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid keeping or reusing the MAE decoder after pretraining for generative tasks — it was trained only for the specific masked reconstruction pretraining task and won't generalize well as a standalone image decoder; if you need a generative model, train a dedicated generative architecture (like a diffusion model) rather than reusing the MAE decoder.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation error is USING THE ENCODER FOR ALL PATCHES during pretraining (including masked tokens with masking applied as a zero-out or special token) rather than TRULY EXCLUDING masked patches from the encoder forward pass — the original paper's key compute efficiency comes from encoding ONLY the 25% visible patches; accidentally including masked patches in the encoder forward pass (even with a zeroed-out embedding) increases compute ~4× and doesn't improve representation quality.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: MAE's ablation on decoder depth shows: a 1-block decoder achieves 83.1% fine-tuned ImageNet accuracy (with ViT-L encoder), while an 8-block decoder (as used in the full model) achieves 85.9% — but a decoder matching the encoder's depth (24 blocks, same size) achieves 85.1%, WORSE than the 8-block decoder despite far more compute; this confirms that an oversized decoder actually interferes with learning (the encoder can 'delegate' too much to the large decoder rather than learning to compress information itself), making the deliberately lightweight 8-block decoder the right design choice.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: BEiT (BERT Pre-Training of Image Transformers, Bao et al. 2021) adapts BERT's masked token prediction to vision by: (1) tokenizing images into DISCRETE VISUAL TOKENS using a pre-trained discrete VAE (dVAE), (2) masking 40% of image patches, and (3) training a ViT to predict the DISCRETE TOKEN IDs of masked patches (classification over a fixed vocabulary of visual tokens) — rather than predicting pixel values as MAE does.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: BEiT was motivated by the observation that predicting raw PIXELS for masked patches may not be the best pretraining objective — pixel prediction forces the model to reconstruct low-level textures and colors, whereas predicting SEMANTIC VISUAL TOKENS (discrete codes from a learned visual vocabulary) encourages the model to recover SEMANTIC CONTENT of masked regions; BEiT was an early successful proof-of-concept for masked visual prediction, predating MAE's simpler approach that showed pixel reconstruction also works well with the right masking ratio.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: Two-stage process: STAGE 1 (offline, pre-done) — train a discrete VAE (dVAE) on images to produce a visual token vocabulary (8192 codes); each 16×16 image patch maps to one of these token IDs; STAGE 2 (BEiT pretraining) — randomly block-mask 40% of patches; feed the masked image (visible patches as pixel embeddings, masked patches as a special [M] token) through a ViT; train to predict the dVAE token ID for each masked patch via cross-entropy; after pretraining, discard the dVAE, fine-tune the ViT on downstream tasks.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: BEiT is primarily of historical/conceptual interest now (predating MAE) — use it to understand the EVOLUTION of masked image modeling (from discrete token prediction → pixel reconstruction); for new projects, MAE (simpler, no dVAE stage needed) or DINOv2 (better frozen features) are preferred; BEiT v2 and BEiT-3 (later versions) remain competitive for multi-modal pretraining.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid BEiT as a primary SSL method for new vision projects given better alternatives (MAE, DINOv2); avoid if the two-stage training (pre-train dVAE, then pretrain BEiT) is a workflow burden without corresponding benefit for your use case; the dVAE pretraining requirement adds complexity that MAE's direct pixel reconstruction eliminates.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: BEiT's performance depends heavily on the QUALITY OF THE VISUAL TOKENIZER (dVAE) — if the dVAE was trained on different data distribution than the target domain, its token vocabulary may be a poor fit, making the pretraining objective less meaningful; this tokenizer-dependency is the key complexity that MAE's simpler design avoids; additionally, BEiT's 40% masking ratio is much lower than MAE's 75%, making the task easier but potentially less challenging for learning rich representations.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: BEiT with ViT-B fine-tuned on ImageNet achieves 83.2% top-1 — competitive with supervised ViT-B (81.8%) — demonstrating that masked token prediction is a valid ViT pretraining objective; but the need to first train a dVAE tokenizer (a multi-day training job itself before BEiT training even begins) motivated the search for simpler alternatives, leading directly to MAE's insight that raw pixel reconstruction at 75% masking achieves similar or better results without any tokenizer pretraining.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: SimMIM (A Simple Framework for Masked Image Modeling, Xie et al. 2021) is a concurrent and complementary work to MAE that also predicts raw pixel values for masked patches but demonstrates these ideas work not just for ViT but for HIERARCHICAL VISION TRANSFORMERS (like Swin Transformer) — showing that masked image modeling is a general pretraining paradigm not tied to isotropic ViT architectures.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: While MAE specifically requires the isotropic ViT (all patches at the same resolution throughout), many practical vision architectures use HIERARCHICAL designs (Swin Transformer, etc.) that progressively downsample feature maps — SimMIM showed that masked prediction pretraining works for these hierarchical architectures too, making masked SSL applicable to the broader family of transformer-based vision models, not just isotropic ViTs.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: SimMIM replaces masked patches with a LEARNABLE MASKED TOKEN (single shared token for all masked positions, different from MAE's approach of excluding them entirely from the encoder); the encoder (Swin or ViT) processes ALL patches (including the masked ones with masked tokens); a LIGHTWEIGHT PREDICTION HEAD (single linear layer in the simplest version, as opposed to MAE's separate decoder transformer) maps the encoded masked positions to pixel values; MSE loss on masked patches; the key finding: even without MAE's elegant separation (encoder on visible, decoder on all), simple pixel prediction with a minimal prediction head pretrains competitive representations.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Use SimMIM when pretraining HIERARCHICAL ViT variants (Swin Transformer, etc.) with masked image modeling — it's the established recipe for these architectures since MAE's design is harder to adapt to hierarchical models; SimMIM is also useful as a reference for understanding that MAE's specific architectural choices (asymmetric encoder/decoder, excluding masked patches from encoder) are important for EFFICIENCY but not necessary for the concept to work.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid SimMIM for isotropic ViT pretraining when MAE is available — MAE's design is more compute-efficient for ViT; also avoid if the task requires dense prediction on hierarchical features (use DINOv2 or task-specific supervised pretraining instead, as masked prediction on hierarchical ViTs may not produce features as semantically rich for dense tasks).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: SimMIM's inclusion of masked tokens in the encoder (unlike MAE, which excludes them) means the encoder processes ALL tokens including uninformative masked tokens — this means the encoder may learn to 'ignore' or reconstruct masked positions based on context, but at the cost of ~4× more encoder computation than MAE; for very large models, this compute cost difference is material.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: SimMIM with Swin-B fine-tuned on ImageNet achieves 84.0% top-1 — surpassing supervised Swin-B (83.5%) — confirming that masked image modeling pretraining provides complementary benefit even over strong supervised baselines for hierarchical ViT architectures; this was an important result showing that the SSL pretraining benefit is architecture-agnostic, not specific to isotropic ViT designs.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: VideoMAE (Tong et al. 2022) extends MAE's masked autoencoder approach to VIDEO by applying masking to SPATIOTEMPORAL PATCHES (3D tubes spanning multiple frames) and using an EXTREMELY HIGH masking ratio (90-95%) — much higher than image MAE's 75% — because video has HIGH TEMPORAL REDUNDANCY (adjacent frames are very similar), making it easy to reconstruct temporal patches from neighboring frames without high-level understanding unless the masking ratio is very high.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: Video pretraining is expensive (videos are much larger than images) and existing video SSL methods required large datasets and complex designs; VideoMAE showed that the same masked autoencoder principle from image MAE extends naturally to video, with the key insight that VIDEO'S TEMPORAL REDUNDANCY means you must use HIGHER masking ratios to prevent trivial reconstruction (just copying from adjacent unmasked frames) — at 90-95% masking, the model must truly understand the scene to reconstruct any given patch.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: Video is divided into SPATIOTEMPORAL TUBES (e.g., 2×16×16 patches spanning 2 consecutive frames); 90-95% of these tubes are masked; the ENCODER processes only the ~5-10% visible tubes with a temporal ViT (ViT extended with temporal self-attention); the DECODER (lightweight, as in image MAE) reconstructs pixel values for all masked spatiotemporal locations; the high masking ratio forces the model to leverage motion patterns, semantic content, and temporal context rather than local pixel continuity; after pretraining, decoder is discarded and encoder is fine-tuned for action recognition, temporal localization, etc.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Use VideoMAE pretraining (or released VideoMAE v2 weights) for video understanding tasks (action recognition, video classification, temporal action detection) where you want SSL-pretrained ViT backbones rather than training from supervised pretraining on Kinetics or similar; VideoMAE enables training on CUSTOM, DOMAIN-SPECIFIC video data (medical video, sports footage, surveillance) without needing large action-labeled datasets.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid VideoMAE if your video task is primarily about STATIC CONTENT or single-frame analysis (use image MAE instead); avoid if compute is highly constrained — video models are substantially larger/slower than image models even with high masking ratios; avoid if you have a specific labeled video dataset large enough for supervised training to dominate (at scale, supervised Kinetics pretraining + fine-tuning can still outperform VideoMAE for action recognition).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: Applying image MAE's 75% masking to video (instead of 90-95%) results in poor pretraining because temporal redundancy makes reconstruction trivial at lower masking ratios — the model can simply copy from adjacent unmasked frames without understanding the scene; this is the most important VideoMAE insight, and using too-low masking ratios is the most common mistake when adapting MAE to video.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: VideoMAE v2 (Wang et al. 2023) with ViT-g (1.9B parameters) pretrained on a combined video dataset achieves 90.0% top-1 on Kinetics-400 action recognition — surpassing previous supervised-pretraining baselines and demonstrating that masked video autoencoding at scale produces general video representations competitive with task-specific supervised pretraining, particularly valuable for domains where labelled video data is scarce.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: Data2Vec (Baevski et al. 2022, Meta AI) is a UNIFIED self-supervised learning framework that uses the SAME ALGORITHM across DIFFERENT MODALITIES (vision, text, audio) — unlike prior SSL methods that are modality-specific (MAE for images, wav2vec 2.0 for speech, BERT for text), Data2Vec trains by predicting CONTEXTUALIZED LATENT REPRESENTATIONS (from a teacher/EMA network) for masked inputs rather than predicting raw pixels, tokens, or waveform features.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: Each modality's SSL had developed its own objectives (contrastive for audio, masked token prediction for text, pixel reconstruction for vision) with different theoretical justifications and hyperparameters; Data2Vec unified these under one principle: predict the TEACHER'S TOP-LAYER REPRESENTATIONS of the full unmasked input using the STUDENT network that sees only the masked input — this forces the student to predict CONTEXTUAL, HIGH-LEVEL features (not raw pixels or tokens) and applies identically to any modality that can be tokenized into patches/frames/subwords.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: TEACHER network: full encoder (EMA of student) processes the FULL, UNMASKED input and produces contextualized top-K layer representations as targets; STUDENT network: same encoder architecture processes the MASKED input (masked tokens replaced with learned mask embedding) and must predict the teacher's representations for the masked positions; LOSS: regression (smooth L1) between student's predictions for masked positions and teacher's representations for those positions; modality-specific: masking and tokenization are adapted per modality (patch masking for images, spectral feature masking for audio, byte-pair token masking for text) but the core prediction objective is identical.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Use Data2Vec when building MULTI-MODAL systems where you want a CONSISTENT SSL framework across modalities rather than maintaining separate per-modality SSL pipelines; Data2Vec 2.0 (improved version) is particularly useful for efficient multi-modal pretraining; also relevant for understanding how SSL objectives can be abstracted across domains.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid Data2Vec as the default choice for any single modality where modality-specific state-of-the-art methods exist and your use case is purely unimodal — specialized methods (MAE for vision, wav2vec 2.0/HuBERT for audio) often outperform Data2Vec on their respective modalities; Data2Vec's value is in CROSS-MODAL CONSISTENCY, not single-modality performance.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: Data2Vec's TARGET REPRESENTATIONS (teacher's contextual features) can be inconsistent early in training when the teacher's EMA has just started and hasn't developed meaningful representations yet — the model may initially predict meaningless targets; this cold-start problem is managed by using a LINEAR COMBINATION of the top-K layers (not just the top layer) as targets, which provides more stable targets early in training when individual layers may fluctuate, but requires careful K tuning.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: Data2Vec applied to SPEECH achieves competitive results with wav2vec 2.0/HuBERT (the prior state-of-the-art speech SSL methods) on LibriSpeech ASR with 10-minute fine-tuning — using the SAME framework code with only modality-specific preprocessing changed; this cross-modal applicability demonstrates Data2Vec's main contribution: an abstraction that lets a single research team maintain and improve ONE SSL algorithm that benefits all three modalities simultaneously rather than developing and maintaining three separate specialized approaches.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: SimCSE (Simple Contrastive Learning of Sentence Embeddings, Gao et al. 2021) and ConSERT (A Contrastive Framework for Self-supervised Sentence Representation Transfer, Yan et al. 2021) adapt contrastive SSL from vision to NLP to improve SENTENCE EMBEDDINGS — they use contrastive learning to create embeddings where SIMILAR sentences are close and DISSIMILAR sentences are far apart, addressing the well-known problem that standard BERT embeddings produce ANISOTROPIC, poorly-clustered sentence representations.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: Standard BERT sentence embeddings (averaging token embeddings or using the [CLS] token) suffer from ANISOTROPY — the embeddings occupy a narrow cone in embedding space, making cosine similarity uninformative (most sentence pairs have high cosine similarity just because all embeddings point in roughly the same direction); contrastive methods fix this by explicitly learning that semantically different sentences should have LOW cosine similarity, resulting in more isotropic, semantically meaningful sentence embeddings useful for retrieval and STS (semantic textual similarity).
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: SIMCSE UNSUPERVISED: the simplest possible contrastive approach — for each sentence, run it through BERT TWICE with different dropout masks to get two different embeddings of the SAME SENTENCE as the positive pair (different dropout → different representations despite identical input); other sentences in the minibatch are negatives; loss: in-batch NT-Xent/InfoNCE; the double-dropout creates minimal but sufficient variation for contrastive learning; SIMCSE SUPERVISED: uses NLI entailment pairs (premise-entailment as positive, premise-contradiction as HARD NEGATIVE); CONSERT: uses different text augmentation strategies (token deletion, reordering, synonym substitution, feature cutoff) instead of double-dropout to create augmented views of sentences.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Use SimCSE (unsupervised variant) when you need better sentence embeddings from BERT/RoBERTa without any labelled data — just fine-tune with in-batch dropout-based contrastive training; use SimCSE supervised when NLI data is available (the supervised variant substantially outperforms unsupervised); use for SEMANTIC SIMILARITY, RETRIEVAL, CLUSTERING of sentences, or as better SENTENCE FEATURES for downstream tasks than raw BERT embeddings.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid SimCSE/ConSERT when state-of-the-art sentence embeddings are needed for large-scale production — modern specialized models (E5, GTE, BGE, or API-based text embeddings like OpenAI's text-embedding-3) significantly outperform SimCSE/ConSERT on BEIR and MTEB benchmarks; SimCSE is primarily valuable as a technique to UNDERSTAND and as a quick in-house improvement over raw BERT when you can't use external embedding APIs.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: The key failure mode for the unsupervised SimCSE approach is DATASET MISMATCH — dropout-based positive pairs are very EASY positives (the same sentence with different random dropout noise), so the model learns to treat very slight variations as equivalent; if the downstream STS task requires distinguishing sentences that are similar but not identical in meaning, the unsupervised dropout-based contrastive objective may not teach the model to make those distinctions; adding HARD NEGATIVES (contradictory sentences) or using richer augmentation strategies (ConSERT) provides stronger training signal for more nuanced similarity judgments.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: SimCSE unsupervised (RoBERTa-large fine-tuned with dropout contrastive, no labels used) achieves Spearman's ρ ≈ 76.7 on STS-B (semantic textual similarity benchmark), compared to ρ ≈ 63.9 for raw RoBERTa-large embeddings — a 13-point improvement from a simple fine-tuning step with NO extra labels; the supervised variant (using NLI entailment/contradiction pairs) pushes to ρ ≈ 86.2, demonstrating that the contrastive objective with good hard negatives dramatically improves sentence embedding quality for semantic similarity tasks.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al. 2020, Facebook AI) and HuBERT (Hidden-Unit BERT, Hsu et al. 2021) are the two dominant self-supervised learning methods for SPEECH AUDIO that produce general-purpose speech representations without transcription labels — wav2vec 2.0 uses CONTRASTIVE learning over quantized speech units; HuBERT uses MASKED PREDICTION of offline-clustered discrete speech units (k-means labels), analogous to BERT for text.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: Supervised ASR (automatic speech recognition) requires large transcribed speech datasets that are expensive to produce and unavailable for most languages; wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT enable pretraining on UNLABELLED SPEECH (cheap to collect) and fine-tuning with only SMALL AMOUNTS of transcribed data (even as little as 10 minutes) — transforming ASR from a data-hungry supervised task to a few-shot adaptation problem; these methods underpin modern multilingual ASR (Whisper builds on these ideas), voice cloning, and speech-based emotion/health models.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: WAV2VEC 2.0: (1) CNN feature extractor produces latent speech representations from raw waveform; (2) QUANTIZATION MODULE maps some features to discrete tokens via product quantization; (3) MASKING: randomly mask spans of the continuous latent representations; (4) TRANSFORMER encoder processes masked features; (5) CONTRASTIVE LOSS: for each masked position, the model must identify the correct quantized token from K distractors; HUBERT: (1) offline clustering (k-means) on MFCC features (or previous HuBERT iteration's features) produces pseudo-labels (discrete speech units); (2) masking continuous speech features; (3) BERT-like prediction of pseudo-labels at masked positions; (4) iterate — use HuBERT's own features for better clustering in next iteration; BOTH: after pretraining, add a CTC or seq2seq head and fine-tune with transcriptions.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Use wav2vec 2.0 or HuBERT pretrained weights (available from Hugging Face's transformers library) when fine-tuning for ASR, speaker identification, speech emotion recognition, or other audio tasks — particularly in LOW-RESOURCE LANGUAGE settings where only limited transcribed data is available; HuBERT generally outperforms wav2vec 2.0 on ASR quality; wav2vec 2.0 is simpler to understand and train from scratch if needed.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid training wav2vec 2.0 or HuBERT from scratch unless you have a domain-specific audio modality not covered by public pretrained models (e.g., non-human speech, industrial sounds, biomedical audio) — pretraining requires days on 32+ GPUs; for standard English/multilingual ASR, published Whisper or HuBERT models fine-tuned with HuggingFace's Transformers library are a faster path to good results.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: HuBERT's ITERATIVE TRAINING is critical to its quality — running only one round (using initial k-means on MFCCs as pseudo-labels) produces significantly worse features than running two or three rounds (where later-round features are derived from the previous HuBERT iteration's learned representations); teams that run only one iteration may see disappointing ASR fine-tuning results and incorrectly conclude HuBERT is not useful for their task; similarly for wav2vec 2.0, the contrastive loss temperature and codebook size are sensitive hyperparameters.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: HuBERT-Large (300M parameters) fine-tuned with only 10 MINUTES of transcribed English speech achieves 8.9% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean — competitive with supervised ASR systems trained on hundreds of hours; this demonstrated that SSL pretraining on unlabelled speech can reduce transcription requirements by 2-3 orders of magnitude, making high-quality ASR achievable for low-resource languages with only a few hours of transcribed speech for fine-tuning.

11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_it_is: SSL representation quality is evaluated using DOWNSTREAM TASK PROBES rather than direct training metrics — since the pretraining loss (reconstruction error, contrastive loss) doesn't directly measure downstream usefulness; the three standard evaluation protocols are: LINEAR PROBE (train a linear classifier on frozen features), FEW-SHOT (train on K examples per class with frozen or lightly-tuned features), and FINE-TUNING (update all parameters end-to-end on downstream task data) — each measures different aspects of representation quality.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.why_it_exists: An SSL method's pretraining loss can be low (good reconstruction) while producing poor transfer features, or high (hard reconstruction) while producing excellent transfer features — the pretraining loss alone is NOT a reliable quality signal; standardized evaluation protocols (linear probe on ImageNet-1K, few-shot on mini-ImageNet, full fine-tuning) allow APPLES-TO-APPLES COMPARISON of SSL methods across papers and let practitioners understand whether a method's representations are primarily useful with/without fine-tuning.
