11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.how_it_works: LINEAR PROBE: freeze the pretrained encoder; train a single fully-connected layer with logistic regression on top using ALL of the downstream dataset's labels; accuracy measures how 'linearly separable' the features are — features that already cluster by class in the pretrained space score high; GOOD FOR: measuring 'out-of-the-box' feature quality without any adaptation; BYOL/DINO score higher than MAE here; FEW-SHOT (K-NN or N-WAY K-SHOT): use K labelled examples per class; compute class centroids in embedding space; assign test examples to nearest centroid; no gradient updates at all; FINE-TUNING: update all encoder parameters with small learning rate (layer-wise lr decay typically) + new classification head; measures whether features are a good INITIALIZATION for task-specific training; MAE scores highest here; CHOICE: if you'll always fine-tune, optimize for fine-tuning accuracy; if you want frozen features for many tasks (DINOv2 as universal encoder), optimize for linear probe.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.use_when: Use ALL THREE evaluation protocols when publishing a new SSL method (the SSL community expects all three); in PRACTICE: choose the evaluation protocol that matches your deployment scenario — if you'll fine-tune on the downstream task, linear probe is less relevant; if you'll use frozen features for retrieval/similarity search, linear probe and k-NN are the right metrics; few-shot evaluation is most relevant when your downstream task has very limited labels.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.avoid_when: Avoid using ONLY the fine-tuning metric when reporting SSL results if the method's advantage is primarily from fine-tuning — some methods (like MAE) show large fine-tuning improvements but weak linear probe results, while others (DINOv2) show the reverse; using only the metric where your method shines gives an incomplete picture; avoid using linear probe accuracy as a PROXY for fine-tuning accuracy when making SSL method selection decisions for a new task.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.what_goes_wrong: A common evaluation pitfall is HYPERPARAMETER LEAKAGE — tuning the linear probe's learning rate on the test set (rather than a validation set) inflates results; another issue is COMPARING MODELS PRETRAINED ON DIFFERENT DATA — a model pretrained on 100M curated images has an inherent advantage on any downstream task compared to one pretrained on 1M images, regardless of SSL method quality; SSL comparison papers must control for data and compute budget to fairly compare methods.
11|🟡 T2 Self-supervised Learning|Masked.real_example: The divergence between linear probe and fine-tuning results for MAE vs. DINO illustrates why both metrics matter: frozen MAE-ViT-L features achieve ~68% ImageNet linear probe (poor), while fine-tuned MAE-ViT-L achieves 87.8% (excellent); frozen DINO-ViT-L features achieve ~81% linear probe (good), while fine-tuned performance is ~83% (smaller improvement); this shows that MAE features are compressed/specialized for reconstruction and need fine-tuning to shine, while DINO features are already semantically organized and work well frozen — a practitioner choosing between them must consider whether they'll fine-tune.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: N-way K-shot classification is the standard PROBLEM FORMULATION for few-shot learning: given N classes (the 'N-way'), each with only K labelled examples (the 'K-shot'), classify new query examples into one of the N classes — the model is evaluated on EPISODES where the N classes are RANDOMLY SAMPLED from a held-out test set, testing generalization to UNSEEN CLASSES not seen during training.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: The N-way K-shot formulation was designed to SIMULATE real-world scenarios where new classes emerge with very few examples and test generalization to NOVEL CLASSES rather than performance on the training set's classes; by evaluating on randomly-sampled N-way K-shot EPISODES from a held-out class set, the protocol measures whether a model can quickly adapt to new class distributions — not whether it can memorize a fixed label space.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: EPISODE STRUCTURE: randomly sample N classes from the test set; for each class, sample K examples as the SUPPORT SET (labelled context) and sample additional examples as the QUERY SET (unlabelled, to classify); the model receives the SUPPORT SET and must classify each QUERY EXAMPLE into one of the N classes; this is done many times (typically 600-2000 episodes) with different random class subsets; METRICS: mean accuracy over episodes ± 95% confidence interval; TYPICAL SETTINGS: 5-way 1-shot (5 classes, 1 labelled example each) and 5-way 5-shot are the standard benchmarks (mini-ImageNet, tiered-ImageNet, Omniglot); TRAINING STYLE: models are also trained EPISODICALLY — using the same N-way K-shot format on training classes to align training distribution with test distribution.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use the N-way K-shot formulation when your ML task involves RAPID ADAPTATION to new classes with very few examples — product catalog expansion (new products with only 2-3 photos), rare species identification, medical condition classification for rare diseases; also use episodic evaluation when comparing few-shot methods to ensure consistent, standardized measurement across different approaches.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid N-way K-shot evaluation when your real use case doesn't match the episode structure — if you'll actually have access to ALL classes at fine-tuning time (even with few examples), standard fine-tuning or linear probing may be more appropriate than few-shot learning; avoid treating 5-way 5-shot accuracy as a universal metric — real applications may have very different N (hundreds of classes) and K (0 or 1 example), which can rank methods differently than the standard 5-way 5-shot benchmark.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: A common few-shot evaluation mistake is DATASET LEAKAGE — using test classes during training (even without the exact test examples) inflates few-shot accuracy by allowing the model to overfit to the test class distribution; proper few-shot evaluation requires strict TRAIN/VALIDATION/TEST CLASS SPLITS where no class appears in more than one split; another issue is VARIANCE — 5-way 1-shot accuracy has HIGH variance between episodes, so always report mean ± 95% CI over 600+ episodes rather than a single point estimate.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: A standard few-shot benchmark: 5-way 1-shot on mini-ImageNet (100 classes, 600 images each; 64 train/16 val/20 test class split); a model achieving 60% accuracy is barely above random (20% = 1/5 classes random baseline for 5-way) with only 1 example per class, while a model achieving 75% is considered strong; the 1-shot vs. 5-shot gap (typically 10-15%) quantifies how much each additional labelled example per class improves classification, providing intuition for how data-hungry a method is.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: Prototypical Networks (Snell et al. 2017) are a simple and effective few-shot learning model that represents each class in the SUPPORT SET by computing the MEAN EMBEDDING of its K examples (the 'prototype'), then classifies query examples by NEAREST-PROTOTYPE distance in the embedding space — the idea is that each class has a representative CENTROID (prototype) and the embedding space should cluster classes around these centroids.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: Prototypical Networks were motivated by the intuition that a GOOD EMBEDDING SPACE should make classes linearly separable by their means — if the embedding space is well-structured, then the mean of K support examples is a good representative of the class, and classification by nearest mean is both simple and powerful; the method is easy to implement, computationally efficient, and remains a strong baseline for few-shot learning despite its simplicity.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: For N-way K-shot: (1) EMBED all support examples: S_n = {f_θ(x): x in class n's support}, n=1..N; (2) COMPUTE PROTOTYPES: c_n = mean(S_n) — the class prototype is the mean of K support embeddings; (3) CLASSIFY QUERY: for query x, compute distances to all prototypes: d(f_θ(x), c_n) for all n; assign to nearest prototype: arg min_n d(f_θ(x), c_n); LOSS during training: softmax cross-entropy over negative distances (treat it as a classification problem, optimizing the embedding to make prototypes well-separated); DISTANCE METRIC: Euclidean distance (authors showed Euclidean outperforms cosine for prototypical networks, unlike k-NN retrieval where cosine is usually preferred).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use Prototypical Networks as a FIRST BASELINE for any few-shot classification problem — the model is simple, interpretable, fast to train, and competitive with much more complex methods on standard benchmarks; especially appropriate when interpretability matters (the prototype is a human-interpretable mean embedding, and you can inspect which support examples contribute to a class's prototype); strong choice when K≥5 (prototypes are more reliable with more support examples).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid Prototypical Networks for EXTREME FEW-SHOT (K=1) cases where a single example determines the prototype — the mean of 1 example IS the single example, losing the averaging benefit; for 1-shot, methods that leverage the embedding space's geometry differently (Matching Networks, MAML) can outperform; also avoid for HETEROGENEOUS CLASSES where the class distribution is multi-modal (the mean prototype may fall in a low-density region between modes, making it a poor class representative).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: The EMBEDDING SPACE QUALITY completely determines Prototypical Networks' performance — if f_θ produces embeddings where classes aren't separated by their means (because the embedding was trained on different classes without episodic training, or the embedding space hasn't generalized to novel test classes), the nearest-prototype classification fails; a common mistake is using embeddings trained with CROSS-ENTROPY on training classes (standard classification) as prototypical network features without EPISODIC TRAINING — this produces class-discriminative features for TRAINING classes but may not generalize well to novel TEST classes.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: On mini-ImageNet 5-way 5-shot, Prototypical Networks achieve ~68% accuracy with a 4-layer ConvNet embedding — significantly above the 20% random baseline and competitive with methods like Matching Networks (72%) despite being simpler; the gap between Prototypical Networks and state-of-the-art few-shot methods (85%+ with pretrained ViT backbones) highlights that the BACKBONE QUALITY matters most — a stronger pretrained embedding lifts Prototypical Networks' performance substantially, as class prototypes become increasingly well-separated with richer feature spaces.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: This note focuses on the INFERENCE MECHANISM of Prototypical Networks and related metric-based few-shot methods: given a query embedding and a set of class prototypes, classify by NEAREST-PROTOTYPE using Euclidean distance — this is the core prediction step that turns a pretrained embedding + a small support set into a classifier without any gradient updates at test time.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: The nearest-prototype classifier is the critical bridge that makes few-shot learning work without fine-tuning at test time — it converts an embedding space into a classifier for NEW CLASSES (not seen during training) using only the K support examples, without needing to retrain or even do gradient descent on new class data; understanding this mechanism clearly (and its distance metric choice) is essential for implementing and debugging metric-based few-shot methods.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: At inference (test episode): compute class prototypes c_n = mean({f_θ(x) : x in support_n}) for each of N classes; for query x, compute Euclidean distances d_n = ||f_θ(x) - c_n||² to all prototypes; assign class: ŷ = argmin_n d_n; SOFTMAX PROBABILITY VERSION: P(y=n|x) = softmax(-d_n) = exp(-d_n) / Σ_k exp(-d_k) (useful for calibrated probabilities); METRIC CHOICE: Euclidean distance empirically outperforms cosine for prototypical networks (because Euclidean is sensitive to both angle AND magnitude, and mean prototypes in a trained space carry magnitude information that's meaningful); k-NN GENERALIZATION: with K=1 and no averaging (1-shot), nearest-prototype reduces to 1-NN with Euclidean distance — the embedding quality is everything.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use nearest-prototype classification whenever you need a GRADIENT-FREE test-time classifier for new classes — it's the standard prediction step for Prototypical Networks, a common baseline in few-shot learning competitions, and a practical approach in production systems that need to add new classes to a recognition system without re-training (e.g., enrolling a new product by averaging 5 photo embeddings to get its prototype, then using nearest-prototype for retrieval/recognition).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid nearest-prototype (with simple mean) when support examples for a class are HIGHLY HETEROGENEOUS (few examples from very different viewpoints, lighting, etc.) — the prototype (mean) may not represent any realistic example and may fall in a low-density region; in such cases, using ALL K support embeddings for nearest-neighbor search (1-NN over the full support set rather than nearest-prototype mean) can be more robust when K is small.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: Using COSINE DISTANCE instead of EUCLIDEAN for prototypical networks is a common mistake — the original paper explicitly showed Euclidean outperforms cosine for the prototypical setting; this is counterintuitive since cosine is standard for semantic similarity, but the averaging step (mean prototype) loses angular information that cosine relies on while Euclidean correctly captures the distance from the mean in the vector space the model was trained to populate; always use Euclidean unless you have a specific reason to use cosine.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: Face recognition systems (FaceNet, ArcFace) use nearest-prototype classification in practice: a new employee's face is enrolled by averaging 5 embedding vectors from 5 photos taken at different angles (creating their 'prototype'); during access control, the live camera embedding is compared by Euclidean distance to all enrolled prototypes, granting access to the nearest match if below a threshold — demonstrating that nearest-prototype is not just an academic few-shot technique but a production pattern used in large-scale biometric systems.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: Matching Networks (Vinyals et al. 2016, DeepMind) is a few-shot learning model that classifies query examples by COMPUTING A WEIGHTED SUM over support set labels using a SOFT ATTENTION MECHANISM over support embeddings — unlike Prototypical Networks' hard mean, Matching Networks assign each query example a label distribution that is the attention-weighted sum of support labels, where attention is based on embedding similarity.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: Matching Networks were motivated by drawing an analogy between few-shot classification and SEQUENCE-TO-SEQUENCE ATTENTION — the key idea is that the relevant support examples for classifying a given query may vary query-by-query (not all support examples are equally informative for all queries), so a SOFT ATTENTION over the support set (rather than a hard mean) should produce better query-specific classification; additionally, Matching Networks introduced the idea of FULL-CONTEXT EMBEDDINGS (using an LSTM to encode support examples in the context of the FULL SUPPORT SET, rather than independently).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: SIMPLE VERSION (attention kernel): embed support S = {(x_i, y_i)} and query x; compute attention weights a(x, x_i) ∝ exp(cosine(f(x), g(x_i))); label prediction: ŷ = Σ_i a(x, x_i) · y_i (soft label mix); FULL CONTEXT VERSION: encode support examples using a bidirectional LSTM (so each support embedding is aware of other support examples — 'full context embeddings'); encode query using attention LSTM over support embeddings; the full-context version is more powerful but more complex; TRAINING: train EPISODICALLY with N-way K-shot episodes sampled from training classes (same format as test-time).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use Matching Networks when you want QUERY-ADAPTIVE classification (different support examples matter differently for different queries) and you have diverse support sets where hard prototype means would lose important structure; Matching Networks are historically important and appear in many few-shot learning papers as a baseline; the soft-attention classification mechanism is directly applicable when you want PROBABILISTIC/SOFT outputs over classes rather than hard nearest-prototype assignment.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid the full-context LSTM variant if implementation complexity and inference time are concerns — the bidirectional LSTM over support and the attention LSTM for queries add significant complexity without always improving results over simpler Prototypical Networks; in most modern few-shot benchmarks, Prototypical Networks with better backbone encoders outperform Matching Networks with complex context encoding.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: The COSINE similarity in the attention kernel (unlike Prototypical Networks' Euclidean) makes Matching Networks sensitive to EMBEDDING MAGNITUDE — if embeddings from different classes have systematically different norms (which can happen without normalization), the attention weights become biased; using L2-normalized embeddings (cosine similarity = dot product of unit vectors) is essential for Matching Networks to work correctly.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: Matching Networks on Omniglot 20-way 1-shot achieves ~88% accuracy vs. ~98% for simple k-NN (different backbone/training regime), illustrating a benchmark where the soft-attention mechanism provides some benefit over very simple baselines but the embedding quality (backbone pre-training) matters more than whether you use hard or soft assignment — a consistent lesson across few-shot learning: better representations matter more than more complex meta-learning algorithms.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: Relation Networks (Sung et al. 2018, Yang et al.) are a few-shot learning model that, instead of using a FIXED distance metric (Euclidean or cosine) to compare query and support embeddings, LEARNS THE COMPARISON FUNCTION — a second neural network (the 'relation module') takes CONCATENATED or SUMMED feature maps of a support example and a query example and outputs a RELATION SCORE (0-1) representing how similar they are.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: Fixed distance metrics (Euclidean, cosine) assume the relevant notion of similarity is predefined and the same for all classes; Relation Networks argue that what constitutes 'similar' may vary by task or class type (spatial relations matter for object classes, texture matters for material classes, etc.) and that a LEARNED comparison function can adapt to what the task requires; by training the relation module end-to-end with the embedding network, both the feature extraction and the similarity metric are jointly optimized for the few-shot classification task.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: Two networks: EMBEDDING MODULE f_φ (CNN encodes each example independently); RELATION MODULE g_φ (a small CNN or MLP that takes the CONCATENATION [f(x_q), f(x_s)] or element-wise operations of query and support embeddings and outputs a scalar relation score r ∈ [0,1]); TRAINING: for N-way K-shot episodes, compute relation scores between each query and each class's K support examples (averaged); train with MSE loss where target is 1 for correct class matches and 0 for incorrect; INFERENCE: assign query to the class with highest average relation score.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use Relation Networks when you believe the SIMILARITY NOTION for your task is complex or task-specific and a learned comparator might capture it better than fixed Euclidean/cosine distance — e.g., few-shot texture recognition (where texture similarity is more complex than global feature Euclidean distance) or few-shot audio comparison; also use as a conceptual baseline when exploring whether learning the comparison function provides benefit over fixed metrics for a new domain.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid Relation Networks when the support set is tiny (K=1) — concatenating one support example's embedding with a query's for a single relation score is high-variance; avoid when compute efficiency is critical (relation scoring requires O(N×K) forward passes through the relation module per query, scaling worse than prototype methods); modern strong baselines (Prototypical Networks with powerful pretrained backbones) typically outperform Relation Networks, so the added complexity is rarely justified.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: Relation Networks' RELATION MODULE is an additional network that must be trained alongside the embedding network — if the relation module overfits the TRAINING CLASSES' similarity patterns (learning, e.g., that background color is predictive of class in training), it will fail when TEST CLASSES have different statistics; regularization on the relation module is important; another failure is UNSTABLE TRAINING when the MSE loss over relation scores is used with extreme cases (very easy positives and negatives early in training don't provide gradient signal; curriculum strategies or better loss functions can help).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: Relation Networks with 4-conv embedding + 2-conv relation module on Omniglot 5-way 1-shot achieves ~99.6% — competitive with other metric-based methods; on mini-ImageNet 5-way 1-shot achieves ~50-51%, similar to Prototypical Networks (~49-60% depending on backbone) but with 2× more parameters and computation; this performance parity at higher cost illustrates why learned comparison functions don't consistently outperform fixed metric methods — the embedding quality (backbone) is the binding constraint, not the comparison mechanism.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: Siamese Networks (Koch et al. 2015, originally for one-shot learning) are networks that learn a PAIRWISE SIMILARITY FUNCTION by processing TWO INPUTS through SHARED WEIGHTS (the 'Siamese' configuration — same network applied to both inputs) and training with a CONTRASTIVE LOSS to output high similarity for same-class pairs and low similarity for different-class pairs; at test time, classify a query by finding the most similar support example.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: Siamese Networks were one of the EARLIEST few-shot/one-shot learning approaches, predating the episodic few-shot formalization; they introduced the key insight that learning a GENERIC SIMILARITY FUNCTION (rather than class-specific classifiers) enables generalization to novel classes — if the network learns 'what makes two handwritten characters similar,' it can apply this knowledge to completely new character classes at test time, classifying by finding the most similar known example.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: Architecture: two IDENTICAL COPIES of an encoder f (sharing weights — a single set of parameters used for both inputs); for a pair (x1, x2): compute representations h1=f(x1), h2=f(x2); compute DISTANCE |h1-h2| (L1 distance in the original paper) or ||h1-h2||²; pass through sigmoid to get similarity score s ∈ [0,1]; LOSS: binary cross-entropy where same-class pairs target 1, different-class pairs target 0; AT TEST TIME (1-shot): compare query to each support example; predict the class of the most similar support example (1-NN over the learned similarity).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Siamese Networks are most useful for VERIFICATION tasks — determining whether two examples belong to the SAME class (yes/no) — which is their natural formulation; common applications: face verification (same person?), signature verification (genuine?), document duplicate detection; understand Siamese Networks historically as the foundation for all metric-based few-shot learning; for CLASSIFICATION tasks, Prototypical Networks or modern metric methods are more accurate.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid Siamese Networks for N-way few-shot classification when N>1 — classifying by finding the single most similar support example is 1-NN over a very small set, which is noisy for K=1 and doesn't benefit from averaging (unlike Prototypical Networks); Siamese training also requires PAIRS, which can be expensive to sample effectively (need balanced positive/negative pairs); modern metric-based few-shot methods that train episodically (Prototypical Networks, Matching Networks) are generally preferred for classification.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: NEGATIVE PAIR SAMPLING strategy significantly impacts Siamese training — if negatives are randomly sampled, most will be EASY NEGATIVES (very dissimilar pairs) that don't provide useful gradient signal; without HARD NEGATIVE MINING (selecting the most similar wrong-class pairs as negatives), Siamese Networks can converge to a trivial solution that correctly handles easy pairs but fails on hard ones (similar-looking examples from different classes); this issue is shared with all contrastive learning methods but is especially acute for Siamese training with small datasets.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: The original Siamese Network applied to the Omniglot dataset (one-shot character recognition with 20 classes per episode) achieved 92% accuracy — the first demonstration that a learned similarity function could generalize to classifying completely new character classes from a single example; this established the foundational idea that few-shot classification doesn't require new classifiers for new classes — just a good enough similarity metric.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning, Finn et al. 2017) is a meta-learning algorithm that learns a MODEL INITIALIZATION such that a small number of GRADIENT STEPS on a NEW TASK's few labelled examples produces a well-adapted model — rather than learning a similarity metric (like Prototypical Networks), MAML learns WHERE IN PARAMETER SPACE to initialize so that gradient descent adapts quickly to any new task.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: Metric-based few-shot methods (Prototypical Networks, Matching Networks) classify by embedding proximity but DON'T UPDATE MODEL PARAMETERS at test time — they rely entirely on the fixed pretrained embedding; MAML represents a different philosophy: the model SHOULD be updated at test time (via gradient descent on the small support set), and the meta-learning objective is to learn an INITIALIZATION that makes those test-time gradient steps MAXIMALLY EFFECTIVE; this 'learning to learn' approach is more expressive and works for ANY gradient-based model (not just metric-based architectures).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: MAML: two nested loops — OUTER LOOP (meta-training): maintains the meta-parameters θ; for each meta-training episode (task T_i): INNER LOOP: compute TASK-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS θ'_i = θ - α·∇_θ L_{T_i}(θ) (one or few gradient steps on task T_i's support set); META LOSS: evaluate task-specific parameters θ'_i on task T_i's QUERY SET; OUTER UPDATE: update θ ← θ - β·∇_θ Σ_{T_i} L_{T_i}(θ'_i) (this gradient flows THROUGH the inner loop, requiring second-order gradients — computing ∇_θ of a gradient, which needs Hessian-vector products); RESULT: θ is initialized at a point where one gradient step on any new task yields good task-specific performance.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use MAML when you need TEST-TIME ADAPTATION (the model should actually update its parameters given new task examples, not just classify by proximity to a fixed embedding); useful for tasks where a few gradient steps genuinely help and metric-based methods plateau; MAML is the foundational reference in meta-learning literature and must be understood conceptually for meta-learning interviews.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid MAML when compute is limited — the second-order gradient computation (Hessian-vector products via reverse-mode AD through the inner loop) is 2-3× more expensive than first-order methods; avoid for classification tasks where metric-based methods (Prototypical Networks + good backbone) already perform well — MAML's added complexity is often not justified for standard few-shot classification benchmarks.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: MAML's SECOND-ORDER GRADIENTS are computationally expensive and can be numerically unstable — this motivated FIRST-ORDER MAML (FOMAML), which ignores second-order terms (treats the inner-loop gradient as a constant), and later Reptile (a cleaner first-order alternative); implementations that inadvertently compute only first-order gradients while claiming to implement full MAML are common; also, MAML is sensitive to the INNER LEARNING RATE α — too large causes overfitting to the few support examples; too small means adaptation is negligible.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: MAML on mini-ImageNet 5-way 1-shot achieves ~48% accuracy with a 4-layer ConvNet — comparable to Prototypical Networks (~50%) but requiring much more computation due to second-order gradients; the value of MAML is not necessarily higher accuracy on standard benchmarks, but its MODEL-AGNOSTIC applicability to REGRESSION, REINFORCEMENT LEARNING, and other settings where metric-based methods don't directly apply — it's the go-to meta-learning algorithm for RL task adaptation (few trial rollouts → fast adaptation to new environment) where no natural embedding similarity exists.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: The MAML INNER LOOP is the fast adaptation step: given a new task's support set (K examples per class), compute gradient-based parameter updates starting from the shared meta-initialization θ to produce TASK-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS θ'_i that are adapted to this particular task — this is the 'learning from the few examples' step that happens at TEST TIME as well as during meta-training.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: The inner loop embodies MAML's core intuition: a few gradient steps on a new task's examples should suffice to adapt the model if the INITIALIZATION is chosen well; the inner loop is the mechanism through which the few-shot learning happens — unlike metric-based methods that don't update parameters at test time, the inner loop explicitly updates model parameters to fit the new task; understanding the inner loop's mechanics (number of steps, learning rate, which parameters to adapt) is essential for implementing and debugging MAML.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: For task T_i with support set D^{tr}_i: START from meta-parameters θ; COMPUTE LOSS on support set: L_i(θ) = loss of model f_θ on D^{tr}_i; GRADIENT STEP: θ'_i = θ - α · ∇_θ L_i(θ) (one step, inner learning rate α); OPTIONALLY REPEAT for multiple inner steps: θ'_i ← θ'_i - α · ∇_{θ'_i} L_i(θ'_i); RESULT: θ'_i is the task-adapted parameters; TYPICAL SETTINGS: 1-5 inner gradient steps, α=0.01-0.1, compute on support set only; IMPORTANT: the inner loop update is DIFFERENTIATED THROUGH for the outer loop — the meta-gradient ∇_θ L_i(θ'_i) requires computing ∇_θ of a gradient (second-order), implemented via second-order autograd or first-order approximation.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Understand the inner loop deeply when implementing MAML variants — the number of inner steps, learning rate, and which parameters are updated (all parameters vs. only task heads) are the primary tunable components; in practice for few-shot CLASSIFICATION specifically, 1-5 inner steps with small α work well; for RL meta-learning, more inner steps may be needed to meaningfully adapt policy parameters.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid many inner loop steps (> 5-10) — too many steps causes OVERFITTING on the support set (the few examples), counteracting the generalization goal; the inner loop should make the model 'aware' of the new task without memorizing the few support examples; with only K examples, even a few gradient steps can cause feature overfitting if the inner learning rate is too high.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: MEMORY EXPLOSION is a common MAML implementation problem: each inner loop step creates a computation graph (for backpropagating through the inner loop in the outer update), so with many inner steps and large models, storing the full unrolled computation graph for Hessian computation exhausts GPU memory; the standard solution is GRADIENT CHECKPOINTING or using FIRST-ORDER MAML (ignoring second-order terms, which works surprisingly well empirically) to avoid storing the full unrolled graph.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: In MAML for 5-way 1-shot image classification: the inner loop starts at θ (meta-initialization) and takes 1 gradient step using the 5 support examples (1 per class) computed with cross-entropy loss; the resulting θ' classifies those 5 classes much better than θ does, even from a single gradient step — demonstrating that with the right initialization, even ONE gradient step enables meaningful adaptation, which is the empirical validation of MAML's core hypothesis.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: The MAML OUTER LOOP is the META-TRAINING step that updates the SHARED INITIALIZATION θ across all tasks simultaneously — it evaluates how well the task-adapted parameters θ'_i (from the inner loop) perform on each task's QUERY SET, and uses gradients flowing THROUGH the inner loop to update θ in the direction that makes future inner-loop adaptations more effective.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: The outer loop is what makes MAML 'meta-learning' rather than just multitask learning — instead of updating θ based on task support-set performance (which would just be multitask learning), the outer loop updates θ based on QUERY SET performance AFTER inner-loop adaptation (performance AFTER adapting to the task) — this crucially trains θ to be a good STARTING POINT for adaptation, not a good model in its current state.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: META-OBJECTIVE: minimize Σ_{T_i ~ p(T)} L_{T_i}(θ'_i) where θ'_i = innerloop(θ, T_i) and evaluation is on QUERY SET (not support set); META-GRADIENT: ∂/∂θ L_{T_i}(f_{θ'_i}(x)) = ∂L/∂f · ∂f/∂θ'_i · ∂θ'_i/∂θ; the LAST TERM ∂θ'_i/∂θ = (I - α·∂²L/∂θ²) involves the HESSIAN of the inner loss — this is the 'second-order' gradient; IMPLEMENTATION: via autograd's double backward pass (e.g., torch.autograd.grad with create_graph=True for outer gradient computation); OUTER STEP: θ ← θ - β · Σ ∇_θ L_{T_i}(θ'_i); each outer step takes ~N tasks simultaneously (mini-batch of tasks), typically 4-32 tasks per outer step.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Understand the outer loop's TASK-QUERY-SET evaluation to avoid a common conceptual error: MAML is NOT doing multitask training on the same data; it's optimizing initialization quality by measuring how well adapting to SUPPORT works when evaluated on SEPARATE QUERY data; this outer loop structure is reusable for any gradient-based optimization problem where you want fast adaptation (supervised learning, RL, neural architecture search).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid using the OUTER LOOP evaluation metric (meta-query-set accuracy) to assess the quality of the adapted model on SUPPORT EXAMPLES — the outer loop trains for query-set generalization after adaptation, not for support-set memorization; if support-set accuracy is high but query-set accuracy after adaptation is poor, the inner loop is overfitting (too many inner steps or too-high inner LR).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: The outer loop can FAIL TO IMPROVE the initialization if the inner learning rate α is incompatible with the outer learning rate β — if α is too large relative to β, the inner loop adapts so aggressively that θ becomes irrelevant to the final performance (all tasks diverge from θ in the inner loop), making the gradient signal for θ noisy and training unstable; if α is too small, the inner loop barely adapts and the outer loop optimizes θ as if it were just multitask training; the α/β relationship is the most critical hyperparameter pair in MAML.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: After 10,000 outer loop steps of MAML training on mini-ImageNet (each step processes 4 tasks of 5-way 1-shot episodes), the meta-initialization θ typically shows near-random performance on held-out test tasks WITHOUT inner-loop adaptation but achieves ~48% accuracy WITH 1 inner step on the 5 support examples — the outer loop has trained θ to be a point where one gradient step dramatically improves performance, not a point that's already good without adaptation; this is the quantitative fingerprint of MAML's 'fast adaptation' property.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: Reptile (Nichol et al. 2018, OpenAI) is a FIRST-ORDER META-LEARNING algorithm that approximates MAML's behavior without computing second-order gradients — it simply trains on each task independently (several gradient steps on the task's support set) and then MOVES THE META-PARAMETERS TOWARD the task-adapted parameters: θ ← θ + ε(θ'_i - θ), where this update is repeated across many tasks and meta-iterations.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: MAML's second-order gradients (Hessian-vector products) are expensive to compute and implement; First-Order MAML (FOMAML) approximates them by ignoring Hessian terms but still requires two forward/backward passes through the inner loop; Reptile is even simpler — its update rule (move θ toward θ') is just SGD on the TASK PARAMETERS with gradient ∝ (θ'_i - θ), which can be shown to approximate MAML's second-order update under certain conditions while being nearly as simple as standard multitask training.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: For each meta-training step: sample task T_i; starting from θ, run K gradient steps (inner loop) on T_i's training data to get θ'_i; update meta-parameters: θ ← θ + ε(θ'_i - θ) where ε is the meta-learning rate; REPEAT across many tasks; INTUITION: the update θ ← θ + ε(θ'_i - θ) moves the meta-initialization toward the task-specific optima of each task; when averaged over many tasks, this moves θ to a CENTRAL REGION of parameter space that is close to ALL tasks' optima simultaneously — which is exactly what MAML tries to achieve; DIFFERENCE FROM FOMAML: Reptile doesn't split data into support/query within each task (uses all task data for inner-loop gradients), making it simpler to implement but slightly different objective.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use Reptile when you want a meta-learning algorithm that's (1) simpler to implement than MAML (no second-order gradients, no support/query split needed), (2) computationally cheaper, and (3) competitive performance on standard few-shot benchmarks; Reptile is a good choice for PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS of meta-learning outside research settings where MAML's full complexity isn't justified.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid Reptile for tasks where the fine distinction between MAML's second-order update and Reptile's first-order approximation matters — in theory, MAML's second-order update more precisely optimizes the meta-objective; in practice, the difference is often small (FOMAML ≈ MAML ≈ Reptile on standard benchmarks), but for very sensitive few-shot tasks or RL meta-learning, full MAML may outperform Reptile.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: Reptile's convergence can be slow compared to MAML/FOMAML because the update direction (θ'_i - θ) doesn't perfectly align with the meta-gradient for the QUERY SET objective (Reptile uses all task data, not a support/query split); this means Reptile may require more meta-training iterations for the same final performance; also, Reptile's performance depends on the INNER LOOP length — too few inner steps (< 5-10) means θ'_i barely moved from θ, giving negligible update signal; too many inner steps causes θ'_i to overfit the task, producing a biased update direction.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: Reptile matches MAML's performance on Omniglot (5-way 5-shot ~99.5%) and is within 1-2% on mini-ImageNet, while requiring no second-order differentiation — making it ~2-3× faster per meta-training step; this near-equivalent performance at much lower implementation complexity made Reptile widely adopted for RAPID PROTOTYPING of meta-learning systems and for domains where MAML's memory requirements for second-order gradients were prohibitive.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: GPT-3 style IN-CONTEXT LEARNING (ICL) is a form of few-shot learning where a LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL performs a new task by conditioning on a FEW EXAMPLES (demonstrations) included in the prompt — without any gradient updates to the model; the model 'learns' from the few examples purely through ATTENTION over the prompt context, making this the most compute-efficient form of few-shot learning (no training, no fine-tuning, no meta-learning, just prompting).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: ICL emerged as a surprising emergent capability of LARGE language models (GPT-3, 175B parameters) — smaller models don't benefit much from in-context examples, but sufficiently large models can pick up task patterns from just 1-10 examples in the prompt; ICL obviates the need for TASK-SPECIFIC TRAINING or META-LEARNING when the target task can be expressed as a natural-language text completion, democratizing few-shot adaptation to anyone with API access to a large LM.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: STRUCTURE: [demonstration_1 input] → [demonstration_1 output] [demonstration_2 input] → [demonstration_2 output] ... [query input] → [?]; the LLM completes the [?] based on the pattern established by the few demonstrations; SELECTION OF DEMONSTRATIONS matters: semantically similar demonstrations to the query (found by k-NN in embedding space) outperform random selection (this is called RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED ICL); ORDERING MATTERS: later demonstrations (closer to the query) have more influence (recency bias of LLMs); THEORY: ICL is understood as implicit Bayesian inference — the LM maintains a posterior over possible tasks given the demonstrations and evaluates the query under that posterior, rather than explicitly learning task parameters.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Use ICL (prompt-based few-shot learning) as the FIRST APPROACH when adapting a large LM to a new task with few examples — it requires no training, no fine-tuning infrastructure, and works immediately for any task expressible as text completion; compare to PARAMETER-EFFICIENT FINE-TUNING (LoRA, etc.) when you have slightly more data — for very few examples (< 20), ICL often matches fine-tuning; for medium-data regimes (50+ examples), fine-tuning typically outperforms ICL.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid ICL when the task requires SPECIALIZED DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE not in the LM's pretraining data (the LM can't learn genuinely new knowledge from a few prompt examples, only task format); avoid when LATENCY is critical — ICL with long prompts (many demonstrations) is slow at inference (the full demonstration text is tokenized and attended to for every query); avoid when the task requires RELIABLE, VERIFIABLE OUTPUTS where the LM's tendency to hallucinate is unacceptable.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: ICL is HIGHLY SENSITIVE to prompt format, example order, and label space verbalization (how you phrase the output classes) — the same task with differently-formatted demonstrations can produce dramatically different accuracy (variance of 10-15% on standard benchmarks); this sensitivity makes ICL unreliable without careful prompt engineering and sensitivity analysis; additionally, ICL doesn't generalize as well as fine-tuning for tasks requiring multi-step reasoning or precise numerical outputs, where chain-of-thought prompting (asking the model to show reasoning steps) is needed to achieve reliable performance.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: GPT-3 with 32 in-context examples achieves 76.2% on SuperGLUE without any gradient updates — matching fine-tuned BERT-large (77.9%) at the time, using no task-specific training; this was the first clear demonstration that sufficiently large LMs could perform few-shot adaptation through prompting alone; the result launched the 'prompt engineering' era and shifted the few-shot learning research focus from metric-based methods and MAML (for smaller models) toward ICL and instruction tuning (for large models), as LM scale made traditional few-shot methods less competitive.

11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_it_is: Mini-ImageNet and tiered-ImageNet are the two STANDARD BENCHMARK DATASETS for evaluating few-shot image classification methods — they provide standardized TRAIN/VALIDATION/TEST CLASS SPLITS that ensure evaluation is on NOVEL CLASSES not seen during training, enabling fair comparison across papers; mini-ImageNet (Vinyals et al. 2016) has 100 classes/600 images each; tiered-ImageNet (Ren et al. 2018) has 608 classes organized into hierarchical semantic categories with train/val/test splits designed to maximize semantic distance between splits.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.why_it_exists: Without standard benchmarks with fixed class splits, each few-shot paper would report results on different data subsets with incomparable splits, making cross-paper comparison impossible; mini-ImageNet provided the first standardized few-shot benchmark; tiered-ImageNet addressed a concern about mini-ImageNet: because mini-ImageNet selects 100 random ImageNet classes, train/val/test classes may be semantically similar (e.g., different dog breeds in both train and test), giving unfair advantage to models that learn class-specific features rather than generalizable representations — tiered-ImageNet uses ImageNet's semantic hierarchy to ensure train/val/test classes come from DIFFERENT HIGH-LEVEL CATEGORIES.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.how_it_works: MINI-IMAGENET: 100 classes (64 train / 16 val / 20 test); 600 images per class (84×84 resolution); standard evaluation: 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot with 600 episodes of 15 query examples per class; all papers use the same Ravi & Larochelle (2017) split for comparability; TIERED-IMAGENET: 608 classes organized into 34 high-level categories; splits ensure high-level categories don't overlap (train: 20 categories; val: 6; test: 8) — physically distinct semantic groups; 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot evaluation; EVALUATION PROTOCOL: sample 600-2000 episodes from test classes; report mean accuracy ± 95% confidence interval over episodes.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.use_when: Always evaluate on mini-ImageNet (and ideally tiered-ImageNet for thoroughness) when publishing a new few-shot image classification method — reviewers expect these benchmarks; use tiered-ImageNet specifically when evaluating whether your method truly generalizes to SEMANTICALLY NOVEL classes rather than just statistically different ones; also use CROSS-DATASET evaluation (train on mini-ImageNet, test on different dataset) for stronger generalization claims.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.avoid_when: Avoid using only mini-ImageNet results for strong generalization claims about novel-class few-shot learning — mini-ImageNet's random class selection means the train/test semantic gap is smaller than in real deployment; avoid treating few-shot benchmark numbers as directly comparable across papers without verifying they use the same backbone and embedding dimension (using a pretrained ViT-L backbone gives 90%+ regardless of few-shot algorithm, making the choice of meta-learning method nearly irrelevant).
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.what_goes_wrong: BACKBONE CONFOUNDING is the most common issue in few-shot benchmark comparisons: a paper reporting 85% on mini-ImageNet 5-way 5-shot with a large pretrained ViT backbone vs. a competing paper's 70% with a 4-layer ConvNet are NOT meaningfully comparable — the backbone accounts for nearly all of the difference, not the few-shot algorithm; always compare methods using the SAME backbone and pretraining data for fair comparison; this backbone-confounding problem led to a period in few-shot learning research where improvements claimed by novel algorithms were largely attributable to simply using larger pretrained backbones.
11|⚪ T3 Few-shot & Meta-learning|Few-sho.real_example: The progress of few-shot classification on mini-ImageNet 5-way 1-shot: Matching Networks (2016): ~44%; Prototypical Networks (2017): ~49%; MAML (2017): ~48%; RelationNet (2018): ~50%; SimpleShot (2019, strong baseline with better backbone): ~62%; FEAT (2020): ~68%; S2M2 (2021): ~72%; Meta-Baseline (2021) + pretrained ViT: ~86%; this trajectory shows that most improvements after 2019 came from BETTER BACKBONES and PRETRAINING rather than fundamentally better few-shot algorithms — a critical context for interpreting few-shot literature.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Bayes' theorem defines the relationship between PRIOR beliefs about model parameters, the LIKELIHOOD of observed data given those parameters, and the POSTERIOR beliefs after observing data: P(θ|X) ∝ P(X|θ) · P(θ) — the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior; this is the foundational equation of Bayesian inference and defines how a Bayesian agent updates beliefs in light of evidence.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Frequentist ML (maximum likelihood estimation) finds the SINGLE parameter value that maximizes P(X|θ) and treats θ as a fixed unknown constant; Bayesian inference treats θ as a RANDOM VARIABLE with a prior distribution, then updates this distribution given data to produce a posterior — this represents UNCERTAINTY about parameters, not a single point estimate, enabling: (1) proper uncertainty quantification in predictions, (2) principled incorporation of prior knowledge, (3) automatic regularization (prior acts as regularizer), and (4) coherent model comparison.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: BAYES THEOREM: P(θ|X) = P(X|θ)·P(θ) / P(X); components — PRIOR P(θ): initial belief about parameters before seeing data (encodes domain knowledge, smoothness assumptions, scale of parameters); LIKELIHOOD P(X|θ): probability of observed data X given parameters θ (same as frequentist model); EVIDENCE P(X) = ∫P(X|θ)·P(θ)dθ: normalizing constant ensuring P(θ|X) sums to 1 (often intractable, computed via approximation); POSTERIOR P(θ|X): updated belief about parameters after observing data; PREDICTION: to predict new point x*, integrate over the posterior: P(x*|X) = ∫P(x*|θ)·P(θ|X)dθ (posterior predictive distribution — averages model predictions over all plausible θ values, weighted by posterior).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use Bayesian inference when UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION is important (not just a point prediction but a distribution over possible outcomes); when you have STRONG PRIOR KNOWLEDGE to incorporate (e.g., parameters must be positive, regularization); for SMALL DATA settings where the prior can meaningfully regularize (Bayesian linear regression with few data points); for PROBABILISTIC PROGRAMMING where you specify a generative story and want to reason about latent variables.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid full Bayesian inference when the posterior is very high-dimensional (e.g., neural network weights — billions of parameters) and exact or approximate inference is computationally intractable without severe approximations (use simpler uncertainty methods like MC Dropout or ensembles instead); avoid when the prior is completely uninformative and data is abundant — Bayesian and frequentist estimates converge anyway, making Bayesian's added complexity unjustified.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: PRIOR SENSITIVITY is the most common Bayesian pitfall — in small-data regimes, the posterior is heavily influenced by the prior; if the prior was chosen for convenience (conjugacy) rather than domain knowledge, the posterior may be a poor approximation of true uncertainty; another issue is EVIDENCE COMPUTATION — P(X) requires integrating over all of parameter space, which is analytically tractable only for conjugate models and requires MCMC or variational inference otherwise, adding significant computational overhead.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Bayesian spam filtering (naive Bayes) illustrates all three components: PRIOR = P(spam) estimated from training set proportion; LIKELIHOOD = P(word|spam) for each word frequency in spam emails; POSTERIOR ∝ prior × likelihood for a new email; the posterior update (given observed words, revise probability of spam) is exactly Bayes' theorem applied in closed form, and the prior P(spam) acts as regularization — without a prior (pure MLE), the model would classify any email containing a rare-but-spam word with 100% spam probability; the prior smooths this.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: A CONJUGATE PRIOR is a prior distribution P(θ) that, when combined with a particular likelihood P(X|θ), produces a POSTERIOR P(θ|X) in the SAME FAMILY of distributions as the prior — the prior and posterior have the same functional form, differing only in hyperparameters; this allows CLOSED-FORM POSTERIOR COMPUTATION without numerical integration, making the otherwise-intractable Bayes computation analytically tractable.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Computing the posterior P(θ|X) = P(X|θ)·P(θ)/P(X) generally requires computing the normalizing constant P(X) = ∫P(X|θ)·P(θ)dθ, which is analytically intractable for most prior-likelihood combinations; conjugate priors make the denominator cancel elegantly, producing a known closed-form posterior; understanding conjugate pairs is essential for BAYESIAN STATISTICS FUNDAMENTALS, for implementing BAYESIAN UPDATES EFFICIENTLY IN ONLINE LEARNING (each new observation updates the hyperparameters, no re-computation from scratch), and as the building blocks of hierarchical Bayesian models.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: CLASSIC CONJUGATE PAIRS: Beta-Binomial (Beta prior for coin-flip probability p, Binomial likelihood → Beta posterior with updated α, β counts); Dirichlet-Multinomial (generalization to K categories — Dirichlet prior → Dirichlet posterior with counts added); Gaussian-Gaussian (Gaussian prior for mean μ, Gaussian likelihood → Gaussian posterior with precision-weighted mean); Normal-Inverse-Gamma (conjugate for both mean and variance of Gaussian); Gamma-Poisson (Gamma prior for rate λ, Poisson likelihood → Gamma posterior); MECHANISM: for Beta-Binomial with prior Beta(α, β) and observed k heads in n flips: posterior is Beta(α+k, β+n-k) — just add the observed counts to the prior hyperparameters; no integration needed.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use conjugate priors for ONLINE LEARNING / STREAMING UPDATES where the prior is updated incrementally as data arrives (each update is just a hyperparameter adjustment — O(1) per observation); for COUNT DATA models (click-through rates, text classification, A/B tests); as ANALYTICAL BASELINE to understand Bayesian behavior before resorting to MCMC for more complex models; for EMPIRICAL BAYES where you estimate hyperparameters from data.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid forcing a conjugate prior when it poorly matches domain knowledge — using a Beta prior for a probability that is physically constrained to be near 0 (extremely rare events) but using a flat Beta(1,1) 'for convenience' misrepresents your prior knowledge; the whole point of conjugate priors is analytical tractability, but if the model complexity requires MCMC anyway (hierarchical models, nonlinear likelihoods), the tractability benefit disappears and you might as well use any prior that captures domain knowledge.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: CONJUGATE PRIOR DOGMATISM — choosing a conjugate prior purely for mathematical convenience without checking if it appropriately represents domain knowledge — is a common Bayesian modeling error; the Beta distribution is always symmetric or unimodal, but a probability parameter that should be strongly concentrated near 0 with a heavy tail toward 1 (skewed) requires a very specific Beta(α << 1, β >> 1) that practitioners often forget to set correctly, defaulting to uninformative Beta(1,1) instead.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Bayesian A/B testing with conjugate priors: Model both conversion rates as Beta distributions (Beta prior for p_control, Beta prior for p_treatment); after observing n_c conversions in N_c visits for control and n_t conversions in N_t visits for treatment, posteriors are Beta(α + n_c, β + N_c - n_c) and Beta(α + n_t, β + N_t - n_t) — updated analytically (no MCMC); the probability that treatment is better P(p_t > p_c) is computed by sampling from both Beta posteriors (closed-form Beta sampling is fast); this allows stopping a test EARLY with a principled probabilistic statement rather than requiring fixed sample sizes, illustrating conjugate priors' practical value for business analytics.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Bayesian linear regression places a PRIOR over the weights w of a linear model y = wᵀx + ε (Gaussian prior P(w) = N(0, λ⁻¹I) on weights; Gaussian likelihood P(y|x,w) = N(wᵀx, σ²)); the resulting POSTERIOR P(w|X,y) is ALSO GAUSSIAN (conjugate) and can be computed in closed form; predictions use the POSTERIOR PREDICTIVE DISTRIBUTION P(y*|x*,X,y) = ∫P(y*|x*,w)P(w|X,y)dw, which is also Gaussian with mean and variance computable in closed form.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Bayesian linear regression provides UNCERTAINTY-AWARE PREDICTIONS — unlike ridge regression (which gives a point estimate equivalent to the MAP of Bayesian linear regression), the Bayesian approach provides a DISTRIBUTION over predictions, quantifying both EPISTEMIC UNCERTAINTY (uncertainty due to limited data — large where data is sparse) and ALEATORIC UNCERTAINTY (irreducible noise σ²); it's the canonical example for teaching Bayesian inference applied to a regression model that practitioners use daily.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: SETUP: likelihood P(y|X,w) = N(Xw, σ²I); prior P(w) = N(0, S₀); POSTERIOR: P(w|X,y) = N(m_N, S_N) where S_N = (S₀⁻¹ + σ⁻²XᵀX)⁻¹ and m_N = S_N(S₀⁻¹m₀ + σ⁻²Xᵀy); POSTERIOR PREDICTIVE: P(y*|x*,X,y) = N(m_Nᵀx*, σ² + x*ᵀS_Nx*) — the predicted variance σ² + x*ᵀS_Nx* increases in regions far from training data (x*ᵀS_Nx* large), capturing EPISTEMIC UNCERTAINTY; NOTE: setting S₀ = λ⁻¹I, the MAP estimate m_N reduces to the RIDGE REGRESSION solution (w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy), showing ridge regression IS Bayesian linear regression with Gaussian prior (just without the uncertainty).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use Bayesian linear regression when you need UNCERTAINTY ESTIMATES for predictions, not just point predictions — e.g., predicting customer lifetime value with confidence bounds; when the connection between ridge regression's regularization and the Gaussian prior helps justify the regularization strength λ in terms of a prior belief about weight scale; as a BUILDING BLOCK for Gaussian Process regression (which is Bayesian linear regression in an infinite-dimensional feature space).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid Bayesian linear regression for NONLINEAR tasks (the linear assumption is limiting) and for VERY HIGH-DIMENSIONAL input spaces where the O(D³) matrix inversion in S_N is computationally intractable; for these cases, either use sparse approximate inference, Gaussian Processes with appropriate kernels, or Bayesian neural networks with variational inference.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: The PRIOR VARIANCE S₀ (equivalent to ridge regularization λ) must be set carefully — a prior that's too DIFFUSE (large S₀) provides little regularization in small-data regimes; too CONCENTRATED (small S₀) prevents the posterior from updating toward the data; in practice, EMPIRICAL BAYES (estimating λ/S₀ by maximizing the marginal likelihood P(y|X) = ∫P(y|X,w)P(w)dw) is commonly used to set the prior automatically from data.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A real estate price model using Bayesian linear regression on 500 training examples produces prediction intervals (95% credible intervals) that widen significantly for houses in neighborhoods with few training examples — the posterior predictive variance x*ᵀS_Nx* is large when x* is far from the training data distribution; this is exactly the behavior you'd WANT for a price-prediction system: high confidence in dense urban areas with many comparable sales, low confidence in rare rural properties with few comparables, naturally communicating where the model's estimates should be trusted.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: MCMC (Markov Chain Monte Carlo) is a family of algorithms for SAMPLING from a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION that is known up to a normalizing constant — exactly the situation with Bayesian posteriors P(θ|X) ∝ P(X|θ)·P(θ) where the normalizing constant P(X) is intractable; MCMC constructs a MARKOV CHAIN whose stationary distribution IS the target posterior, so after a warm-up period (burn-in), samples from the chain are (approximately) samples from the posterior.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Exact Bayesian inference requires computing ∫P(X|θ)·P(θ)dθ (the evidence) which is analytically intractable for most realistic models (non-conjugate likelihoods, hierarchical models, Bayesian neural networks); MCMC provides a general-purpose approach to approximate the posterior by SAMPLING rather than computing it analytically — any expectation under the posterior (predictions, uncertainty estimates, model comparisons) can then be approximated by averaging over MCMC samples; MCMC is the gold standard for EXACT ASYMPTOTIC approximation (converges to the true posterior as the chain runs longer, unlike variational inference which introduces approximation bias).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: GENERAL FRAMEWORK: start at θ₀; at each step, propose a new θ' from a proposal distribution q(θ'|θ); ACCEPT or REJECT the proposal according to an acceptance rule that ensures detailed balance (guaranteeing the chain converges to the target distribution); SPECIFIC ALGORITHMS: Metropolis-Hastings (symmetric proposal, accept/reject ratio); Gibbs sampling (sample each variable from its full conditional — always accepts); HMC/NUTS (use gradient information to make proposals in high-dimensional spaces — covered in subsequent notes); CONVERGENCE: check using diagnostics (R-hat, ESS) after sufficient burn-in; PREDICTIONS: for each posterior sample θ_i, compute P(x*|θ_i) and average (posterior predictive).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use MCMC when you need ACCURATE POSTERIOR SAMPLES for a model of moderate complexity (tens of parameters to a few thousand) and can afford the compute — MCMC produces unbiased samples from the true posterior (asymptotically), unlike variational inference which has approximation bias; use PyMC or Stan for probabilistic programming that automatically implements NUTS (the best MCMC algorithm for most problems); use when model uncertainty estimates need to be trustworthy for high-stakes decisions.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid MCMC for VERY HIGH-DIMENSIONAL parameter spaces (Bayesian neural networks with millions of parameters) — chains mix poorly and the number of samples required for reliable estimates grows exponentially with dimension; avoid when SPEED is critical — MCMC is orders of magnitude slower than optimization-based methods (MLE, MAP, variational inference) and doesn't parallelize easily; for neural networks, use MC Dropout, deep ensembles, or variational inference instead.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: CONVERGENCE FAILURE is the primary MCMC risk — chains can get stuck in a local region of the posterior for many steps without exploring the full distribution (POOR MIXING); this produces biased posterior estimates even after many iterations; diagnosis: run MULTIPLE CHAINS from different starting points and check R-hat (potential scale reduction factor — should be < 1.01 for good convergence) and effective sample size (ESS — should be > 100 per chain); a chain with R-hat > 1.1 should NEVER be used for inference; automatic diagnostics in PyMC make this easy to check.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A clinical researcher modeling patient survival times with a Bayesian hierarchical model (hospital-level random effects, patient-level covariates) uses PyMC with NUTS to draw 2000 posterior samples after 1000 burn-in steps across 4 chains; checking R-hat < 1.01 for all parameters confirms convergence; the posterior distribution over the treatment effect coefficient directly gives the probability that the treatment is beneficial — P(β_treatment > 0 | data) — without requiring frequentist p-values or confidence intervals, making the clinical evidence statement more natural and directly interpretable.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Metropolis-Hastings (MH) is the foundational MCMC algorithm that constructs a Markov chain sampling from a target distribution π(θ) ∝ p(θ) (known up to normalization) using a PROPOSAL DISTRIBUTION q(θ'|θ) and an ACCEPT/REJECT step that ensures the chain's stationary distribution is exactly π(θ); it's the algorithm from which all more sophisticated MCMC methods (Gibbs, HMC, NUTS) are derived or can be understood as improvements upon.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: MH provides a GENERAL-PURPOSE recipe for sampling from ANY distribution known up to a normalizing constant — a remarkably powerful result since it means exact Bayesian posterior inference is possible for any model as long as you can evaluate P(X|θ)·P(θ) pointwise; the accept/reject mechanism (accepting moves that increase probability, sometimes accepting moves that decrease probability) ensures the chain doesn't get stuck at a mode and explores the full posterior distribution.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: ALGORITHM: (1) at current θ, propose θ' ~ q(θ'|θ); (2) compute acceptance ratio: α = min(1, [π(θ')·q(θ|θ')] / [π(θ)·q(θ'|θ)]); for symmetric proposals (q(θ'|θ)=q(θ|θ'), e.g., Gaussian random walk): α = min(1, π(θ')/π(θ)) = min(1, p(θ')/p(θ)) — normalizing constant CANCELS; (3) accept θ'←θ' with probability α, otherwise stay at θ; PROPOSAL DESIGN matters: a Gaussian random walk proposal N(θ'|θ, σ²I) with small σ accepts often but explores slowly (high autocorrelation); large σ proposes far but rejects often; OPTIMAL acceptance rate ~23% for random-walk MH in high dimensions (set σ to achieve this).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use MH (via probabilistic programming libraries) when the target distribution is simple enough that random-walk proposals work (few to ~20 dimensions); understand MH as the CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATION for all MCMC — understanding why the accept/reject step works (detailed balance condition) is essential for Bayesian statistics; use MH-within-Gibbs for hierarchical models where some full conditionals are available analytically but others aren't.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid hand-implementing random-walk Metropolis-Hastings for HIGH-DIMENSIONAL posteriors (> 20 dimensions) — step sizes need careful tuning and the random walk doesn't scale well (the curse of dimensionality means the fraction of good proposals shrinks rapidly); use NUTS instead (via PyMC/Stan), which is MH with gradient-guided proposals that scale much better; also avoid for MULTIMODAL posteriors without mode-jumping proposals — random walk MH will get stuck in one mode.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: The most common MH failure is STEP SIZE MISCALIBRATION — if σ is too small, acceptance rate approaches 100% but the chain moves slowly (high autocorrelation, very high ESS needed per unit compute); if σ is too large, acceptance rate approaches 0% and the chain barely moves; neither regime gives useful samples per unit compute; ADAPTIVE MH (tuning σ during burn-in to target 23% acceptance) is standard in libraries but must be disabled after burn-in to ensure valid MCMC theory applies (adapting proposals during the sampling phase violates the stationarity guarantee).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: For Bayesian logistic regression with 5 features (6 parameters including intercept), a Gaussian random-walk MH with σ=0.1 achieves ~30% acceptance rate and produces converged posteriors after ~10,000 steps (1000 burn-in, 9000 samples); inspecting the trace plots (parameter values vs. step) shows good mixing (rapid oscillation around the posterior mode) and R-hat ≈ 1.00 across 4 chains — a healthy MCMC run; this illustrates that for low-dimensional Bayesian regression, basic MH is adequate and easy to implement without probabilistic programming frameworks.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Gibbs sampling is an MCMC algorithm for multivariate distributions that samples each variable in turn from its FULL CONDITIONAL DISTRIBUTION (the distribution of one variable given ALL other variables at their current values) — rather than proposing all variables jointly; it's a special case of Metropolis-Hastings where the acceptance probability is always 1 (proposals from full conditionals are always accepted).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: In many Bayesian models (especially HIERARCHICAL MODELS), the JOINT posterior P(θ₁, θ₂, ..., θ_k | X) is intractable, but the FULL CONDITIONAL distributions P(θᵢ | θ_{-i}, X) (the distribution of each parameter given all others and the data) are tractable and often have closed form (especially with conjugate priors at each level); Gibbs sampling exploits this structure to sample from the joint posterior by repeatedly sampling from the tractable conditionals, avoiding the need for proposals or acceptance/rejection.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: ALGORITHM: initialize all parameters θ₁, θ₂, ..., θ_k; for each iteration: sample θ₁ ~ P(θ₁ | θ₂, ..., θ_k, X); sample θ₂ ~ P(θ₂ | θ₁, θ₃, ..., θ_k, X); ... sample θ_k ~ P(θ_k | θ₁, ..., θ_{k-1}, X); REPEAT; each sweep through all variables constitutes one Gibbs 'step'; CONDITIONAL TRACTABILITY: for conjugate hierarchical models (e.g., LDA topic model, Bayesian GMM), each full conditional is a known distribution (Dirichlet, Normal, Gamma); COLLAPSED GIBBS: integrate out some variables analytically, sampling only the remaining ones — produces better mixing by reducing dimensionality.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use Gibbs sampling for HIERARCHICAL BAYESIAN MODELS where conjugate prior structures make full conditionals available analytically — canonical examples: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for topic modeling, Gaussian Mixture Models (Bayesian GMM), Bayesian hidden Markov models; Gibbs sampling is also implemented within PyMC for discrete variables (like mixture assignments) that gradient-based NUTS can't sample from directly.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid Gibbs sampling when full conditionals are NOT analytically tractable (then MH or HMC/NUTS within Gibbs is needed instead); avoid for models with HIGHLY CORRELATED parameters — Gibbs sampling mixes poorly when variables are strongly correlated (the chain takes many steps to move from one end of the correlation to the other, causing high autocorrelation and low ESS); block Gibbs (sampling correlated variables jointly) or HMC can help.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: SLOW MIXING DUE TO CORRELATION is the primary Gibbs failure mode — for a bivariate Gaussian with high correlation ρ ≈ 0.99, Gibbs sampling requires ~10,000 steps to traverse the full posterior while HMC/NUTS would do it in ~10 steps; this isn't a theoretical failure (Gibbs will eventually converge) but a practical one (convergence takes so long the sampler appears to be stuck); BLOCK SAMPLING (sampling correlated variables jointly using a multivariate conditional) or reparameterizing to reduce correlation (e.g., centering hierarchical models) are standard fixes.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for topic modeling is typically trained with COLLAPSED GIBBS SAMPLING: integrate out the topic-word and document-topic distributions analytically (conjugate Dirichlet-multinomial), then only sample the topic assignment z_{d,n} for each word in each document; the full conditional P(z_{d,n}=k | z_{-d,n}, w) ∝ (count of topic k in document d + α_k) × (count of word w in topic k + β_w) is a simple categorical distribution — computed and sampled in O(K) time; this makes LDA training on millions of documents feasible with Gibbs sampling where other MCMC algorithms would be impractical.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is an MCMC algorithm that uses GRADIENT INFORMATION from the log-posterior (∂/∂θ log P(θ|X)) to make LARGE, GEOMETRY-AWARE PROPOSALS in parameter space — simulating Hamiltonian dynamics (like a frictionless ball rolling over the energy landscape) to propose points far from the current position while maintaining a high acceptance rate; this makes HMC dramatically more efficient than random-walk Metropolis-Hastings in HIGH-DIMENSIONAL spaces.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Random-walk MH in D dimensions has acceptance rates that decrease exponentially with D (step size must shrink as D grows), making it impractical for posteriors with more than ~20 parameters; HMC avoids this by using the GRADIENT OF THE LOG-POSTERIOR to follow the curvature of the distribution — proposals travel along contours of equal probability rather than randomly, enabling large moves that still get accepted because they respect the posterior geometry; HMC made Bayesian inference practical for models with hundreds to thousands of parameters.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: HMC introduces MOMENTUM variables p (same dimension as θ, Gaussian prior P(p) = N(0,M)); HAMILTONIAN H(θ,p) = -log P(θ|X) + pᵀM⁻¹p/2 (potential energy = negative log posterior; kinetic energy = momentum term); LEAPFROG INTEGRATION: simulate Hamiltonian dynamics for L steps of size ε: p ← p + ε/2 · ∇θ log P(θ|X); θ ← θ + ε · M⁻¹p; p ← p + ε/2 · ∇θ log P(θ|X); after L leapfrog steps, accept/reject with standard MH acceptance probability (to correct for numerical integration error); PARAMETERS TO TUNE: step size ε, number of leapfrog steps L, mass matrix M (often set to identity or diagonal).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use HMC (via PyMC or Stan, which implement NUTS — the automatic version) for any continuous-parameter Bayesian model where MCMC is needed and the posterior has more than ~20 parameters; HMC is the default recommendation for modern Bayesian workflows — it's far more efficient than random-walk MH and handles correlated posteriors much better than Gibbs sampling; essentially always use NUTS over raw HMC (NUTS automates the L and ε tuning that raw HMC requires).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid HMC for DISCRETE PARAMETERS (topic assignments, mixture components, tree structures) — HMC requires continuous gradients; for models with discrete variables, use RJMCMC, discrete MH, or Gibbs for those variables while using HMC/NUTS for continuous ones (PyMC handles this automatically); avoid for posteriors with VERY SHARP GRADIENTS or DISCONTINUITIES (e.g., sharp priors or step-function likelihoods) where leapfrog integration becomes numerically unstable.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: DIVERGENCES in HMC are a critical warning sign: a divergence occurs when the leapfrog integrator goes into a region of extremely high curvature (log-posterior gradient changes very rapidly), causing the numerical integration to go wildly off the true Hamiltonian trajectory; divergences indicate the sampler is NOT accurately exploring that part of the posterior — posterior estimates from regions with divergences are BIASED; fixes: increase target acceptance probability (NUTS), reparameterize the model (non-centered parameterization for hierarchical models), or use a smaller step size ε; NEVER ignore divergences when using HMC/NUTS.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A hierarchical Bayesian model for predicting conversion rates across 100 websites (each with different sample sizes) using HMC/NUTS in PyMC: the partial-pooling structure means the 100 website-level parameters are correlated through a shared hyperprior — random-walk MH would require ~100,000 steps for decent mixing; NUTS draws 1,000 samples after 1,000 warmup steps in a few minutes, with R-hat < 1.01 and no divergences; the efficient sampling is enabled by NUTS following the posterior curvature through gradient-guided leapfrog steps that traverse the correlated parameter space efficiently.
