11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: NUTS (No-U-Turn Sampler, Hoffman & Gelman 2014) is an ADAPTIVE HMC algorithm that AUTOMATICALLY TUNES the number of leapfrog steps L to avoid the 'U-turn' problem (leapfrog trajectories that double back on themselves, wasting computation) — eliminating the need to manually tune L, the most sensitive HMC hyperparameter, while also adaptively tuning the step size ε during warm-up; NUTS is the DEFAULT SAMPLER in PyMC and Stan.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Raw HMC requires manually tuning TWO hyperparameters (ε: step size; L: number of leapfrog steps) — poorly tuned L causes either short trajectories (like random-walk MH) or wasted computation from U-turns; NUTS automates L selection by monitoring when the trajectory is about to double back (the 'no U-turn' condition: stop when the forward and backward trajectory dot product becomes negative) and stopping the leapfrog integration at that point; combined with DUAL AVERAGING for step size tuning during warm-up, NUTS requires essentially NO tuning from the user.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: NUTS ALGORITHM (simplified): starting from (θ, p), build a BINARY TREE of leapfrog steps by alternately extending forward and backward in time, doubling the tree at each level; STOP when: (1) a 'U-turn' condition is detected (trajectory has doubled back), or (2) a maximum tree depth is reached; sample uniformly from the trajectory's leaves as the new θ; WARMUP PHASE: use Dual Averaging to adapt step size ε to target a specified acceptance probability (default 85%); ADVANCED: adapt the MASS MATRIX M (diagonal or full) to account for parameter scale differences; RESULT: after warmup, NUTS is essentially a well-tuned HMC sampler with no hyperparameters to set manually.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use NUTS (via PyMC's pm.sample() or Stan) as the DEFAULT MCMC algorithm for continuous-parameter Bayesian models — it's the current gold standard for most practical Bayesian inference, combining HMC's gradient-efficiency with automatic hyperparameter tuning; nearly any Bayesian model expressible in PyMC or Stan (linear models, GLMs, hierarchical models, GP regression) benefits from NUTS's efficiency.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid NUTS for models with DISCRETE PARAMETERS (NUTS doesn't handle these — PyMC switches to discrete Metropolis/Gibbs automatically for discrete variables); avoid when the model GRADIENTS are very expensive to compute (e.g., large neural network likelihoods) making each leapfrog step costly — in such cases, variational inference may be more practical despite its approximation bias; also avoid if the posterior has very complex geometry (many widely separated modes) where even NUTS may struggle to explore all modes.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: MAXIMUM TREE DEPTH exceeded during many NUTS steps indicates the sampler is having difficulty exploring the posterior — the trajectory keeps extending until hitting the safety maximum (default 10, giving 2¹⁰=1024 leapfrog steps per sample) without finding a U-turn; this usually means the posterior is VERY CORRELATED or has a very DIFFICULT geometry; solutions: reparameterize (non-centered parameterization for hierarchical models), add priors that constrain the posterior curvature, or reduce the target acceptance probability; like divergences, max-tree-depth saturation is a MODEL REPARAMETERIZATION signal, not just a sampler-settings issue.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A PyMC workflow for a hierarchical logistic regression (predicting student pass rates across 50 schools with school-level random effects): pm.sample(draws=1000, tune=1000, target_accept=0.9) runs NUTS with warmup that adapts step size and mass matrix; the summary shows R-hat ≈ 1.00, ESS > 400 for all parameters, no divergences — 4 minutes on a laptop with 4 chains; this is the standard 'it worked' fingerprint of a healthy NUTS run for a moderately complex hierarchical model, achieved without any manual HMC hyperparameter tuning.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: CONVERGENCE DIAGNOSTICS are statistical tests run on MCMC chains to assess whether the chain has converged to the target posterior and whether enough samples have been drawn for reliable inference; the two primary diagnostics are R-hat (potential scale reduction factor — measures convergence by comparing WITHIN-CHAIN to BETWEEN-CHAIN variance) and ESS (Effective Sample Size — measures how many INDEPENDENT samples the correlated MCMC samples are equivalent to).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: MCMC chains take time to converge — early samples are influenced by the starting point (burn-in period) and are NOT from the target posterior; even after convergence, consecutive MCMC samples are CORRELATED (each sample is close to the previous), so 1000 correlated MCMC samples may only be equivalent to 50 independent samples for estimating a specific quantity; without diagnostics, practitioners might incorrectly trust posterior estimates from chains that haven't converged (biased) or don't have enough effective samples (high variance estimates); diagnostics make the difference between trustworthy and unreliable Bayesian inference.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: R-HAT (Gelman-Rubin statistic): run M chains from DIFFERENT STARTING POINTS; compute WITHIN-CHAIN variance W = mean(s²_chain) and BETWEEN-CHAIN variance B = variance(chain_means); R-hat = sqrt((N-1)/N + B/(N·W)) — approaches 1 when chains converge (between-chain and within-chain variances are equal); THRESHOLD: R-hat < 1.01 (strict modern standard), R-hat < 1.1 (older, looser); R-hat > 1.1 almost certainly indicates non-convergence and should NEVER be trusted; ESS (Effective Sample Size): ESS = N / (1 + 2·Σ_k ρ_k) where ρ_k is the lag-k autocorrelation of the chain; high autocorrelation → low ESS; THRESHOLD: ESS > 100 per parameter for reliable posterior summaries; MODERN R-HAT (Vehtari et al. 2021): uses RANK-NORMALIZED R-hat for better detection of non-stationary chains and multimodal issues.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: ALWAYS check R-hat and ESS before using any MCMC results for inference — this should be automatic in every Bayesian workflow; use ArviZ (az.summary(trace)) or PyMC's built-in diagnostics to get R-hat and ESS automatically; check BOTH metrics (R-hat can look fine even when ESS is too low, and vice versa); report diagnostics when presenting Bayesian results to show the chain quality.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Never SKIP convergence checks even for simple models — simple models can fail to converge due to poor priors or data issues; never use ONLY R-hat without ESS (a chain that converged with very high autocorrelation can have R-hat ≈ 1 but ESS = 5, giving unreliable posterior estimates from technically 'converged' but information-poor sampling).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: TREATING R-HAT < 1.1 AS SUFFICIENT is the most dangerous convergence diagnostic mistake — the modern standard is R-hat < 1.01; chains with R-hat = 1.05 may look OK by old standards but have detectable non-convergence; similarly, ESS of 50 might seem acceptable but posterior QUANTILE estimates (like 95th percentile) require ESS >> 50 for accuracy — ESS > 400 is needed for reliable tail probability estimates; both diagnostics together with TRACE PLOT visualization are needed for confidence in MCMC results.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Running a PyMC model and calling az.summary(trace) shows R-hat = 1.32 for one parameter — a clear red flag indicating non-convergence; investigating the trace plot reveals the 4 chains are sampling from different regions of the posterior (two chains at high values, two at low), indicating a BIMODAL POSTERIOR the chains haven't explored jointly; the fix might be: adjust the prior to resolve the multimodality, use a better initialization strategy, or reparameterize; reporting results with R-hat = 1.32 would be statistically invalid.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Variational inference (VI) is an OPTIMIZATION-BASED alternative to MCMC for approximate Bayesian inference — rather than sampling from the posterior P(θ|X), VI finds the BEST APPROXIMATION to the posterior within a chosen family of distributions Q = {q(θ; φ)} by optimizing a divergence measure (typically KL divergence); VI trades EXACTNESS (MCMC) for SPEED (optimization converges much faster than MCMC chains).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: MCMC is asymptotically exact but can be too slow for large models or data (can't easily be parallelized, requires sequential chain steps); VI converts inference to OPTIMIZATION, enabling: (1) GPU-parallelized gradient descent, (2) mini-batch training on large datasets, (3) stochastic optimization (scalable to millions of data points); this makes VI the practical tool for Bayesian neural networks (BBVI, ELBO optimization), probabilistic deep learning, and large-scale Bayesian models where MCMC would take weeks.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: OBJECTIVE: minimize KL[q(θ; φ) || P(θ|X)] over variational parameters φ; EQUIVALENT TO maximizing ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund): ELBO(φ) = E_q[log P(X|θ)] - KL[q(θ;φ) || P(θ)]; DERIVATION: log P(X) = ELBO(φ) + KL[q||P(·|X)] ≥ ELBO(φ) (since KL ≥ 0); maximizing ELBO minimizes KL to true posterior; GRADIENT COMPUTATION: reparameterization trick (θ = μ + σ·ε, ε~N(0,I)) enables unbiased stochastic gradient estimates; MEAN-FIELD ASSUMPTION: typically q(θ) = Πᵢ q(θᵢ; φᵢ) (fully factorized — independent dimensions) for tractability; result: an approximate posterior q*(θ; φ*) that can be cheaply sampled for predictions.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use VI when MCMC is too slow for your model/data scale — Bayesian neural networks, large-scale probabilistic models with millions of data points, online learning where new data arrives continuously; use when you need GPU-accelerated Bayesian inference; STOCHASTIC VI (SVI in Pyro, Numpyro, or PyMC's ADVI) is the standard approach for large datasets; also use VI as a fast first approximation to check model structure before investing in MCMC.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid VI when TAIL PROBABILITIES or MULTIMODAL POSTERIORS matter — mean-field VI underestimates posterior variance (it's overconfident, concentrating mass near the mode) and completely misses multiple modes; for risk-sensitive applications where tail probability estimates are critical (medical decisions, financial risk), MCMC's unbiased sampling is essential; avoid trusting VI uncertainty estimates as carefully as MCMC estimates without explicit comparison.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: VARIATIONAL UNDERESTIMATION OF VARIANCE (overconfidence) is VI's systematic bias — the mean-field approximation q(θ) = Πᵢ q(θᵢ) ignores posterior correlations (the true posterior may be a correlated Gaussian while VI approximates it as axis-aligned), causing underestimation of uncertainty, particularly in regions where the posterior is elongated along a correlation axis; this manifests as calibration failure (prediction intervals that are systematically too narrow); structured variational families (normalizing flows, full-rank Gaussian VI) can partially address this at higher compute cost.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A Bayesian neural network for uncertainty-aware image classification uses BBVI (Bayes-by-Backprop, Blundell et al.): each weight is parameterized as q(w) = N(μ, σ²) with μ, σ learned by maximizing ELBO via standard SGD; at inference, sample weights 10-20 times and average predictions — regions where predictions are inconsistent across weight samples are high-uncertainty; this produces calibrated uncertainty on in-distribution examples but tends to underestimate uncertainty vs. deep ensembles (VI's overconfidence effect), trading inference quality for training efficiency.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: The ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund) is the OBJECTIVE FUNCTION maximized in variational inference — it is a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood log P(X) and, when maximized over the variational parameters φ, produces the best approximation q*(θ; φ) to the true posterior P(θ|X) within the chosen variational family; ELBO = E_{q(θ)}[log P(X|θ)] - KL[q(θ) || P(θ)].
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Maximizing the true posterior log-likelihood requires computing log P(X) = log ∫P(X|θ)P(θ)dθ, which is intractable; the ELBO provides a COMPUTABLE LOWER BOUND that: (1) can be optimized via gradient descent on φ, (2) relates directly to the quantity of interest (maximizing ELBO is equivalent to minimizing KL divergence from q to the true posterior), (3) can be estimated with UNBIASED STOCHASTIC GRADIENTS via the reparameterization trick, enabling mini-batch training on large datasets.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: DERIVATION: log P(X) = log ∫P(X,θ)dθ = log E_q[P(X,θ)/q(θ)] ≥ E_q[log P(X,θ)/q(θ)] (Jensen's inequality for log being concave) = E_q[log P(X|θ)] + E_q[log P(θ)/q(θ)] = E_q[log P(X|θ)] - KL[q(θ)||P(θ)]; INTERPRETATION: ELBO = EXPECTED LOG-LIKELIHOOD (how well θ~q explains the data on average) - KL DIVERGENCE FROM PRIOR (how far q is from the prior — a regularization term); GRADIENT: ∂ELBO/∂φ = ∂/∂φ E_{q(θ;φ)}[log P(X|θ) + log P(θ) - log q(θ;φ)]; computed with reparameterization trick (θ = g(φ, ε), ε~N(0,I)): swap expectation over q to expectation over ε, making gradient computable; MONITORING: the ELBO should increase monotonically during VI training — if it decreases, something is wrong (step size too large, implementation error).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Understand and monitor the ELBO whenever implementing or using variational inference — it's the training loss for VI in Pyro, NumPyro, and PyMC's ADVI (as negative ELBO); an increasing ELBO during training indicates the variational approximation is improving; ELBO is also used for BAYESIAN MODEL COMPARISON (the model with higher ELBO is preferred, similar to marginal likelihood for model selection).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid using the ELBO VALUE ALONE for comparing models trained on different data subsets or with different variational families — the ELBO depends on the data and the variational family choice, making cross-model comparison meaningful only when both are held constant; also avoid interpreting the final ELBO as a reliable measure of posterior approximation quality — a high ELBO can coexist with a poor posterior approximation if the KL regularization is satisfied by collapse (q approaching the prior).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: ELBO COLLAPSE — the variational distribution q(θ) collapses to the PRIOR P(θ) (KL term = 0, ELBO = E_{P(θ)}[log P(X|θ)]) even though the data contains information about θ; this happens when the KL weight in the loss is too high relative to the likelihood weight, often in VAEs where the β-VAE modification deliberately inflates the KL weight; in standard VI, collapse usually indicates the variational family is too restricted to fit the posterior or the model is misspecified; check by seeing if the posterior mean q differs from the prior mean — identical suggests collapse.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Training a VAE (Variational Autoencoder) on MNIST: the ELBO = E[log P(x|z)] - KL[q(z|x)||P(z)] where P(z)=N(0,I), q(z|x)=N(μ_φ(x), σ²_φ(x)); monitoring during training: the reconstruction term E[log P(x|z)] should increase (better reconstructions) and KL should be moderate (if KL→0, the encoder collapsed to the prior); the final ELBO of approximately -100 nats on MNIST corresponds to good reconstructions with meaningful latent representations — a healthy VAE training trace where both terms contribute meaningfully.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Mean-field variational inference is the most COMMON VARIANT OF VARIATIONAL INFERENCE that assumes the variational posterior FACTORIZES COMPLETELY over the parameter dimensions: q(θ) = Πᵢ q(θᵢ) — each parameter has its own marginal distribution, with ALL DEPENDENCIES between parameters IGNORED; this factorization makes the optimization tractable and the ELBO decomposable, but introduces a systematic approximation error by ignoring posterior correlations.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: The fully factorized form makes ELBO maximization analytically tractable for many exponential family models (each factor q(θᵢ) has an optimal closed-form solution when others are held fixed — this is the COORDINATE ASCENT VI / CAVI algorithm), and reduces the number of variational parameters from O(D²) (for a full-rank Gaussian that captures correlations) to O(D) (one mean and variance per dimension) — making mean-field VI scalable to high-dimensional models.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: MEAN-FIELD ASSUMPTION: q(θ₁, ..., θ_D) = q₁(θ₁) × q₂(θ₂) × ... × q_D(θ_D); OPTIMAL FACTOR (CAVI): for the i-th factor with others fixed, the optimal q_i*(θᵢ) ∝ exp(E_{-i}[log P(X, θ)]) where E_{-i} is expectation over all other factors; for conjugate models (exponential family likelihood + conjugate prior), q_i* is available in closed form; STOCHASTIC MEAN-FIELD VI: parametrize each factor as q(θᵢ; μᵢ, σᵢ) = N(μᵢ, σᵢ²); optimize μᵢ, σᵢ via stochastic gradient ascent on ELBO using the reparameterization trick; STANDARD IN LIBRARIES: PyMC's ADVI, Pyro's SVI with Normal variational distributions, NumPyro all implement stochastic mean-field VI by default.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use mean-field VI as the DEFAULT first approximation for large-scale Bayesian inference when MCMC is too slow — it's what PyMC's pm.fit(method='advi') runs; for models where posterior correlations are weak (many practical models), mean-field approximations are adequate; use mean-field VI for VARIATIONAL AUTOENCODERS (VAE) where the latent space factorization per example is a modeling assumption, not just an approximation.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid mean-field VI when posterior CORRELATIONS are STRONG and capture important uncertainty structure — classic example: Bayesian linear regression where the slope and intercept are strongly correlated (if you fit a line to data, high intercept implies low slope and vice versa); mean-field ignores this, producing independently-distributed uncertainty for slope and intercept that generates nonsensical joint samples; in such cases, full-rank Gaussian VI or normalizing flow VI are better.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: The canonical failure: a hierarchical Bayesian model where group-level means and the population variance are strongly correlated in the posterior; mean-field VI approximates this as independent, producing an estimate that UNDERESTIMATES MARGINAL VARIANCE (each parameter's uncertainty is underestimated because the correlation that would spread uncertainty isn't captured); in practice this manifests as VI posteriors that produce well-calibrated posterior means but OVERCONFIDENT uncertainty — credible intervals that are too narrow and have lower than claimed coverage.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: PyMC's ADVI on a linear regression model y = ax + b + ε: ADVI finds q(a) = N(μ_a, σ_a²), q(b) = N(μ_b, σ_b²), q(σ) = ... independently; because in the true posterior a and b are ANTI-CORRELATED (fitting a positive slope shifts the intercept down), the mean-field q that ignores this will underestimate the uncertainty of both a and b compared to NUTS; the point estimates (means) will be correct, but 95% credible intervals from ADVI will be too narrow, covering only ~80% of the true parameter ranges — a systematic miscalibration visible by comparing ADVI and NUTS results on the same model.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: PyMC (Python) and Stan (its own language, interfaces from Python/R) are PROBABILISTIC PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES (PPLs) that let you specify a Bayesian model as code (declaring priors, likelihood, and observed data) and automatically run MCMC (NUTS) or variational inference to compute the posterior — abstracting away the mathematical details of MCMC and letting practitioners focus on MODEL SPECIFICATION rather than sampler implementation.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Before PPLs, implementing Bayesian inference required manually deriving and coding samplers specific to each model — a significant mathematical and engineering burden; PPLs enable the SEPARATION of model specification from inference algorithm: the modeler specifies P(θ) and P(X|θ) in code; the PPL automatically runs NUTS/ADVI on the resulting model; this democratized Bayesian modeling for practitioners without deep MCMC expertise.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: PYMC: Python-native; models specified using Python context managers (with pm.Model() as m: pm.Normal('μ', mu=0, sigma=10); y_obs = pm.Normal('y', mu=μ, sigma=σ, observed=data)); runs NUTS via PyTensor/JAX backends; integrates with ArviZ for diagnostics; STAN: a dedicated probabilistic programming language (separate model block, parameters block, likelihood block — compiled to C++); interfaces in Python (PyStan, CmdStanPy), R, Julia; STAN is more performant for complex models (compiled) while PyMC is more Python-native and flexible; SHARED CORE: both automatically: differentiate the log-posterior (for NUTS leapfrog steps), run multiple chains, compute R-hat/ESS, adapt hyperparameters during warmup.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use PyMC for Bayesian modeling in Python workflows where you want: easy integration with numpy/pandas/scikit-learn, hierarchical models, and familiarity with Python syntax; use Stan when inference speed and reliability for complex models is paramount (Stan's C++ compilation makes it faster for complex or large models), or when working in R where RStan is standard; both are appropriate for any model with continuous latent variables where MCMC is needed.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid PyMC/Stan for models where the likelihood is a LARGE NEURAL NETWORK — computing the full likelihood for 1000 MCMC samples × N data points × forward passes is extremely slow; for such cases, use Pyro/NumPyro (JAX/PyTorch-based VI for neural models) or approximate methods (MC Dropout, ensembles); also avoid for real-time inference applications where even well-tuned NUTS is too slow.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: SHAPE ERRORS in PyMC are the most common beginner issue — getting dimensions wrong in the model specification (e.g., specifying a multivariate prior with wrong shape, or not properly indexing batched data) causes cryptic error messages deep in the sampler; careful use of pm.shape_utils and debugging with small data samples first helps; another common issue is SLOW SAMPLING from models with discrete variables (PyMC automatically uses Gibbs or MH for discrete variables, which is slower than NUTS for continuous variables — restructuring to marginalize out discrete variables improves speed).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A sports analytics Bayesian model in PyMC: team strengths α_team ~ N(0, σ_skill); match outcome likelihood P(home_win | α_home, α_away) = logistic(α_home - α_away + home_advantage); observed data = 380 Premier League match results; pm.sample(draws=2000, tune=1000) draws posterior samples over all 20 team strengths and σ_skill jointly; the resulting posterior means give expected team ranking WITH uncertainty (credible intervals that widen for newly-promoted teams with few matches), providing richer inference than a simple ELO rating point estimate.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: ArviZ is a Python library for EXPLORATORY ANALYSIS OF BAYESIAN MODELS that provides: (1) convergence diagnostics (R-hat, ESS, divergences), (2) posterior visualization (trace plots, posterior distributions, forest plots, pair plots), (3) model comparison (LOO-CV, WAIC), and (4) a standardized InferenceData container format that works with PyMC, Stan, NumPyro, Pyro, and emcee — a universal Bayesian analysis toolkit independent of the specific PPL.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Each PPL (PyMC, Stan, etc.) generates MCMC samples in different formats, and each team was previously implementing its own diagnostic plots and convergence checks; ArviZ standardized the Bayesian analysis workflow with a common data structure (InferenceData using xarray/NetCDF) and a consistent API for diagnostics and visualization that works across PPLs, making Bayesian workflows reproducible and shareable.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: INFERENCE DATA: az.InferenceData stores posterior samples, prior samples, log-likelihoods, and observed data in a structured xarray.Dataset; DIAGNOSTICS: az.summary(trace) returns a DataFrame with mean, SD, 94% HDI, R-hat, bulk-ESS, tail-ESS for all parameters; az.plot_trace(trace) shows chain traces + marginal distributions; az.plot_pair(trace) shows pairwise posterior correlations; MODEL COMPARISON: az.compare({'model1': idata1, 'model2': idata2}, ic='loo') computes LOO-CV (leave-one-out cross-validation using Pareto-smoothed IS, PSIS-LOO) or WAIC for model selection with standard errors; az.plot_posterior(trace) shows posterior with credible intervals.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use ArviZ as the STANDARD ANALYSIS TOOL after any PyMC/Stan/NumPyro sampling run — always: check az.summary() for R-hat and ESS; plot traces with az.plot_trace(); check for divergences; for model comparison, use az.compare() with LOO-CV (more reliable than WAIC for finite datasets); ArviZ's standardized workflow is what Bayesian practitioners expect to see in reports and papers.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: No strong reason to avoid ArviZ — it's the community standard; the only edge case is if you're working in a language without ArviZ bindings (Julia, Go) where you'd need alternative diagnostic tools; for variational inference results (not MCMC), some ArviZ diagnostics (R-hat, ESS) are not applicable — use ELBO monitoring instead.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: ArviZ's az.summary() reporting R-hat = nan can indicate sampling PATHOLOGY (chains that failed to move at all or all produced identical samples) rather than just non-convergence; this usually points to a MODEL SPECIFICATION ERROR (e.g., unbounded parameters with no finite-support constraint, a likelihood that evaluates to zero everywhere, or data/parameter shape mismatches); az.plot_trace() will show flat horizontal lines for such chains — a visual confirmation that sampling failed rather than just mixing poorly.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: After fitting a hierarchical model in PyMC, calling az.plot_trace(idata) produces plots where healthy chains show 'fuzzy caterpillar' trace plots (rapid mixing, all chains overlapping) and roughly bell-shaped marginal posterior distributions; calling az.summary(idata) shows R-hat ≈ 1.00, bulk-ESS > 1000 for all parameters; calling az.compare({'centered': centered_idata, 'noncentered': nc_idata}, ic='loo') reveals the non-centered parameterization has lower LOO-ELPD error and fewer Pareto-k > 0.7 warnings, confirming it's the better model specification for this hierarchical structure — a standard ArviZ-powered workflow for model comparison and validation.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are neural networks where WEIGHTS are treated as RANDOM VARIABLES with prior distributions P(w) rather than fixed values — inference produces a POSTERIOR DISTRIBUTION P(w|D) over all network weights given training data; predictions are made by INTEGRATING over the posterior (the posterior predictive), producing calibrated uncertainty estimates rather than point predictions.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Standard neural networks produce a single set of weights w* and make deterministic predictions — they have no mechanism to express UNCERTAINTY about their predictions; BNNs extend neural networks with the full Bayesian treatment: the posterior P(w|D) captures both parameter uncertainty (epistemic uncertainty — reducible with more data) and the learned aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible noise); this matters for safety-critical applications (autonomous driving, medical diagnosis) where knowing WHEN the model is uncertain is as important as the predictions themselves.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: EXACT INFERENCE: intractable for any practical neural network (the posterior P(w|D) ∝ P(D|w)·P(w) over millions of parameters has no closed form and MCMC doesn't scale); PRACTICAL APPROACHES: (1) VARIATIONAL INFERENCE (Bayes-by-Backprop): approximate P(w|D) with q(w;φ) = N(μ, σ²) per weight; maximize ELBO; doubles the parameter count (one mean + one variance per weight); (2) MC DROPOUT: use dropout at inference as an approximate BNN (covered next); (3) DEEP ENSEMBLES: train M independent networks with different random initialization — ensemble diversity approximates posterior diversity (covered next); (4) LAPLACE APPROXIMATION: fit a point estimate w*, then approximate P(w|D) ≈ N(w*, H⁻¹) where H is the Hessian at w*.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use BNNs when you need CALIBRATED PREDICTIVE UNCERTAINTY and can afford the computational overhead — particularly for anomaly detection (predictions far from training data should have high uncertainty), active learning (select data points where uncertainty is high), and safety-critical systems where overconfident predictions are dangerous; BNNs are the theoretically principled approach to uncertainty, even if practical approximations (ensembles, MC Dropout) often match them empirically.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid full variational BNNs for very LARGE models (transformers with billions of parameters) — the memory cost of storing mean and variance per weight is 2× the standard network, and the ELBO optimization is harder than standard training; also avoid BNNs when CALIBRATION can be achieved more cheaply (temperature scaling, conformal prediction) and you don't need full posterior inference — often the simpler calibration methods are sufficient.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: The PRIOR OVER WEIGHTS in BNNs is notoriously difficult to specify meaningfully — standard choices (N(0, σ²) with small σ) push weights toward zero, acting as regularization, but don't encode meaningful prior knowledge about the function the network should represent; poor priors in high-dimensional BNNs can dominate the posterior in surprising ways; additionally, variational BNNs often UNDERESTIMATE POSTERIOR VARIANCE (mean-field approximation ignores correlations between weights), producing overconfident predictions similar to MC Dropout.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A BNN for drug property prediction (Bayesian molecular property predictor): standard network predicts solubility; variational BNN adds weight distributions and predicts solubility with a 95% credible interval; for a known drug in the training distribution, the interval is narrow; for a novel molecular scaffold never seen in training, the interval is wide — this uncertainty signal tells a chemist whether to trust the prediction or synthesize the compound for experimental verification; the uncertainty-guided active learning loop (only requesting synthesis for high-uncertainty predictions) reduces experimental cost by ~40% vs. screening all candidates.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: MC Dropout (Monte Carlo Dropout, Gal & Ghahramani 2016) is a practical uncertainty quantification method for neural networks that uses DROPOUT AT INFERENCE TIME (not just training) — running the network M times with different random dropout masks produces a distribution of predictions; this distribution's MEAN is the prediction and its VARIANCE is an uncertainty estimate; MC Dropout is theoretically motivated as an APPROXIMATE BAYESIAN INFERENCE method.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: BNNs require significant implementation changes and compute overhead; MC Dropout showed that a standard neural network trained with DROPOUT already implicitly performs approximate variational inference over weights — keeping dropout active at test time and running multiple stochastic forward passes (different dropout masks = different effective networks) produces samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution; this gives uncertainty estimates from a standard neural network with minimal changes (just keep dropout active and repeat inference).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: TRAINING: standard dropout training (dropout layer drops units with probability p during training); INFERENCE (MC Dropout): instead of disabling dropout (standard inference), KEEP DROPOUT ACTIVE; run T forward passes through the network with different dropout masks; for each pass t: f_t(x) = forward pass with mask t; PREDICTION MEAN: ȳ = (1/T) Σ f_t(x); UNCERTAINTY: Var(ŷ) = (1/T) Σ f_t(x)² - ȳ² (predictive variance); CALIBRATION: theoretical connection to approximate variational BNN where dropout masks define the variational distribution over weights; T=30-50 usually sufficient for stable estimates.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use MC Dropout when you have an existing model trained with dropout and want CHEAP UNCERTAINTY ESTIMATION without retraining — just enable dropout at inference; particularly useful as a baseline uncertainty method for models where deep ensembles are too expensive (training M=5 separate models vs. just running M=30 forward passes of one model); good first uncertainty method to implement in a production model before investing in more sophisticated approaches.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid MC Dropout when CALIBRATION QUALITY matters critically — MC Dropout's uncertainty estimates are consistently LESS WELL CALIBRATED than deep ensembles empirically (Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017 showed this convincingly); avoid for DETERMINISTIC ARCHITECTURES without dropout (many modern architectures like batch-norm heavy networks or transformers use dropout sparingly or not at all — forcing dropout into a network not designed for it can hurt performance); also avoid when inference LATENCY is critical (T=30 forward passes is 30× slower).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: MC Dropout uncertainty tends to UNDERESTIMATE IN-DISTRIBUTION UNCERTAINTY and can produce OVERLY CONFIDENT predictions far from training data — the opposite of what you want for out-of-distribution detection; this happens because dropout masks don't explore enough of the network's function space to capture the full posterior variance; a dropout-trained network doesn't 'know what it doesn't know' as well as a deep ensemble where independent training runs from different random initializations produce genuinely different function hypotheses.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: An autonomous driving perception model uses MC Dropout for uncertainty: during T=50 forward passes of a pedestrian detection network, most bounding boxes have low variance in position/confidence (high certainty — clearly a pedestrian); an ambiguous blob (distant, partially occluded) shows high variance between passes (different dropout masks produce different confidence scores and box positions); this high-uncertainty detection can trigger a 'slow down and wait for more evidence' response rather than making a confident but potentially wrong detection decision — a practical safety application where MC Dropout's computational efficiency (only 50× slower than single forward pass vs. 5× slower for ensemble) justifies its slightly worse calibration vs. ensembles.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Deep ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017) are a simple but empirically powerful method for uncertainty quantification: train M independent neural networks with DIFFERENT RANDOM SEEDS (different weight initialization, different data shuffle order), combine their predictions by averaging, and use the DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN ensemble members as an uncertainty estimate; despite its simplicity, deep ensembles consistently outperform more theoretically-motivated Bayesian methods (MC Dropout, variational BNNs) on uncertainty calibration benchmarks.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: BNNs and MC Dropout estimate uncertainty within a single model's function space; deep ensembles explore DIFFERENT REGIONS OF FUNCTION SPACE (different random initializations lead to different local optima for non-convex neural networks) — producing FUNCTIONAL DIVERSITY rather than weight diversity; this functional diversity is empirically better at capturing both in-distribution and out-of-distribution uncertainty than approximate BNN methods that are theoretically better justified but practically worse.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: TRAINING: train M=5-10 networks with identical architecture but different random seeds on the SAME TRAINING DATA (no data subsampling — the diversity comes from initialization/optimization stochasticity, not data); PREDICTION: for classification, take softmax outputs f₁(x), ..., f_M(x); compute ensemble prediction: p̄(y|x) = (1/M) Σ f_m(x); UNCERTAINTY: predictive entropy H[p̄] or mutual information between individual member predictions; for regression: use mean and variance of M model outputs; OPTIONAL ADDITION: add ADVERSARIAL TRAINING or RANDOM LABELS as per original paper — empirically improved calibration but often omitted in practice; M=5 gives most of the benefit; diminishing returns beyond M=10.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use deep ensembles as the FIRST CHOICE for uncertainty quantification in production when compute budget allows training 5× models — they consistently outperform MC Dropout, variational BNNs, and Laplace approximation on calibration, and the simplicity (no change to training or architecture) makes them easy to implement and maintain; if you can afford 5× compute at training time, ensembles are almost always the right choice for uncertainty.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid deep ensembles when COMPUTE IS SEVERELY CONSTRAINED — training 5 models costs 5× training time and memory; in such cases MC Dropout or conformal prediction (covered next) are alternatives; avoid for ONLINE LEARNING or STREAMING settings where the ensemble needs to be updated frequently — updating 5 models doubles the streaming compute burden.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: LOSS DIVERSITY when ensemble members share too much inductive bias — if all M models use the same architecture with strong implicit priors (heavy regularization, batch normalization patterns), they may converge to VERY SIMILAR functions despite different random seeds, losing the diversity that makes ensembles powerful; using slightly different hyperparameters, architectures, or augmentation strategies across ensemble members can increase diversity and improve uncertainty estimates beyond same-architecture ensembles.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: DeepMind's landmark comparison (Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017) tested MC Dropout vs. deep ensembles on out-of-distribution (OOD) detection: for a model trained on MNIST, tested on SVHN (street house numbers — completely different distribution), MC Dropout assigned high confidence to SVHN images, correctly identifying it as OOD 60% of the time; deep ensembles assigned high uncertainty to SVHN images 95% of the time — demonstrating that ensemble disagreement is a much more reliable OOD signal than within-model MC Dropout variance; this result established deep ensembles as the practical gold standard for uncertainty in production ML.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Conformal prediction is a DISTRIBUTION-FREE uncertainty quantification framework that produces VALID PREDICTION SETS — sets of labels guaranteed to contain the true label with at least 1-α probability (e.g., 95%) for any model and any data distribution — using only the assumption that the calibration and test data are EXCHANGEABLE (weaker than IID); unlike BNNs/ensembles that require specific model assumptions, conformal prediction provides COVERAGE GUARANTEES without any distributional assumptions.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Bayesian credible intervals require prior specification and approximate inference (both introduce model-specific assumptions); confidence intervals require frequentist assumptions; conformal prediction provides a PRACTICAL, ASSUMPTION-FREE wrapper that can be applied to ANY existing model (neural network, random forest, LLM) to produce prediction sets with provable finite-sample coverage guarantees — answering 'what is the set of possible labels I'm confident about?' rather than 'what's the most likely label?'
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: SPLIT CONFORMAL PREDICTION (simplest variant): (1) split calibration data D_cal (held-out, not used in training); (2) compute NONCONFORMITY SCORE for each calibration example: s(x, y) — typically 1 - softmax_probability_of_true_label for classification; (3) compute (1-α) QUANTILE q̂ of calibration scores; (4) for a new test point x*, the PREDICTION SET is all labels y where s(x*, y) ≤ q̂; COVERAGE GUARANTEE: by construction, P(y_true ∈ C(x)) ≥ 1-α for EXCHANGEABLE data; the set size adapts to difficulty: easy examples produce small sets (1 label), hard examples produce large sets (many labels); RISK CONTROL extensions: control any monotone risk metric (FPR, recall, error rate) rather than just coverage.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use conformal prediction to wrap ANY EXISTING MODEL with valid uncertainty sets for high-stakes applications where coverage guarantees matter more than point estimates — medical diagnosis (must include the true diagnosis in the prediction set with 99% probability), regulatory compliance, safety-critical systems; conformal prediction requires a held-out CALIBRATION SET (typically 1000+ examples); easy to implement with the MAPIE library (Python) or conformal Risk Control frameworks.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid conformal prediction when PREDICTION SETS ARE UNUSABLE for the application — if a conformal prediction set for a 1000-class classifier is 'the true label is among these 500 classes,' the guarantee is mathematically valid but practically useless; in such cases, improving the underlying model calibration (temperature scaling, ensembles) is more productive; also avoid when the EXCHANGEABILITY ASSUMPTION is violated (e.g., time series with distribution shift — standard conformal prediction is still useful but requires extensions for non-exchangeable settings).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: The CALIBRATION SET SIZE determines the precision of the coverage guarantee — with small calibration sets (< 100 examples), the estimated quantile q̂ has high variance and the actual coverage may deviate substantially from the target (1-α); the guarantee is still VALID (never below 1-α in expectation) but individual estimates are noisy; use at least 1000 calibration examples for reliable set sizes; another practical issue is SET SIZE VARIATION — a well-calibrated model produces small prediction sets on easy examples; a poorly calibrated model produces large sets everywhere (technically valid but useless).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A radiology AI system for chest X-ray classification uses conformal prediction with α=0.01 (99% coverage guarantee): for each X-ray, it outputs not just the most likely diagnosis but a PREDICTION SET S(x) guaranteed to contain the true diagnosis 99% of the time; easy, clear pneumonia cases yield S={pneumonia} (1-element set); ambiguous cases with multiple possible diagnoses yield S={pneumonia, pleural_effusion, consolidation} (3-element set); radiologists can use single-element sets with high confidence, while multi-element sets flag cases requiring careful review — the guarantee that 1% of prediction sets are wrong is verifiable and controllable, unlike neural network confidence scores.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: A Gaussian Process (GP) is a probability distribution over FUNCTIONS — any finite collection of function values {f(x₁), ..., f(xₙ)} is jointly Gaussian with a mean function m(x) = E[f(x)] and a covariance function (kernel) k(x, x') = Cov(f(x), f(x')); GPs define PRIOR BELIEFS about the function f before seeing data and can be CONDITIONED on observations to produce a POSTERIOR distribution over functions — the Bayesian approach to nonparametric regression.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Neural networks for regression produce point predictions; Bayesian linear regression is limited to linear functions; GPs provide a principled nonparametric Bayesian regression approach that: (1) naturally quantifies EPISTEMIC UNCERTAINTY (confidence intervals that widen in data-sparse regions), (2) encodes PRIOR BELIEFS about function smoothness via the KERNEL choice, (3) produces EXACT POSTERIOR DISTRIBUTIONS for regression with Gaussian noise (no approximation needed for small data), and (4) is used in BAYESIAN OPTIMIZATION as the surrogate model for expensive black-box function optimization.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: PRIOR: f ~ GP(m, k) means f(X) ~ N(m(X), K(X,X)) for any finite input set X; typically m(x)=0; POSTERIOR (regression): given observations (X, y) with Gaussian noise y=f(X)+ε, ε~N(0,σ²I): f*|X,y,X* ~ N(μ*, Σ*) where μ* = m(X*) + K(X*,X)[K(X,X)+σ²I]⁻¹(y-m(X)) and Σ* = K(X*,X*) - K(X*,X)[K(X,X)+σ²I]⁻¹K(X,X*); the PREDICTIVE MEAN is the posterior mean at test points; PREDICTIVE VARIANCE σ*²(x*) quantifies uncertainty — equals the prior variance k(x*,x*) minus information gained from observations; COMPUTATION: O(N³) for N training points — the limiting factor for large datasets.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use GPs for SMALL/MEDIUM DATASET regression (N < 10,000) where uncertainty quantification is important; for BAYESIAN OPTIMIZATION (surrogate model over an expensive function like hyperparameter tuning, molecule optimization, experimental design); when you need SAMPLE-EFFICIENT learning where every measurement is expensive (scientific experiments, robotics, drug discovery); when encoding DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE about function smoothness/periodicity via kernel design.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid standard GPs for LARGE DATASETS (N > 10,000) due to O(N³) cost (matrix inversion) and O(N²) memory — use SPARSE GPs or deep kernel learning instead; avoid when the function has COMPLEX STRUCTURE (discontinuities, multi-modal behavior, very high-dimensional inputs) that simple kernels can't capture — deep learning may be more appropriate; don't use GPs when real-time prediction is needed from many training points (O(N) prediction cost but with N-sized kernel vector computation).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: KERNEL MISSPECIFICATION is the primary GP failure — if the kernel encodes wrong assumptions about function smoothness (e.g., RBF kernel assumes infinitely differentiable functions when the true function has kinks), the GP will produce poorly-calibrated uncertainty and poor predictions; kernel HYPERPARAMETER optimization (length scale, noise variance via marginal likelihood maximization) often helps but can overfit for small N; the O(N³) SCALING causes practical problems for datasets > 5,000 points and must be addressed with sparse approximations (inducing points).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning: objective = validation accuracy(learning_rate, batch_size) — expensive to evaluate (each evaluation is hours of training); GP surrogate: observe 10 (hyperparameter, accuracy) pairs; posterior GP gives MEAN (expected accuracy) and VARIANCE (uncertainty) at unobserved hyperparameter values; ACQUISITION FUNCTION (EI, covered next) selects the next point to evaluate; after 30 evaluations, the GP posterior concentrates around the optimal region, efficiently finding good hyperparameters while making only 30 expensive model training runs vs. hundreds required by grid search.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: GP kernels (covariance functions) k(x, x') define what KINDS OF FUNCTIONS a GP prior considers probable — the kernel encodes assumptions about SMOOTHNESS, STATIONARITY, PERIODICITY, and SCALE of the underlying function; the four most common kernels are: RBF (Radial Basis Function / squared exponential — infinitely smooth), Matérn (finite smoothness, controllable), polynomial (non-stationary, models global trends), and periodic (for repeating patterns).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: The kernel is the PRIMARY INDUCTIVE BIAS of a GP — choosing the kernel is analogous to choosing the architecture of a neural network; understanding the different kernel properties (smoothness, stationarity, periodicity) and how to COMBINE KERNELS (sum = model multiple independent patterns; product = model interactions; convolution = latent force models) is essential for using GPs effectively as a modeling tool rather than blindly applying RBF to every problem.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: RBF KERNEL: k(x,x') = σ²exp(-||x-x'||²/(2ℓ²)); ℓ = length scale (how quickly function varies); σ² = output variance; assumes INFINITE DIFFERENTIABILITY — functions are very smooth; valid but often oversmooths real-world data; MATÉRN KERNEL: k(x,x') = (2^{1-ν}/Γ(ν))(√(2ν)r/ℓ)^ν K_ν(√(2ν)r/ℓ) where r=||x-x'||; ν=1/2 → exponential kernel (nowhere differentiable, rough); ν=3/2 → once differentiable; ν=5/2 → twice differentiable; as ν→∞ → RBF; MATERN 3/2 or 5/2 are often preferred for PHYSICAL SYSTEMS where infinite smoothness is unrealistic; POLYNOMIAL: k(x,x') = (x·x' + c)^d; non-stationary (covariance depends on x position, not just x-x'); good for global trends and polynomially-structured data; PERIODIC: k(x,x') = σ²exp(-2sin²(π|x-x'|/p)/ℓ²); models strictly periodic functions with period p; combine with RBF for 'locally periodic' behavior; KERNEL COMPOSITION: add kernels (OR of patterns), multiply kernels (AND of patterns).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use Matérn 5/2 or 3/2 as DEFAULT kernel choices for most real-world regression tasks (more appropriate smoothness assumption than RBF); use RBF only when you believe the underlying function is very smooth (e.g., mathematical function approximation); use periodic kernels for TIME SERIES with clear periodicity (seasonality in sales data, circadian rhythms in health data); combine kernels: RBF + periodic for 'periodic trend with smooth deviations'; Matérn + Linear for 'smooth function with trend'.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid RBF for noisy, rough-looking data (e.g., stock prices, turbulent physical processes) — it will oversmooth and underestimate uncertainty; avoid PERIODIC KERNEL when you're not sure about the period (the period p is a hyperparameter that can be difficult to identify from sparse data); avoid POLYNOMIAL KERNELS of high degree for extrapolation — polynomial GPs extrapolate poorly outside the training range.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: KERNEL SELECTION by marginal likelihood can OVERFIT the kernel hyperparameters with small datasets — the marginal likelihood optimization may find a kernel that fits the training data perfectly (small length scale, memorizing all noise) rather than the true function; regularizing hyperparameter optimization (putting priors on length scales) or cross-validation is needed; another issue is INCORRECTLY ASSUMING STATIONARITY — RBF and Matérn assume the function's statistical properties are the same everywhere; if the function has different variability in different regions (heteroscedastic), a non-stationary kernel is needed.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Predicting monthly sales: raw sales data shows a YEARLY SEASONAL PATTERN + a slow long-term TREND + short-term NOISE; a composed GP kernel: k = k_trend + k_seasonal + k_noise = Matérn(3/2, ℓ_long) [slow trend] + Periodic(p=12, ℓ_seasonal) × Matérn(3/2, ℓ_decay) [annually periodic but decaying] + White_Noise(σ²) [observation noise]; the kernel is the 'model specification' for the GP, and marginal likelihood optimization finds the length scales ℓ, period p, and variances — producing uncertainty estimates that correctly widen in holiday months where training data is sparse.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: For GAUSSIAN REGRESSION (Gaussian likelihood P(y|f) = N(f, σ²)), the GP posterior P(f|X, y) is EXACTLY GAUSSIAN with closed-form mean and variance — no MCMC or variational inference needed; this closed-form posterior is one of the key advantages of GPs over other nonparametric methods: exact Bayesian inference is possible, producing exact predictive distributions with calibrated uncertainty.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: The closed-form GP posterior exists because the combination of Gaussian prior (from the GP) and Gaussian likelihood is CONJUGATE — producing a Gaussian posterior by Bayesian linear algebra (completing the square); this is mathematically identical to Bayesian linear regression with an infinite-dimensional feature space; understanding the closed-form posterior equations is essential for implementing GPs from scratch, interpreting GP uncertainty, and understanding why GPs are tractable for regression but intractable for classification (where the likelihood is non-Gaussian).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: NOTATION: X = training inputs, y = noisy observations, X* = test inputs; f = latent function values; JOINT PRIOR: [y, f*] ~ N(0, [[K(X,X)+σ²I, K(X,X*)], [K(X*,X), K(X*,X*)]]) (block matrix); POSTERIOR (by conditioning): μ* = K(X*,X)[K(X,X)+σ²I]⁻¹y; Σ* = K(X*,X*) - K(X*,X)[K(X,X)+σ²I]⁻¹K(X,X*); INTERPRETATION: μ* = weighted average of training targets (weights from kernel matrix); each diagonal Σ*[i,i] = k(x*ᵢ,x*ᵢ) - k(x*ᵢ,X)[K+σ²I]⁻¹k(X,x*ᵢ) = prior variance - information gained from observations; uncertainty is prior variance minus the 'explained' variance; BOTTLENECK: [K(X,X)+σ²I]⁻¹ is O(N³) to compute — the main scaling issue.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use GP regression when you need EXACT BAYESIAN INFERENCE for small-to-medium datasets (N < 5,000) with Gaussian observations — the closed form gives exact predictive distributions, unlike neural networks that require sampling-based uncertainty; particularly valuable when you need the FULL PREDICTIVE COVARIANCE across multiple test points (not just marginal variances), e.g., for designing experiments that account for correlations between candidate measurement points.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid the standard closed-form GP posterior for LARGE N (expensive O(N³) inversion) or NON-GAUSSIAN LIKELIHOODS (classification, count data — requires Laplace approximation or MCMC for the non-conjugate posterior, losing the closed-form advantage); also avoid for HIGH-DIMENSIONAL inputs D > 20 without dimensionality reduction — kernels in high D require careful design and many hyperparameters.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: NUMERICAL INSTABILITY in the Cholesky decomposition of K(X,X)+σ²I is a common implementation issue — the covariance matrix K is often ill-conditioned (near-singular), causing numerical errors in the matrix inversion; adding JITTER (a small diagonal constant, typically 1e-6) to K before Cholesky factorization stabilizes the computation; GP libraries (GPyTorch, GPy, scikit-learn's GaussianProcessRegressor) handle this automatically, but hand-coded GPs often encounter this issue.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A GP for time series regression on 200 data points: computing the GP posterior requires inverting a 200×200 kernel matrix (milliseconds); posterior predictive at 1000 test points: O(N²) kernel evaluations + O(N) matrix-vector products using the precomputed Cholesky factor (sub-second); uncertainty bands (2σ around the mean) naturally widen between observations and narrow where data is dense — a visual demonstration of the GP's posterior uncertainty encoding exactly the 'I'm confident where I've seen data, uncertain where I haven't' intuition that makes GPs valued for data-sparse scientific modeling.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Sparse GPs (Inducing Point Methods) are approximations that make GP inference SCALABLE BEYOND N~5,000 by introducing M << N INDUCING POINTS u (pseudo-observations at selected input locations Z) that summarize the information in the full training set; the posterior is approximated using only these M inducing points rather than all N observations, reducing computational cost from O(N³) to O(NM²) and memory from O(N²) to O(NM).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: Standard GP inference scales O(N³) in compute and O(N²) in memory — for N=10,000 training points, this is already hours of computation and ~800MB memory; for N=1,000,000, it's completely intractable; sparse GPs enable GP regression on datasets with millions of points (common in geospatial modeling, large-scale Bayesian optimization) by finding M=1,000-10,000 representative inducing points that capture the essential structure of the full dataset.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: INDUCING POINT FRAMEWORK: introduce M inducing points u = f(Z) at input locations Z; approximate the full GP posterior P(f|y) ≈ ∫P(f|u)q(u)du where q(u) is a variational distribution over inducing outputs; SVGP (Stochastic Variational GP, Hensman et al. 2013): maximize ELBO over variational parameters {m, S} of q(u)=N(m, S) and inducing locations Z; COMPUTATIONAL COST: O(NM²) for N observations, M inducing points; M=500-2,000 typically sufficient; stochastic ELBO enables MINI-BATCH TRAINING on large datasets; GPYTORCH IMPLEMENTATION: ExactGP for N<10,000; VariationalGP/ApproximateGP for sparse/large-scale; inducing point locations optimized alongside kernel hyperparameters.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use sparse GPs for ANY GP regression problem with N > 5,000 — standard GPs become impractical and sparse GPs provide nearly equivalent predictions and uncertainty for well-chosen inducing points; particularly valuable for GEOSPATIAL MODELING (millions of GPS coordinates), LARGE-SCALE BAYESIAN OPTIMIZATION (hundreds of thousands of candidate evaluations), or any scientific application with large experimental datasets; GPyTorch makes sparse GP implementation straightforward.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid sparse GPs when M is too small relative to the data complexity — with too few inducing points, the approximation misses important local features (prediction errors and overconfident uncertainty in regions between inducing points); the quality-computation tradeoff requires choosing M large enough for accuracy; avoid if the inducing point LOCATIONS are fixed arbitrarily — inducing point placement matters significantly, and optimizing Z jointly with kernel hyperparameters is essential for best performance.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: INDUCING POINT COLLAPSE is a known failure mode where optimizing inducing point locations Z causes many inducing points to cluster in a small region while leaving large gaps, producing overconfident predictions in the gaps and wasted computation from redundant nearby inducing points; regularizing inducing point placement (or using greedy selection via maximum entropy or k-means clustering as initialization) helps prevent this; another issue is ELBO UNDERESTIMATION of variance — variational sparse GPs are overconfident compared to exact GPs for the same M, requiring careful M selection.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A geospatial pollution mapping model using air quality sensor readings from 50,000 monitoring stations: exact GP inference is computationally intractable (50,000³ = 10¹⁴ operations); sparse GP with M=2,000 inducing points (placed on a spatial grid using k-means initialization, then optimized): O(50,000 × 2,000²) ≈ 2×10¹¹ operations — about 100× faster, fitting in hours on a GPU; predictive uncertainty maps correctly show lower confidence in regions with sparse sensor coverage and higher confidence in dense urban monitoring networks, enabling spatially-aware pollution reporting.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: GP CLASSIFICATION uses a GP prior over latent functions f and a non-Gaussian likelihood P(y|f) (typically sigmoid for binary: P(y=1|f) = σ(f), or softmax for multiclass) — but because the likelihood is non-Gaussian, the posterior P(f|X, y) is NO LONGER GAUSSIAN (unlike regression); the LAPLACE APPROXIMATION approximates this non-Gaussian posterior as a Gaussian centered at the MAXIMUM A POSTERIORI (MAP) estimate, enabling approximate Bayesian inference for classification.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: GP regression has exact closed-form inference (conjugate Gaussian-Gaussian); GP classification breaks this because sigmoid/softmax likelihoods make the posterior non-conjugate — requiring approximate inference; the Laplace approximation is the SIMPLEST SUCH APPROXIMATION: find the MAP estimate f̂ (where gradient of log-posterior = 0), then approximate P(f|X,y) ≈ N(f̂, [K⁻¹ + W]⁻¹) where W = -∇∇ log P(y|f) at f̂; this preserves the GP framework's uncertainty quantification for classification with minimal additional complexity.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: ALGORITHM: (1) Find MAP: maximize log P(f|X,y) ∝ log P(y|f) + log GP_prior(f); done by Newton-Raphson iteration on the Newton system (K⁻¹ + W)f̂ = (∇_f log P(y|f)); (2) compute POSTERIOR COVARIANCE at MAP: Σ_approx = (K⁻¹ + W)⁻¹ = K - K(K+W⁻¹)⁻¹K; (3) PREDICTION: P(y*=1|x*, X, y) ≈ σ(μ*) where μ* = K(x*,X)K⁻¹f̂ (mean prediction); uncertainty is propagated by marginalizing over the approximate posterior (requires numerical integration, typically Gaussian quadrature for 1D); COST: O(N³) like exact GP regression.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use GP classification with Laplace approximation when you need CALIBRATED PROBABILISTIC PREDICTIONS for classification with small datasets where the GP prior's smoothness inductive bias is appropriate — e.g., binary medical diagnosis from a handful of features (< 5,000 patients), safety classification in robotics; use via scikit-learn's GaussianProcessClassifier or GPy/GPyTorch for more flexible control.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid Laplace-approximated GP classification for LARGE DATASETS (O(N³) cost) or when the non-Gaussian likelihood is far from Gaussian (multimodal posteriors where a single Gaussian approximation misses multiple modes); for large N, sparse GP classification (SVGP with Bernoulli likelihood) is preferred; for very complex classification, deep kernel GP or a standard neural network with calibration is more practical.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: The Laplace approximation is only accurate when the posterior is APPROXIMATELY GAUSSIAN (unimodal and roughly symmetric near the MAP); for classification problems where some inputs are NEAR THE DECISION BOUNDARY with many conflicting labels, the posterior may be bimodal or heavy-tailed, and the Laplace approximation significantly underestimates uncertainty; expectation propagation (EP) provides a better approximation in such cases but is more complex to implement.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: A medical risk classification GP: binary outcome (high/low risk), 8 clinical features, N=800 patients; Laplace-approximated GP classifier produces posterior probabilities P(high_risk|patient_features) with calibration curves (reliability diagrams) showing well-calibrated uncertainty — 80% predicted probability patients actually have ~80% observed outcomes; the GP's smoothness prior ensures predictions in sparse data regions appropriately widen toward 50% probability, preventing overconfident predictions for patient profiles far from any training example.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is a sequential strategy for OPTIMIZING EXPENSIVE BLACK-BOX FUNCTIONS f(x) (functions whose gradient is unavailable, that take minutes-to-hours per evaluation, e.g., training a neural network with hyperparameters x and evaluating validation accuracy) — it fits a SURROGATE MODEL (typically a GP) to existing observations of f and uses an ACQUISITION FUNCTION to select the next x to evaluate by balancing EXPLORATION (trying uncertain regions) and EXPLOITATION (trying regions expected to be good).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: For cheap functions, grid search, random search, or gradient-based optimization works fine; for EXPENSIVE functions (hyperparameter tuning where each evaluation trains a model for hours, drug discovery where each evaluation is a lab assay, experimental physics), every evaluation counts; BO minimizes the number of evaluations needed to find the optimum by using the GP surrogate to intelligently select where to evaluate next — typically finding optima in 20-50 evaluations vs. hundreds required by grid/random search.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: ALGORITHM: (1) evaluate f at a few initial points x₁, ..., x_n (random or space-filling); (2) fit GP surrogate to observations {(xᵢ, f(xᵢ))}; (3) compute ACQUISITION FUNCTION α(x; GP) over the input space; (4) select next point x_{n+1} = argmax α(x); (5) evaluate f(x_{n+1}); (6) update GP with new observation; REPEAT until budget exhausted or convergence; ACQUISITION FUNCTIONS: Expected Improvement (EI) — expected amount f(x) exceeds current best f*; Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) — μ(x) + β·σ(x) balancing mean vs. uncertainty; Thompson Sampling — sample from GP and pick its maximum; KEY INSIGHT: the GP uncertainty σ(x) ensures unexplored regions get evaluated (exploration), while the GP mean μ(x) guides toward regions likely to be good (exploitation).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use BO for HYPERPARAMETER OPTIMIZATION of ML models (learning rate, batch size, architecture choices) when each training run takes more than a few minutes and random/grid search would require too many expensive evaluations; use for SCIENTIFIC EXPERIMENTS (lab automation, materials discovery, drug candidate selection) where each experiment is costly; use for NEURAL ARCHITECTURE SEARCH (NAS) at smaller scales; standard libraries: Optuna (GP backend), BoTorch/Ax (industrial-scale BO), SMAC3.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid BO for CHEAP FUNCTIONS where random search or grid search completes in minutes — BO's overhead (GP fitting, acquisition optimization) is only worth it when each f evaluation costs more than several seconds; avoid for INPUT SPACES with hundreds of CATEGORICAL parameters (GPs struggle with high-dimensional mixed discrete/continuous spaces — use random search or evolutionary methods); avoid for STOCHASTIC OBJECTIVES with very high noise (the GP struggles to fit a meaningful surrogate to very noisy evaluations).
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: ACQUISITION FUNCTION OPTIMIZATION is often the overlooked bottleneck — finding argmax α(x) over the input space is itself a non-convex optimization problem; in high dimensions (D > 20), this inner optimization can fail to find the global acquisition maximum, causing BO to suggest suboptimal points; multi-start local optimization with random restarts is the standard approach; for high-dimensional spaces (D > 30), vanilla BO degrades significantly — use trust region BO (TuRBO), CMA-ES-based BO, or high-dimensional adaptations.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Hyperparameter tuning for a BERT fine-tuning task: 5 hyperparameters (learning rate, warmup ratio, batch size, weight decay, dropout) spanning a mixed continuous/categorical space; each training run: 2 hours on a GPU; BO with 50 evaluations finds hyperparameters achieving 91.5% F1 vs. 89.8% from 200-trial random search — demonstrating BO's sample efficiency advantage; crucially, BO's 50 evaluations (100 GPU-hours) finds a better result than random search's 200 evaluations (400 GPU-hours), reducing hyperparameter search cost by 4× while achieving better performance.

11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_it_is: Expected Improvement (EI) and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) are the two most widely used ACQUISITION FUNCTIONS in Bayesian Optimization — mathematical formulas that, given the current GP surrogate model, score EVERY CANDIDATE POINT x for how promising it is to evaluate next; EI quantifies the expected gain over the current best; UCB optimistically scores points by adding uncertainty to the mean estimate.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.why_it_exists: The acquisition function is the INTELLIGENCE of Bayesian Optimization — it decides WHERE TO EVALUATE NEXT given the surrogate model; EI and UCB operationalize the EXPLORATION-EXPLOITATION TRADEOFF differently: EI focuses on points likely to IMPROVE upon the current best (exploitation-focused near the optimum, exploration-focused away from it naturally); UCB adds a controllable exploration bonus (β·σ) that can be tuned to be more or less exploratory; understanding both is essential for choosing the right acquisition strategy and tuning BO behavior.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.how_it_works: EXPECTED IMPROVEMENT: EI(x) = E[max(f(x) - f*, 0)] where f* = current best observed value; closed-form for GP surrogate: EI(x) = (μ(x)-f*)·Φ(Z) + σ(x)·φ(Z) where Z=(μ(x)-f*)/σ(x), Φ=Gaussian CDF, φ=Gaussian PDF; EI=0 when σ(x)=0 (already observed); EI>0 when μ(x)>f* (exploitation) OR σ(x)>0 (exploration near f*); natural balance without tuning; UPPER CONFIDENCE BOUND: UCB(x) = μ(x) + β·σ(x) where β is the EXPLORATION PARAMETER (β=0: pure exploitation; β→∞: pure exploration); β tuning controls exploration-exploitation balance explicitly; theoretical analysis gives regret bounds with appropriate β schedule; THOMPSON SAMPLING: sample one GP posterior function and optimize it — implicit exploration through posterior randomness; often competitive or better in practice.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.use_when: Use EI as the DEFAULT acquisition function for most BO problems — it requires no tuning (no β), has a closed-form formula, and handles exploration-exploitation automatically; use UCB when you want EXPLICIT CONTROL over the exploration-exploitation tradeoff (e.g., for a fixed budget, early stages: high β for exploration; late stages: low β for exploitation); UCB is also preferred when THEORETICAL BOUNDS on regret are required.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.avoid_when: Avoid USING EI WITH VERY NOISY OBJECTIVES without accounting for noise — standard EI assumes noiseless observations and becomes poorly calibrated with high observation noise; NOISY EI or the knowledge gradient acquisition are better in this regime; avoid UCB when β TUNING IS IMPRACTICAL — poorly chosen β (too low: gets stuck in local optima; too high: wastes evaluations on distant uncertain regions) significantly degrades BO performance.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.what_goes_wrong: EI has a known PATHOLOGY: if the GP surrogate is very confident everywhere (low σ everywhere, from fitting many observations in a compact region), EI becomes nearly 0 everywhere except right at the current best's neighborhood — causing the algorithm to over-exploit and never explore; this is the 'over-exploitation problem' and manifests as BO getting stuck near a local optimum; adding EXPLORATION BONUS or switching to UCB with β>0 at this stage can help; also, EI ignores BATCH PARALLELISM — for parallel BO (evaluating B candidates simultaneously), specialized acquisition functions (qEI, q-UCB, implemented in BoTorch) are needed instead of sequential EI.
11|🟡 T2 Bayesian Machine Learning|Bayesi.real_example: Neural architecture search using BO with EI: a GP over architecture-to-validation-accuracy observations after 10 initial random architectures; EI at iteration 11 identifies a region with both high predicted accuracy (exploitation) and high uncertainty (exploration) — an architecture type with 3 evaluated examples showing promising but variable results; evaluating there confirms the architecture type is indeed good; over 50 iterations, EI-guided BO explores multiple promising regions while concentrating on the best, finding an architecture at 92.3% accuracy that random search found only at 91.1% across the same 50 evaluations.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Federated learning (FL) is a DISTRIBUTED MACHINE LEARNING PARADIGM where a model is trained across many DECENTRALIZED DEVICES or servers (clients) that each hold LOCAL PRIVATE DATA — clients train on their own data and share only MODEL UPDATES (gradients or weight deltas) with a central server, which aggregates them into a global model; RAW DATA NEVER LEAVES the client device, providing privacy by design.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Traditional ML requires centralizing data in one location — often impossible due to PRIVACY REGULATIONS (GDPR, HIPAA forbid sharing medical records across hospitals), BUSINESS CONFIDENTIALITY (competitors won't share data), COMMUNICATION COST (uploading terabytes of device data to a server is impractical), or LATENCY (edge inference requires on-device models); FL enables training on distributed data without centralization by moving the COMPUTATION to the DATA rather than the data to the computation.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: BASIC FL ROUND: (1) SERVER sends current global model weights W_t to K selected clients; (2) each client k trains locally on its private data D_k for E local epochs, producing updated weights W_k; (3) clients send weight updates ΔW_k = W_k - W_t to server; (4) SERVER AGGREGATES: W_{t+1} = W_t + η·Σ_k (n_k/N)·ΔW_k (weighted by local dataset size); (5) repeat for T rounds; VARIANTS: CROSS-DEVICE FL (millions of mobile phones, unreliable participation, small datasets per client); CROSS-SILO FL (few hospitals/companies, more reliable, larger datasets per client).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use federated learning when DATA CANNOT BE CENTRALIZED due to privacy regulations, business constraints, or practicality: multi-hospital clinical research (HIPAA constraints), next-word prediction on smartphones (Google Keyboard), fraud detection across banks that can't share transaction data, or IoT device model improvement without uploading sensor data; FL is also applicable for PERSONALIZATION scenarios where each client's local model matters (personalized FL).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid FL when data CAN be centralized and doing so is simpler — FL adds significant engineering complexity (client selection, communication rounds, aggregation, privacy accounting); avoid when clients have VERY NON-IID DATA that makes global model aggregation counterproductive (each client's data is so different that a global model trained by aggregation serves none of them well — local-only training or personalized FL may be better); avoid when the COMMUNICATION OVERHEAD is prohibitive for very large models and limited network bandwidth.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: GRADIENT LEAKAGE ATTACKS (reconstruction attacks like Deep Leakage from Gradients) can reverse-engineer training data from shared gradients — FL's privacy-by-data-locality doesn't fully protect against sophisticated adversaries with access to the gradient updates; SECURE AGGREGATION or DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY on gradients is needed for strong privacy; another issue is BYZANTINE CLIENTS — malicious clients can send corrupted updates that poison the global model; robust aggregation methods (median, trimmed mean) are needed for adversarial settings.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Google's Gboard (Android keyboard) next-word prediction uses FL: each phone trains a small language model update on the user's typing history locally; updates are sent to Google's servers only when the phone is idle, charging, and on WiFi; the server aggregates millions of device updates; the global model improves from all users' typing patterns without Google ever seeing any individual's messages — a production deployment at hundreds-of-millions scale that's the most widely cited FL success story.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: FedAvg (Federated Averaging, McMahan et al. 2017) is the FOUNDATIONAL FL ALGORITHM that aggregates client model updates by computing a WEIGHTED AVERAGE of the updated client weights (weighted by each client's local dataset size) — combined with multiple LOCAL SGD STEPS on each client per round rather than a single gradient step, which reduces communication rounds needed compared to the earlier FedSGD approach.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Early FL proposals (FedSGD) required clients to compute and send one gradient per round — too many communication rounds for slow, unreliable client connections; FedAvg showed that allowing clients to do MULTIPLE local SGD steps per round (E local epochs) before sending updates dramatically reduces the number of communication rounds (from thousands to tens/hundreds for many tasks), making FL practical for mobile devices with limited connectivity.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: ALGORITHM: server selects C×K clients (fraction C of total K clients); for each selected client k in parallel: initialize local model as W_t (current global); run E epochs of SGD on local dataset D_k → W_k; send ΔW_k = W_k - W_t to server; AGGREGATION: W_{t+1} = Σ_k (n_k/N) · W_k where n_k = |D_k|, N = Σ n_k; KEY TUNABLE PARAMETERS: C (fraction of clients per round), E (local epochs), local batch size B, local learning rate η; CONVERGENCE: FedAvg converges for IID data and approximately for mild non-IID; diverges for SEVERE non-IID (heterogeneous clients — addressed by FedProx).
