11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use FedAvg as the BASELINE aggregation algorithm for any FL system — it's the standard against which all FL improvements are measured; for cross-silo FL (few clients, roughly IID data), FedAvg often works well without modification; FedAvg with DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY (add Gaussian noise to gradients before aggregation, clip gradient norms) is the standard privacy-preserving FL baseline.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid FedAvg for SEVERELY NON-IID DATA distributions — multiple local epochs cause 'client drift' where each client's model moves far from the global optimum toward its local data distribution, and averaging drifted models produces poor global models; use FedProx or SCAFFOLD in such settings; avoid when clients have VASTLY DIFFERENT DATASET SIZES — the n_k/N weighting can give disproportionate influence to a few large clients, requiring client weighting strategies.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: CLIENT DRIFT is FedAvg's primary failure: with many local epochs E on non-IID data, each client's model drifts toward its local data optimum; averaging drifted models from different data distributions produces a global model that's worse than any individual client's local model for IID data — the opposite of the intended benefit; reducing E (fewer local steps) or using a smaller local learning rate reduces drift but requires more communication rounds; SCAFFOLD and FedProx were developed specifically to address this.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: A healthcare consortium of 10 hospitals runs FedAvg for a chest X-ray classification model: each hospital has ~500-2000 X-rays; 3 hospitals per round are selected; each trains for E=5 local epochs; the server averages their updates weighted by dataset size; after 50 rounds, the global model achieves 89% AUC on a held-out test set — better than any individual hospital's local model (limited data) and without any raw X-ray data leaving the hospitals; this demonstrates FedAvg's core value: privacy-preserving model improvement from distributed medical data.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: FedProx (Li et al. 2020) is an improvement to FedAvg for HETEROGENEOUS FL settings — it adds a PROXIMAL REGULARIZATION TERM to each client's local objective that prevents client models from drifting too far from the global model during local training: L_client(w) = L_local(w) + (μ/2)||w - w_t||² where w_t is the current global model and μ is the proximal parameter.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: FedAvg's client drift problem (clients diverging from the global optimum during multiple local training steps) becomes severe when clients have HETEROGENEOUS DATA (non-IID distributions) and VARIABLE SYSTEM RESOURCES (some clients complete more local work than others per round — 'systems heterogeneity'); FedProx addresses BOTH: the proximal term prevents DATA HETEROGENEITY-induced drift (keeps local models near the global model), and it naturally handles SYSTEMS HETEROGENEITY by allowing clients to do different amounts of work (those with fewer resources do fewer local steps, but the proximal term keeps them close to the global model regardless).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: CLIENT OBJECTIVE: instead of minimizing local loss L_local(w), minimize L_local(w) + (μ/2)||w - w_t||²; the proximal term (μ/2)||w - w_t||² penalizes deviation from the initial global model w_t; with μ=0: FedProx reduces to FedAvg; with μ→∞: all clients return the global model unchanged (no local learning); PRACTICAL μ: μ ∈ [0.01, 1] balances convergence (large μ) vs. local learning (small μ); SYSTEMS HETEROGENEITY: clients with fewer resources can terminate early (fewer local steps) — the proximal term still constrains their updates to be near w_t, ensuring they contribute useful updates despite incomplete optimization.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use FedProx (over FedAvg) when you observe DIVERGENCE or poor convergence in FedAvg training due to non-IID client data distributions — FedProx's proximal term stabilizes training; also use in CROSS-DEVICE FL settings with variable client resources where some clients regularly fail to complete a fixed number of local steps; μ can be tuned on a small validation set or treated as a hyperparameter in the FL system.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid FedProx with large μ when CLIENT SPECIALIZATION IS DESIRED — the proximal term actively prevents clients from learning local patterns that deviate from the global model, which may be harmful in settings where personalization matters (each client should develop its own specialized model); for personalized FL, methods like FedBN or FedPer (keeping some layers local) are better; also avoid if data is roughly IID — the extra μ hyperparameter adds complexity without meaningful benefit over FedAvg.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: MU TUNING can be challenging — too-small μ doesn't prevent client drift (behaves like FedAvg); too-large μ prevents clients from learning anything useful from their local data (all updates are near zero because w remains close to w_t); in practice, a grid search over μ ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1} using a small fraction of the FL rounds as a validation period is standard; some implementations use ADAPTIVE μ schedules (increasing μ over training as the global model becomes better-calibrated).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: A federated NLP training setup with 1000 smartphone clients, each with personal message histories (highly non-IID — some users text formally, others informally): FedAvg with E=5 local epochs diverges after round 20 (global perplexity increasing); switching to FedProx with μ=0.1 stabilizes training (global perplexity decreasing throughout), converging to 82 perplexity vs. FedAvg's final 95 perplexity despite identical data and compute budget — demonstrating FedProx's advantage on strongly heterogeneous client distributions.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Non-IID (not independently and identically distributed) data is the CENTRAL CHALLENGE of federated learning — in real FL deployments, each client's local dataset has a DIFFERENT DISTRIBUTION (a hospital specializes in cardiac patients; a user's phone has their personal photos; a bank serves a specific region's customers), and standard FL algorithms designed for IID data fail or perform poorly when client distributions differ significantly.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: In centralized ML, data is mixed from all sources (IID assumption approximately holds); in FL, each client only has local data from its OWN DISTRIBUTION — clients cannot see each other's data; when a model trained exclusively on local data at each client 'drifts' toward that client's distribution during local training, and these drifted models are averaged, the result is a GLOBAL MODEL that doesn't represent ANY individual client's distribution well — the 'mean of a distribution mixture' may not be representative of any component distribution.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: TYPES OF NON-IID: LABEL SKEW (clients have different label distributions — hospital A has 80% cardiac, hospital B has 60% pulmonary); FEATURE SHIFT (same labels but different feature distributions — different MRI machine calibration); QUANTITY SKEW (clients have very different amounts of data); COVARIATE SHIFT (input distributions differ across clients); IMPACT ON ALGORITHMS: each local SGD step on non-IID data moves the model toward the local optimum; averaging K models that moved toward K DIFFERENT optima produces a model that's suboptimal for all; METRICS: degree of heterogeneity measured by 'quantity of label imbalance' or Wasserstein distance between client distributions; MITIGATION: FedProx (proximal regularization), SCAFFOLD (control variates), FedNova (normalized averaging), personalized FL (keep some layers local), data sharing (share a small IID subset), or clustered FL (group similar clients).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Always characterize the DEGREE OF NON-IID in a FL system before choosing an algorithm — if client label distributions have high overlap (mild non-IID), FedAvg likely works; if distributions are very different (severe non-IID), SCAFFOLD, FedProx, or personalized FL is needed; use standard benchmarks for non-IID simulation: Dirichlet distribution partitioning of datasets (Dirichlet(α) with small α creates severe heterogeneity, large α approaches IID).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid IGNORING non-IID characterization when designing a FL system — assuming IID (and using FedAvg) when data is severely non-IID will produce a global model significantly worse than a centralized model trained on the same data; always measure and report the degree of non-IID in FL experiments to give context for performance numbers.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: The MOST DANGEROUS non-IID failure mode is SILENT DEGRADATION — FedAvg may appear to converge (loss decreases) in non-IID settings but to a POOR LOCAL MINIMUM far from the true global optimum; the global model has lower accuracy than expected and may perform poorly on specific subpopulations (the clients whose local distribution the global model underrepresents after averaging); detecting this requires FEDERATED EVALUATION across multiple client distributions, not just a single centralized test set.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Federated training of an NLP sentiment classifier across 20 companies (non-IID because each company's customers write reviews with different vocabulary, formality, and sentiment base rate): FedAvg with 5 local epochs achieves 78% accuracy on the global test set (which mixes all companies' distributions); a centralized model on the same data achieves 86%; the 8% gap is entirely explained by non-IID client drift — clients in different sentiment quartiles (mostly positive vs. mostly negative reviewers) train models that diverge, and averaging them produces a mediocre global model; using SCAFFOLD reduces the gap to 3%, and personalized FL (per-company top layers) eliminates the gap entirely at the cost of no longer having a single global model.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Communication efficiency refers to techniques for REDUCING THE DATA TRANSMITTED between FL clients and the server — since sharing full model gradients/updates can require transferring hundreds of MB per round per client, communication is often the BOTTLENECK for large-scale FL; GRADIENT COMPRESSION methods reduce transmission size via QUANTIZATION (representing gradients with fewer bits), SPARSIFICATION (only sending the largest-magnitude gradient components), or SKETCHING (sending a compressed summary).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: FL's practical scalability depends on efficient communication: a ResNet-50 has 25M parameters × 4 bytes = 100MB per update; uploading 100MB over a mobile data connection per training round (with potentially hundreds of rounds) is impractical; compression reduces this by 10-1000× with minimal accuracy loss; communication efficiency is also important for CROSS-SILO FL between organizations over limited-bandwidth VPN connections and for CROSS-DEVICE FL with resource-constrained IoT devices.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: QUANTIZATION: represent gradients as K-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats (K=8: 4× compression; K=1: 32× compression for 1-bit SGD); STOCHASTIC ROUNDING ensures unbiased quantization estimates; SPARSIFICATION: top-K sparsification — only send the top-K% of gradient values by magnitude, set rest to 0 (K=0.1% → 1000× compression); ERROR FEEDBACK: accumulate the quantization/sparsification error locally and add it to the next round's gradient (prevents persistent bias from compression); RANDOM SPARSIFICATION: randomly select gradient components to send (less effective than top-K but requires no coordination); FEDERATED DISTILLATION: instead of model updates, clients share predictions on public data, further reducing communication at the cost of requiring a public dataset.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use gradient compression when COMMUNICATION BANDWIDTH is a bottleneck in your FL system — profile communication time vs. computation time per round; if communication dominates, apply quantization (8-bit: negligible accuracy loss, 4× speedup) or top-K sparsification (1% sparsification: ~100× communication reduction, minimal accuracy impact with error feedback); quantization is almost always safe to apply; aggressive sparsification (< 1%) requires error feedback to avoid bias accumulation.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid aggressive compression (< 4-bit quantization, < 0.1% sparsification) without ERROR FEEDBACK — biased gradient estimates from compression without error correction cause persistent convergence problems that aren't obvious from training loss curves; also avoid compression for CROSS-SILO FL with high-bandwidth connections where computation (not communication) is the bottleneck — the compression overhead (encoding/decoding) may cost more than the bandwidth saving.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: ERROR ACCUMULATION without error feedback is the primary compression failure mode — if the QUANTIZATION ERROR is not accumulated locally and carried forward, each round's gradient estimate is biased; over many rounds, small biases compound and prevent convergence to the true optimum; this is especially severe for top-K sparsification where you're ignoring 99.9% of gradients per round; error feedback (adding last round's compression error to current gradient before compressing) eliminates this bias at zero communication overhead cost.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Google's research on FL for Gboard applied 1-bit quantization + error feedback to mobile keyboard model training: communication bandwidth reduced by 32× with <1% accuracy degradation (from 97.2% to 96.9% word accuracy); across 1 million devices per training round, this saves ~3.2GB of total upload bandwidth per round compared to 32-bit gradients — enabling more frequent training rounds within the same mobile data budget and faster convergence of the global keyboard model.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Differential Privacy (DP) applied to Federated Learning adds CALIBRATED NOISE to the model updates (gradients) before aggregation, providing a MATHEMATICAL PRIVACY GUARANTEE that the server cannot infer individual clients' private data from the updates — even if the server is adversarial; this addresses the GRADIENT LEAKAGE vulnerability of basic FL where sophisticated adversaries can reconstruct training data from shared gradients.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Basic FL (FedAvg, FedProx) sends model gradients or weight updates to the server; these updates LEAK INFORMATION about local training data — gradient leakage attacks (e.g., iDLG, GradInversion) have shown that individual training images can be reconstructed from gradients with high fidelity; DP-FL plugs this hole by providing a provable bound (ε-DP or (ε,δ)-DP) on how much information about any INDIVIDUAL CLIENT's data is leaked in the update, enabling use of FL in settings with strict privacy regulations (GDPR, HIPAA) where gradient leakage would be unacceptable.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: DP-FL combines two mechanisms: (1) GRADIENT CLIPPING: before sending an update, each client clips the L2 norm of their gradient to C (∀||ΔW_k||₂ > C: ΔW_k ← ΔW_k · C/||ΔW_k||₂) — bounding the maximum influence of any single client; (2) GAUSSIAN NOISE ADDITION: server adds Gaussian noise N(0, σ²C²I) to the aggregated gradient before updating the model, where σ is the noise multiplier (larger σ → more privacy, more noise); PRIVACY ACCOUNTING: uses Rényi DP or PRV accountant to track the TOTAL PRIVACY BUDGET ε spent across all rounds (each round spends some ε, and rounds compose to give total ε); CLIENT-LEVEL vs. SAMPLE-LEVEL DP: client-level (each client's contribution protected) is the standard for FL; USER-LEVEL DP where each SAMPLE is protected requires larger noise.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use DP in FL when: (1) regulatory requirements mandate provable privacy guarantees (HIPAA-compliant medical FL); (2) the server is not fully trusted (cross-organization FL where a participating party controls the server); (3) the data is highly sensitive and gradient leakage attacks are a realistic threat model; set the privacy budget ε based on regulatory requirements (ε < 1 is strong; ε < 10 is moderate; ε > 10 provides weak guarantees).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid strong DP (very low ε < 0.1) unless absolutely required — the utility-privacy tradeoff is steep: very low ε requires so much noise that model accuracy may drop by 5-20% vs. non-DP FL; in trusted server settings (the server is the organization training the model on its own devices), DP-FL's overhead may not be justified; in such cases, SECURE AGGREGATION (covered next) may provide sufficient protection without the accuracy hit.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: PRIVACY BUDGET EXHAUSTION is the core practical challenge — each FL round spends some ε, and running many rounds to achieve good model accuracy depletes the budget quickly; the fundamental tension: more rounds → better model accuracy AND more privacy budget spent; using a GOOD PRIVACY ACCOUNTANT (Rényi DP composition, PRV accountant) instead of naive composition gives tighter bounds and allows more rounds within the same ε budget; NOISE SCALE MISCALIBRATION (too-small σ: doesn't provide meaningful DP guarantees; too-large σ: model fails to learn) requires careful calibration using tools like Google's DP library or Opacus.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Google's Gboard production FL uses (ε,δ)-DP with ε ≈ 8.9 (moderate privacy) per training run — providing provable protection that any single user's typing data influences the shared model updates by at most a controlled, bounded amount; the ε value was chosen to balance privacy (reasonably strong guarantee) with utility (keyboard model accuracy maintained above acceptable threshold); this is one of the few public examples of production DP-FL deployment with a stated privacy budget.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Secure Aggregation (SecAgg) is a CRYPTOGRAPHIC PROTOCOL for federated learning where clients submit ENCRYPTED model updates that the server can only AGGREGATE (sum) — but cannot read any individual client's update; the server learns only the sum of client updates, not any individual contribution, using SECRET SHARING or SECURE MULTI-PARTY COMPUTATION (SMPC) techniques without requiring the clients to trust the server.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: In basic FL, the server sees each client's individual gradient update — even without raw data, this leaks per-client information; SecAgg ensures the server can ONLY LEARN THE AGGREGATE (FedAvg's sum), not individual contributions; this is complementary to DP-FL (which adds noise to the aggregate, protecting against what can be inferred from the AGGREGATE) — SecAgg protects against what can be inferred from INDIVIDUAL UPDATES, which DP-FL alone doesn't address.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: SECRETSHARE-BASED SECAGG (Bonawitz et al. 2017, used by Google): PAIRWISE MASKING — each client pair (i,j) agrees on a shared random mask r_{ij}; client i adds Σ_{j≠i} r_{ij} to its update (r_{ij} added, r_{ji} subtracted for pair j); when the server sums all masked updates, the masks CANCEL OUT (r_{ij} + r_{ji} = 0 in expectation for all pairs), leaving only the true sum of updates; if a client DROPS OUT, other clients can be asked to reveal their mask shares for the dropped client (using a secret-sharing scheme that allows reconstruction only if the client has dropped, not otherwise); COST: O(n²) communication per round for n clients (pairs of keys), manageable for cross-silo FL but heavy for cross-device FL with millions of clients.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use SecAgg in FL settings where the server is NOT FULLY TRUSTED by all clients — cross-organization FL where one party controls the server; regulatory settings where demonstrating that no single client's data is visible to the aggregating party is required (some GDPR interpretations require this); combine SecAgg + DP-FL for comprehensive protection: SecAgg hides individual updates from the server; DP-FL protects the aggregate from inference attacks.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid SecAgg for VERY LARGE CLIENT POPULATIONS (millions of devices) — the O(n²) pairwise key setup is impractical at extreme scale; lightweight SecAgg variants (FastSecAgg, compressed SecAgg) reduce this cost but add implementation complexity; avoid when the overhead of cryptographic operations is prohibitive for resource-constrained clients (small IoT devices with limited compute for key agreement and masking operations).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: DROPOUT HANDLING is SecAgg's primary practical challenge — clients may disconnect during a round; SecAgg protocols must handle partial client dropout while maintaining security (not revealing individual updates for clients who DO complete) — this requires a robust secret-sharing scheme and a recovery phase that adds protocol complexity and latency; COLLUSION between clients and server is another threat: if enough clients collude with the server, individual updates can be reconstructed (k-out-of-n secret sharing provides k-colluder resistance).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: A federated clinical NLP system across 5 hospitals uses SecAgg: each hospital trains locally on its clinical notes and encrypts its model update using pairwise masks agreed with other hospitals; the aggregation server (operated by a neutral third party) sums the masked updates — seeing only the aggregate weight change, not any hospital's individual model update; the sum is identical to standard FedAvg aggregation, so model quality is unaffected; hospital compliance officers can point to SecAgg as the technical mechanism ensuring the aggregating server never sees individual hospital models or infers their clinical distributions.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Personalised Federated Learning (PFL) produces CLIENT-SPECIFIC MODELS rather than a single global model — recognizing that in FL's non-IID setting, a single global model often performs WORSE than a locally-trained model for clients with distinctive data distributions; PFL approaches produce models that balance GLOBAL KNOWLEDGE (from all clients' data) with LOCAL ADAPTATION (fitting each client's own distribution).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Standard FL's goal (one global model for all clients) is counterproductive when clients are FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT — a hospital specializing in pediatric patients shouldn't use the same model as one specializing in geriatric patients; PFL addresses this by allowing client-specific components while still SHARING KNOWLEDGE across clients (sharing is still valuable — a pediatric hospital benefits from seeing patterns in geriatric data it would never observe locally, even if it shouldn't blindly adopt a model optimized for geriatric data).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: COMMON PFL APPROACHES: (1) LOCAL FINE-TUNING: train global model via standard FL, then each client fine-tunes on its local data (fast, simple, effective); (2) FEDBN / FEDBN++: share everything except BATCH NORMALIZATION statistics, which are kept local (BN statistics encode data distribution — keeping them local allows the model to adapt to each client's distribution while sharing learned features); (3) PER-FEDAVG (meta-learning approach): train a global model initialization (using MAML-style meta-learning) that's designed to be quickly fine-tuned per client with a few local steps; (4) FEDPER: split network into shared FEATURE EXTRACTOR (trained globally) + local HEAD (trained locally per client); (5) CLUSTERED FL: group clients by distribution similarity, train a global model per cluster.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use PFL when there's EVIDENCE that a global model underperforms individual clients' local models — measure 'global model performance on each client's local test set' vs. 'local model performance'; if local models consistently outperform the global model for most clients, PFL is needed; particularly important for PERSONALIZATION USE CASES (personalized news recommendations, personalized keyboard models, personalized medical risk scores) where individual variation is the point.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid PFL when the goal is a SINGLE DEPLOYABLE MODEL that works across all clients (e.g., a shared API endpoint serving all clients with one model) — PFL requires managing and serving per-client models, increasing deployment complexity significantly; avoid for CROSS-DEVICE FL with millions of clients where maintaining per-client model state is impractical; also avoid if local data is VERY SCARCE per client (< 100 examples) — local fine-tuning on tiny local datasets overfits quickly.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: LOCAL OVERFITTING is PFL's primary failure — local fine-tuning on small local datasets quickly memorizes local idiosyncrasies rather than genuinely adapting; a client with 50 training examples who fine-tunes a 100M-parameter model for many epochs will overfit catastrophically; EARLY STOPPING, strong L2 regularization toward the global model, or limiting fine-tuning to the final few layers (not the full network) are standard mitigations; also, PFL's EVALUATION is tricky — standard FL evaluation uses a global test set, but PFL should be evaluated on each client's local test set to correctly capture the per-client improvement.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: A messaging app deploys PFL for next-word prediction: a global RNN backbone is trained via FedAvg on all users' (anonymized) typing patterns; each user's phone then fine-tunes only the final LSTM layer locally on their personal typing history for 5 epochs (small local fine-tuning); the personalized model captures user-specific vocabulary (technical jargon for a software engineer, medical terminology for a nurse) while the global backbone provides general language understanding; evaluation shows 12% reduction in word prediction error vs. the global model alone.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: This is the INTRODUCTORY, CONCEPTUAL overview of Flower (flwr) as a federated learning framework — a more detailed, API-level look at Flower's architecture and specific features appears later in the Federated Learning Frameworks subtopic; here the focus is on WHY Flower was created and how it fits into the FL ecosystem as an OPEN-SOURCE, FRAMEWORK-AGNOSTIC FL library that enables research and development of FL systems in Python.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Before Flower, FL research required either modifying Google's TensorFlow Federated (TFF), using PySyft (OpenMined), or building custom FL infrastructure from scratch — each option tied to a specific ML framework (TF or PyTorch) or involved significant boilerplate; Flower was created to be FRAMEWORK-AGNOSTIC (works with PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, scikit-learn, or any Python ML library) and SCALABLE (simulation mode for single-machine research; deployment mode for real distributed systems) with a simple, consistent API for implementing FL strategies.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: ARCHITECTURE: SERVER runs a Strategy (FedAvg, FedProx, FedOpt, or custom) that orchestrates training rounds; CLIENTS implement the fl.client.NumPyClient interface with fit() and evaluate() methods (or fl.client.Client for lower-level control); SIMULATION MODE: fl.simulation.start_simulation() runs all clients in-process (no networking) for fast research experiments; DEPLOYMENT MODE: clients connect to server over gRPC; BUILT-IN STRATEGIES: FedAvg, FedProx, FedOpt (server-side momentum), QFedAvg, custom strategies via inheriting from fl.server.strategy.Strategy; can run 1,000+ simulated clients on a single machine for scalable FL research.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Use Flower when you need a QUICK START for FL research or development in Python with any ML framework — Flower is the easiest to get started with (pip install flwr; 50-line example works); particularly valuable for researchers who want to compare multiple FL algorithms quickly (built-in strategies) or implement custom strategies without building FL infrastructure; also use for CROSS-SILO FL deployment where all participants can install the Flower client.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid Flower in production cross-device FL at VERY LARGE SCALE (millions of mobile devices) — Flower is designed for research and smaller deployments; for production mobile FL at Google/Apple scale, specialized infrastructure is needed; the Flower framework is best for research, prototyping, and small-to-medium cross-silo deployments.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: Flower's simulation mode runs ALL CLIENTS IN ONE PROCESS — if a simulated client's training allocates GPU memory (training a large model), memory isn't released between clients (within a round), which can cause out-of-memory errors when simulating many clients with GPU training; using CPU for simulation or carefully managing model/tensor memory release between client.fit() calls is needed; also, Flower's gRPC communication in deployment mode has DEFAULT TIMEOUTS that may be too short for clients with slow computation (long local training jobs) — adjusting server timeout parameters is often needed.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: A research team comparing FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD on a non-IID CIFAR-10 benchmark uses Flower simulation mode: define one Python class implementing the client training logic; run fl.simulation.start_simulation(client_fn, num_clients=100, config=..., strategy=FedAvg()) — all 100 clients simulated on one machine; switch to FedProx by changing just the strategy argument; results stored in TensorBoard; the same client code works for all three strategy comparisons — Flower's strategy abstraction enabling quick algorithmic comparison with minimal code changes.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: This note covers the two CANONICAL REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS of federated learning that appear most frequently in FL literature and interviews: (1) HOSPITAL COLLABORATION — multiple healthcare institutions training shared medical AI models without sharing patient records; (2) KEYBOARD PREDICTION — Google's production FL deployment for next-word and next-sentence prediction on Android devices; these represent the two primary FL deployment patterns: cross-silo (few trusted organizations) and cross-device (millions of consumer devices).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Understanding FL's motivating applications is essential for contextualizing its design choices — the hospital scenario explains why FL was designed to handle non-IID data (different hospitals treat different patient populations) and why regulatory compliance (HIPAA) motivated privacy-preserving aggregation; the keyboard scenario explains why FL was designed for extreme scale (millions of devices), unreliable participation, and minimal communication; together they represent the TWO ARCHETYPES around which FL research and tooling is organized.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: HOSPITAL COLLABORATION (cross-silo FL): typically 5-50 hospitals; each has thousands of labeled records; using FedAvg or FedProx; INFRASTRUCTURE: each hospital runs a Flower, NVIDIA FLARE, or OpenFL client locally; a neutral aggregation server (or hospital consensus round) handles aggregation; DP may be added for regulatory compliance; EXAMPLES: Intel-sponsored COVID-19 chest CT model across 8 sites (Nature Communications 2021), FeTS (Federated Tumor Segmentation) across 71 institutions; KEYBOARD PREDICTION (cross-device FL): millions of Android phones; each phone has personal typing history (highly non-IID); hourly training rounds; only phones idle+charging+WiFi participate; DP-FL with moderate ε; gradient compression for bandwidth; ServerModel aggregates from ~100K participating devices per round; personalized fine-tuning on device; result: Gboard model improves from user typing patterns without Google accessing message content.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when: Reference these applications when explaining FL's design goals in interviews or project planning — hospital collaboration explains the REGULATORY MOTIVATION and cross-silo design; keyboard prediction explains the SCALE and communication efficiency motivation; when designing a new FL system, map it to one of these archetypes to identify which FL challenges (non-IID, communication, privacy, scale) are primary.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when: Avoid treating these as the only FL applications — FL is increasingly used in financial services (banks training fraud models without sharing transaction data), manufacturing (factories training predictive maintenance models across facilities), and autonomous vehicles (cars sharing driving-data-derived model updates); the hospital and keyboard examples are canonical but not exhaustive.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong: A common misunderstanding about production FL applications is that they're PURELY FL — in practice, HYBRID APPROACHES are common: Google's Gboard uses FL for model improvement but still relies on server-side processing for some personalization; hospital FL systems often use a small SHARED VALIDATION DATASET (centralized) that all hospitals contribute a few examples to for global model evaluation; neither system is pure FL in the academic sense, illustrating that practical FL often mixes centralized and federated components to balance privacy and utility.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: The FeTS (Federated Tumor Segmentation) challenge (2021-2022): 71 medical institutions across 6 continents trained a glioblastoma (brain tumor) segmentation model using FL; no patient scans left any institution; the federated model achieved Dice coefficient of 0.855 on the test set — MATCHING the performance of a centralized model trained with all data aggregated, while preserving data locality; this is the most rigorous empirical demonstration that FL can achieve centralized-model-level accuracy on a real clinical task with multiple diverse institutions.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: ε-differential privacy (ε-DP) is a formal mathematical guarantee that the probability of any output from an algorithm changes by at most a factor of e^ε whether or not any single individual's record is included in the dataset.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Without a formal privacy definition, 'anonymized' datasets repeatedly proved re-identifiable. ε-DP provides a worst-case, composable guarantee that is provably resistant to arbitrary auxiliary information.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works: A randomized mechanism M satisfies ε-DP if for all adjacent datasets D, D' (differing in exactly one record) and all possible outputs S: Pr[M(D) ∈ S] ≤ e^ε · Pr[M(D') ∈ S]. Small ε (e.g. 0.1) = strong privacy (outputs barely change), large ε (e.g. 10) = weak privacy. ε=0 means perfect indistinguishability (useless). ε=∞ means no protection. Typical production values range 1–10.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- You need a mathematically provable privacy guarantee
- Releasing aggregate statistics, ML model parameters, or query results over sensitive data
- Regulatory or auditing requirements demand a quantified privacy bound
- Building privacy-preserving ML pipelines (DP-SGD, DP-FTRL)
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- ε is set so high (>100) it provides no meaningful protection — cosmetic compliance
- The threat model requires hiding that a person is *in the dataset at all* (DP only bounds inference from outputs)
- You need exact answers — DP always adds noise, so deterministic correctness is incompatible
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Choosing ε without understanding the scale — ε=1 on a 1M-row dataset vs a 100-row dataset have very different empirical privacy risks
- Composition blindness: running many DP queries with ε=1 each accumulates budget (basic composition: k queries costs kε total)
- Neighbouring-dataset definition mismatch: replace-one vs add/remove changes the sensitivity calculation
- Forgetting the δ term: pure ε-DP is often too noisy; most production systems use (ε, δ)-DP
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Apple's iOS keyboard and emoji usage analytics use local DP with ε=4 per day, collecting frequency data for billions of users without Apple's servers ever seeing individual keystrokes. The DP guarantee is derived directly from this formal definition.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Sensitivity (Δf) is the maximum amount a function's output can change when a single record is added or removed from the dataset. It is the key quantity that determines how much noise must be added to achieve DP.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Noise must be calibrated to sensitivity: if adding/removing one record could swing the output by 1000, you need 1000× more noise than if it could only swing by 1. Sensitivity formalizes this worst-case swing.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
**L1 sensitivity** (for Laplace mechanism): Δ₁f = max_{D,D'} ||f(D) - f(D')||₁
**L2 sensitivity** (for Gaussian mechanism): Δ₂f = max_{D,D'} ||f(D) - f(D')||₂
Examples:
- COUNT query: Δ₁=1 (one record changes count by at most 1)
- SUM of values in [0,1]: Δ₁=1
- SUM of unbounded values: Δ₁=∞ (must clip first)
- MEAN of N values clipped to [0,1]: Δ₁=1/N
Clipping is the primary tool for bounding sensitivity before adding noise.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Before applying any DP mechanism — sensitivity must be computed first
- When deciding how much to clip gradients in DP-SGD (gradient clipping sets Δ₂)
- When choosing between Laplace (L1) and Gaussian (L2) mechanisms
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Never skip sensitivity analysis assuming the output 'looks small' — the guarantee requires a provable worst-case bound
- Don't use unbounded sensitivity functions without clipping; the resulting noise would be infinite
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Clipping threshold too low → high bias (model learns clipped gradients, not true gradients)
- Clipping threshold too high → high sensitivity → high noise → poor utility
- L1 vs L2 confusion: Laplace needs L1 sensitivity, Gaussian needs L2 — mixing them breaks the proof
- Sensitivity changes with query composition; recompute at each step
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: In DP-SGD (Abadi et al. 2016), gradient clipping norm C=1.0 sets the L2 sensitivity of per-sample gradients to 1.0. The Gaussian mechanism then adds noise σ·C to the summed gradient, where σ is chosen from the privacy accountant given the target (ε, δ).

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: The Gaussian mechanism achieves (ε, δ)-differential privacy by adding zero-mean Gaussian noise N(0, σ²I) calibrated to the L2 sensitivity of the query, where δ > 0 allows a small probability of the guarantee failing.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Pure ε-DP often requires impractically large Laplace noise for high-dimensional or multi-query settings. The Gaussian mechanism trades a tiny failure probability δ (e.g. 10⁻⁵) for much lower noise, enabling useful ML models.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
Given query f with L2 sensitivity Δ₂, release M(D) = f(D) + N(0, σ²·I) where:
- σ ≥ Δ₂ · √(2 ln(1.25/δ)) / ε   (classic formula)
- In practice, use a privacy accountant (Rényi DP or moments accountant) which gives tighter σ values
Key properties:
- (ε, δ)-DP with δ > 0 (must be cryptographically small, e.g. 1e-5 to 1e-8)
- Composes gracefully: total (ε, δ) can be computed via Rényi DP accounting across T steps
- Works in high dimensions because noise scales with L2 norm, not L1
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- High-dimensional outputs (ML gradients, embedding tables)
- Many compositions (SGD with many steps — use moments accountant)
- When L2-bounded sensitivity is natural (gradient clipping)
- Need tighter accounting than Laplace allows
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- When δ must be exactly 0 (pure ε-DP) — use Laplace instead
- Very low-dimensional scalar queries where Laplace is simpler and equally efficient
- When the noise distribution shape matters (Gaussian tails vs Laplace tails)
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Setting δ too large (e.g. δ=0.01) means a 1% chance of no privacy guarantee — should be << 1/N where N is dataset size
- Forgetting that σ scales with sensitivity: doubling the clipping norm doubles σ for the same (ε, δ)
- Using the classic σ formula instead of a moments accountant → unnecessarily large noise for SGD
- Not accounting for composition: each training step consumes privacy budget
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: TensorFlow Privacy and Opacus both implement the Gaussian mechanism for DP-SGD. Google's DP library uses the moments accountant (Abadi et al. 2016) which computes much tighter (ε, δ) bounds over T steps of SGD than naive composition, enabling training ResNet-50 on MNIST with ε=3, δ=10⁻⁵.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: The Laplace mechanism achieves pure ε-differential privacy by adding Laplace-distributed noise Lap(0, Δf/ε) to the true query output, where Δf is the L1 sensitivity of the function f.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: It is the canonical, simplest DP mechanism and the building block for understanding all others. It achieves pure ε-DP (no δ failure probability), making the guarantee unconditional.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
Release M(D) = f(D) + Lap(Δ₁f / ε), where Lap(b) is Laplace with scale b.
- PDF: p(x) ∝ exp(-|x|/b)
- Variance: 2b² = 2(Δ₁f/ε)²
- Smaller ε → larger scale b → more noise
- Vector outputs: add independent Lap(Δ₁f/ε) to each coordinate
Proof sketch: the ratio of output probabilities for adjacent D, D' is bounded by e^(|f(D)-f(D')|/b) ≤ e^(Δ₁f/b) = e^ε.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Low-dimensional scalar or small-vector statistics (counts, means, histograms)
- When pure ε-DP (δ=0) is required
- Simple query answering pipelines: total sales, average age, histogram of ratings
- Local DP: each user adds Laplace noise before sending data
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- High-dimensional outputs (ML gradients): L1 sensitivity explodes → impractical noise
- Many compositions: Laplace composition gives looser bounds than Gaussian + moments accountant
- Non-scalar outputs where L2 sensitivity is more natural than L1
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Forgetting to clip before computing sensitivity: unbounded SUM has Δ₁=∞ → infinite noise
- Using Laplace for gradient descent: high-dimensional gradient noise makes convergence impractical vs Gaussian
- Publishing exact sensitivity values alongside noisy outputs: helps attackers calibrate attacks
- Integer rounding after noise addition: introduces bias and can slightly degrade DP bound
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: The US Census Bureau used Laplace noise (via the TopDown algorithm) for the 2020 Census DP prototype. For a county-level count with Δ=1, ε=0.25 gives Lap(4) noise — adding roughly ±8 people (2 std devs) to any single count.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: The privacy budget is the total ε (and δ) allocated for all DP queries/mechanisms run on a dataset. Composition theorems govern how the budget accumulates across multiple DP operations.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: DP guarantees compose: running two ε-DP mechanisms on the same data costs 2ε total. Without accounting, you might think you have strong privacy while actually spending budget 100× over, destroying the guarantee.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
**Basic composition**: k mechanisms with parameters (ε₁,δ₁),...,(εₖ,δₖ) compose to (Σεᵢ, Σδᵢ)-DP. Worst case but simple.
**Advanced composition** (Dwork, Rothblum, Vadhan 2010): k mechanisms each (ε,δ₀)-DP compose to (ε√(2k ln(1/δ)), kδ₀+δ)-DP. Better for large k.
**Moments accountant / Rényi DP**: tightest bounds for SGD. Converts to (ε,δ)-DP at end of training. Used in Opacus, TF Privacy.
**Zero-Concentrated DP (zCDP)**: intermediate framework that converts cleanly to (ε,δ)-DP.
Budget management: once you've spent your total ε, you must stop querying or accept that the privacy guarantee degrades.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Any pipeline with multiple DP queries or training steps — must track total budget
- Deciding how many SGD steps to run given a target ε
- Comparing mechanisms: moments accountant often allows 10× more SGD steps than basic composition for the same ε
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Don't use basic composition when moments accountant applies — it's needlessly pessimistic for iterative algorithms
- Don't ignore composition and apply ε independently to each query — this is a common mistake that breaks the guarantee
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Budget exhaustion mid-training: model stops improving before convergence if ε is set too small
- Not tracking δ composition: small δ per step can accumulate to large total δ
- Reusing the dataset after budget exhaustion without disclosure
- Forgetting that data-dependent hyperparameter tuning (early stopping on validation loss) also consumes privacy budget if validation set overlaps training
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Training a DP language model for 10,000 SGD steps with per-step noise σ=1.1, clipping C=1, and batch size 256 from a 60,000-sample dataset: basic composition gives ε≈137, but the moments accountant gives ε≈3.0 at δ=10⁻⁵ — a 45× tighter estimate, making the model actually usable (Abadi et al. 2016, MNIST experiment).

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Central DP adds noise once at the aggregator after collecting raw user data; local DP has each user randomize their own data before sending it, so the server never sees true values. They offer different trust assumptions.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Central DP requires trusting the data collector (server/aggregator) but achieves far better accuracy. Local DP eliminates that trust but requires much more noise per user to achieve the same ε — the fundamental privacy-utility tradeoff splits along this axis.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
**Central DP**: User → raw data → Trusted Aggregator → adds noise → public release. Noise = Lap(Δf/ε) or Gaussian scaled to global sensitivity. Used when data collection is regulated but internal analysts are trusted.
**Local DP**: User applies randomized response or RAPPOR before sending. Each user's datum satisfies ε-LDP (local DP). Aggregator sees only noisy responses. Classic mechanism: randomized response — send true value with probability p = e^ε/(1+e^ε), random with probability 1-p.
Accuracy difference: central DP noise ∝ 1/n (mean of n users), local DP noise ∝ 1/√n — variance is much worse.
**Shuffle model**: middle ground — shuffle + anonymize before aggregation, achieving central-DP accuracy from locally-randomized data.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Central DP: you have a trusted server (internal analytics, medical research with IRB)
- Local DP: users cannot trust the server (third-party data brokers, adversarial collection contexts)
- Local DP: browser/device analytics at massive scale (Apple, Google RAPPOR)
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Local DP with small datasets (n < 10,000): the accuracy is too poor to extract signal
- Central DP when the aggregator itself is an adversary or subject to subpoena without controls
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Confusing ε in local vs central: ε=1 local is far weaker protection per-user than ε=1 central due to noise scale differences
- Using local DP for rare events: frequency estimation of rare values requires enormous n to detect signal above noise
- Shuffle model implementation bugs: non-random shuffles (predictable ordering) defeat anonymization
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Apple uses local DP with ε=4/day for keyboard analytics. Google's RAPPOR (2014) uses local DP for Chrome browser histogram collection, with ε=ln(3) per report, collecting millions of reports to estimate population-level frequencies.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: DP-SGD (Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent) is a modification of SGD that clips per-sample gradients and adds Gaussian noise to the gradient sum before the parameter update, achieving (ε, δ)-DP for the trained model.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Trained model weights can memorize sensitive training data (model inversion, membership inference attacks). DP-SGD bounds the influence of any single training example on the final model parameters, providing a formal guarantee against such attacks.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
Each SGD step:
1. Compute per-sample gradient gᵢ for each sample i in the minibatch
2. Clip each: g̃ᵢ = gᵢ / max(1, ||gᵢ||₂/C)  — bounds L2 norm to C
3. Sum: G = Σ g̃ᵢ
4. Add noise: G̃ = G + N(0, σ²C²I)
5. Update: θ ← θ - η·G̃/B  (B = batch size)

σ is chosen via a privacy accountant (moments accountant/Rényi DP) given target (ε, δ) and T total steps.
Key hyperparameters: clipping norm C, noise multiplier σ, batch size B, steps T, target ε.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Training ML models on sensitive data where model release is planned
- Federated learning: each client runs DP-SGD locally before sending updates
- Healthcare, financial, or legal data where membership inference must be bounded
- Compliance contexts requiring quantified privacy guarantees for released models
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Very small datasets (<1000 samples): DP noise dominates and model won't converge
- When ε requirements are extremely tight (ε<0.1): accuracy collapses
- Tasks where model accuracy is critical and no large dataset exists; consider synthetic data augmentation first
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Per-sample gradient computation is slow: naive implementation is O(B) times slower than batch gradient; use ghost clipping or vmap for efficiency
- Clipping norm too small → high bias (gradients crushed); too large → sensitivity increases, needing more noise
- Not using a privacy accountant: basic composition overestimates ε by 10-100×, causing you to stop training too early
- Learning rate needs retuning: DP models typically need larger LR and more epochs to compensate for noise
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Abadi et al. (2016) 'Deep Learning with Differential Privacy' trained a CNN on MNIST achieving 97% accuracy with ε=2.93, δ=10⁻⁵. Google used DP-SGD to train language models for Gboard (keyboard next-word prediction) at ε~4.7, released as a landmark production deployment of DP in ML.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: Opacus is Meta's open-source PyTorch library for training neural networks with differential privacy using DP-SGD. It handles per-sample gradient computation, clipping, noise addition, and privacy accounting with minimal code changes.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Implementing DP-SGD correctly from scratch is error-prone (per-sample gradients, accountant math). Opacus wraps any PyTorch optimizer and model, handles the engineering, and integrates with standard training loops.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
```python
from opacus import PrivacyEngine

model = MyModel()
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
train_loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=256)

privacy_engine = PrivacyEngine()
model, optimizer, train_loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=train_loader,
    epochs=10,
    target_epsilon=3.0,
    target_delta=1e-5,
    max_grad_norm=1.0,  # clipping norm C
)

for batch in train_loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(batch))
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()  # clips + adds noise internally

epsilon = privacy_engine.get_epsilon(delta=1e-5)
print(f'Final ε = {epsilon:.2f}')
```
Uses Rényi DP accountant internally. Supports LSTM, Transformers, CNNs. Requires BatchNorm → GroupNorm replacement (BatchNorm uses batch statistics, breaking per-sample independence).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- PyTorch-based training pipelines needing DP-SGD with minimal refactoring
- Research experiments with DP (standard benchmark tool in DP-ML papers)
- Federated learning: run on each client before FedAvg aggregation
- Production ML on sensitive tabular/text/image data
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Non-PyTorch stacks: use TensorFlow Privacy instead
- Models with layers unsupported by Opacus (some custom CUDA ops)
- When model accuracy is paramount and DP noise is unacceptable — evaluate privacy budget feasibility first
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- BatchNorm breaks DP (shares statistics across batch): replace with GroupNorm or LayerNorm before using Opacus
- Per-sample gradient hooks increase memory usage by O(B): reduce batch size or use gradient accumulation
- Module compatibility: Opacus wraps modules with grad sample hooks — some third-party layers need custom GradSampleModule implementations
- Forgetting that `privacy_engine.get_epsilon()` call itself doesn't spend budget — just queries the accountant
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Meta used Opacus to train DP versions of their internal models. The Opacus paper (Yousefpour et al. 2021) shows training BERT-base on SST-2 (sentiment) with ε=3 achieves 92.5% accuracy vs 93.5% non-private — a 1% accuracy cost for strong DP guarantees.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: The privacy-utility tradeoff is the fundamental tension in DP where stronger privacy (smaller ε) requires more noise, which reduces the accuracy/usefulness of the released output. It is an inherent mathematical constraint, not an engineering limitation.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: DP noise is proportional to sensitivity/ε. Smaller ε → more noise → less accurate outputs. This is not a bug — it reflects that privacy and perfect accuracy are incompatible when the dataset is small or the query is sensitive.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
Key factors determining where you land on the curve:
- **n (dataset size)**: larger n amortizes noise better. For mean queries, noise = Δ/(n·ε) — 10× more data → 10× less noise impact
- **ε level**: halving ε doubles noise
- **Query type**: some queries have lower sensitivity (counts vs sums of large values)
- **Composition**: more queries → less budget per query → more noise each

Empirical rule of thumb for DP-SGD on ImageNet-scale data:
- ε=10: ~2-5% accuracy drop vs non-private
- ε=3: ~5-10% accuracy drop
- ε=1: >15% accuracy drop
- ε<0.5: typically unusable

Mitigations: public pre-training + DP fine-tuning (only fine-tuning step is DP), larger batches, lower clipping norm.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Evaluating whether DP is feasible for a given use case: model the expected accuracy at target ε before committing
- Comparing DP approaches: central vs local, different accountants
- Reporting to stakeholders: always report both ε and accuracy degradation together
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Don't treat the tradeoff as avoidable with better engineering — for a given n and ε, there is a lower bound on error
- Don't deploy DP models without measuring utility loss; a model with DP that doesn't work is worse than no model
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Setting ε=0.01 for 'strong privacy' without checking if the model trains at all
- Reporting accuracy without disclosing ε — meaningless for comparison
- Ignoring the public pre-training trick: fine-tuning from a public checkpoint (e.g., GPT-2) with DP often achieves much better accuracy than training from scratch
- Conflating ε with 'percentage of privacy lost' — ε is a worst-case log-odds ratio, not an intuitive percentage
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Google's DP language model for Gboard (2017): training from scratch with DP was poor quality. Solution: pre-train on public web text, then DP fine-tune on private keyboard data. Final model achieved production-level quality at ε≈4.7, demonstrating that public pretraining largely bypasses the utility cliff.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: GDPR (EU data law) and HIPAA (US health data law) impose legal obligations on how personal and health data is processed. Differential privacy can serve as a technical safeguard but does not automatically guarantee compliance — the legal frameworks have additional requirements.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Organizations processing EU personal data (GDPR) or US protected health information (HIPAA) face steep penalties for violations. DP provides a quantifiable privacy measure that can support compliance arguments and demonstrate data minimization practices.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
**GDPR relevance**:
- Article 5: data minimization and purpose limitation — DP mechanisms add noise to prevent excess data disclosure
- Article 25: privacy by design — DP-SGD and aggregation noise are built-in technical measures
- Article 89: research exemption allows processing if 'appropriate safeguards' are in place — DP can be cited as one
- Pseudonymization (Recital 26): DP-released statistics may not be 'personal data' if re-identification is computationally infeasible

**HIPAA relevance**:
- Safe Harbor de-identification: 18 identifiers removed. DP noise on aggregate statistics is a complementary technique but doesn't replace Safe Harbor or Expert Determination paths
- Expert Determination (§164.514(b)(1)): a statistician certifies that re-identification risk is 'very small' — DP ε is a quantitative input to this determination

**Key limitation**: no regulatory body has formally specified an ε threshold that guarantees compliance. ε=1 may suffice or not depending on dataset size, adversary model, and jurisdiction.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Documenting privacy safeguards for GDPR Article 30 records of processing activities
- Supporting an Expert Determination argument under HIPAA
- Publishing aggregate statistics from health records (census, registry data)
- Building a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) that requires technical privacy measures
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Using DP as a sole compliance strategy without legal review — GDPR and HIPAA have organizational, contractual, and procedural requirements DP cannot address
- Claiming 'GDPR compliant' based only on DP without DPA review or legal counsel sign-off
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Assuming DP eliminates all legal obligations: data subjects still have rights (access, deletion) even if released statistics are DP
- Setting ε too large (ε=100) and claiming DP compliance — courts and DPAs may scrutinize whether the protection is meaningful
- Not documenting the DP mechanism in processing records: regulators expect audit trails
- Ignoring retention limits: DP on outputs doesn't address requirements to delete raw data on schedule
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: The US Census Bureau's 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance System used DP with a formal ε budget, publishing detailed methodology to satisfy both statistical transparency requirements and privacy law obligations. NIH's All of Us research program cites DP mechanisms in its IRB protocols as a technical safeguard supporting HIPAA Expert Determination for genomic data releases.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: DoWhy is Microsoft Research's Python library for causal inference that enforces a four-step workflow: model (build a causal DAG), identify (find an identification strategy), estimate (compute the effect), and refute (run falsification tests). It unifies the graphical (Pearl) and potential outcomes (Rubin) frameworks.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: Ad hoc causal analyses often skip identification (assuming what's estimable) or refutation (testing whether results are artifacts). DoWhy makes these steps explicit and provides standardized APIs for multiple estimators and refutation tests.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
```python
import dowhy
from dowhy import CausalModel

model = CausalModel(
    data=df,
    treatment='T',
    outcome='Y',
    common_causes=['X1', 'X2'],   # confounders
    graph='digraph { X1 -> T; X1 -> Y; T -> Y; X2 -> Y }'  # optional
)

# Step 1: Identify — finds backdoor adjustment set
identified_estimand = model.identify_effect(proceed_when_unidentifiable=True)

# Step 2: Estimate
estimate = model.estimate_effect(
    identified_estimand,
    method_name='backdoor.propensity_score_matching'
)
print(estimate.value)  # ATE

# Step 3: Refute — random common cause test
refutation = model.refute_estimate(
    identified_estimand, estimate,
    method_name='random_common_cause'
)
print(refutation)  # should not change estimate significantly
```
Built-in estimators: linear regression, IPW, matching, IV, RDD. Refutation tests: random cause, placebo treatment, data subset, add unobserved confounder.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Causal analysis in Python with explicit assumption encoding
- Research pipelines requiring reproducible identification + estimation + refutation
- Comparing multiple estimators on the same causal problem
- Teaching or auditing causal assumptions
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Pure prediction without causal interpretation: overkill
- When causal DAG is completely unknown: DoWhy requires at least a partial DAG or variable role specification
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Graph misspecification: wrong DAG → wrong identification → biased estimates despite correct code
- Treating refutation tests as proof of correctness: passing refutation is necessary but not sufficient
- Ignoring the `proceed_when_unidentifiable=True` flag: if identification fails, estimates are not causally valid
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: A/B test complement: an e-commerce team uses DoWhy to estimate the causal effect of homepage redesign on purchases from an observational dataset where redesign was rolled out unevenly. DoWhy's backdoor adjustment for user segment, device type, and prior purchase history produces an ATE with refutation tests confirming robustness.

11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_it_is: The Synthetic Control Method constructs a counterfactual for a single treated unit by finding an optimal weighted combination of untreated control units that matches the treated unit's pre-treatment outcomes and characteristics. It was designed for comparative case studies with only one treated unit.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.why_it_exists: DiD requires many treated and control units. When only one unit receives treatment (one country, one state, one city), synthetic control provides a rigorous alternative that explicitly constructs the counterfactual from donor pool units.
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.how_it_works:
1. Define a donor pool: J untreated control units with T₀ pre-treatment periods
2. Find weights W* = (w₁,...,wⱼ) ≥ 0, Σwⱼ=1 minimizing distance between treated unit's pre-treatment outcomes and the weighted average: Σwⱼ·Xⱼ ≈ X_treated
3. Counterfactual = Σwⱼ·Yⱼt for post-treatment periods t > T₀
4. Treatment effect τt = Y_treated,t - Σwⱼ·Yⱼt

Inference: permutation tests ('placebo' synthetic controls for each donor unit — if the treated unit's gap is unusually large, it's significant).

Implemented in: `SyntheticControlBenchmarks`, `gsynth` (R), `pysyncon` (Python).
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.use_when:
- Single treated unit with multiple pre-treatment periods
- Policy evaluation for one region/country/firm
- When parallel trends is implausible but pre-treatment fit can be achieved
- Strong pre-treatment match is possible (good donor pool)
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.avoid_when:
- Poor pre-treatment fit: synthetic control interpolates from donor pool, can't extrapolate
- Very few pre-treatment periods (<10): can't assess pre-treatment fit quality
- Interference between treated and control units (spillovers invalidate the donor pool)
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.what_goes_wrong:
- Overfitting to pre-treatment period: perfect pre-treatment fit doesn't guarantee good counterfactual
- Bad donor pool: units too dissimilar to form a plausible counterfactual
- Small donor pool limits permutation inference power
- Extrapolation: if post-treatment outcomes go outside the convex hull of control units, interpolation fails
11|🟡 T2 Privacy, Federation & Causality|.real_example: Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller (2010): effect of California's Proposition 99 tobacco control program (1988). Synthetic California = weighted average of Colorado, Connecticut, Montana, Nevada, Utah. Synthetic control matched CA's cigarette sales perfectly pre-1988. Post-1988 gap (≈25 packs/capita/year) = treatment effect of the policy.

11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_it_is: Test-time compute scaling is the paradigm of allocating additional computation at inference time — through chain-of-thought reasoning, repeated sampling, tree search, or verifier-guided rollouts — to improve output quality without retraining the model. It is the mechanism behind 'thinking' models like o1/o3.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.why_it_exists: Training compute scaling (more parameters, more data) has diminishing returns and is increasingly expensive. Test-time compute offers a complementary axis: a single trained model can achieve dramatically better performance on hard problems by spending more compute at query time.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.how_it_works:
**Chain-of-thought (CoT)**: generate intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. Emerges at ~100B parameters; few-shot CoT examples elicit it in smaller models.

**Self-consistency**: sample multiple reasoning paths independently, take majority vote on final answer. Effective because different reasoning paths make independent errors.

**Best-of-N (BoN)**: generate N candidate answers, select the best using a verifier or process reward model (PRM). O1-style models train a PRM that scores each reasoning step.

**Tree/MCTS search**: expand reasoning as a tree, backtrack on dead ends, use value estimates at each node. DeepMind's AlphaCode 2 uses a code execution verifier as the tree search signal.

**Process Reward Models (PRM)**: trained to assign rewards to each step of reasoning (not just the final answer), enabling fine-grained search guidance.

Scaling curve: for math olympiad problems, BoN with N=1000 matched GPT-4 accuracy at 10× GPT-4's inference cost, using a GPT-3.5-scale model.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.use_when:
- Hard reasoning problems: math, code, scientific question answering
- When accuracy matters more than latency (research, medical diagnosis)
- When a verifier exists (code execution, math checker) to validate reasoning steps
- Budget inference: allocate compute proportional to estimated query difficulty
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.avoid_when:
- Latency-sensitive applications: 1000× more tokens = 1000× more time
- Tasks where multiple samples show high variance with no reliable selection signal
- Simple lookups or factual questions: no benefit, just cost
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_goes_wrong:
- Reward hacking: PRM can be gamed by formatting/structural patterns that score well without correct reasoning
- Verifier dependency: test-time search is only as good as the signal used to select candidates
- Overthinking: for simple questions, extended reasoning causes more errors than direct answers (OpenAI o1 known issue)
- Cost explosion: poorly calibrated compute allocation can make cheap queries expensive
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.real_example: OpenAI o1 (2024): trained with RL to use extended chain-of-thought reasoning before answering. On AIME 2024 (competitive math), GPT-4o scores 13%; o1 scores 83% by spending ~30s of internal reasoning per problem. The model 'thinks before it speaks' using a private scratchpad of intermediate steps, exemplifying test-time compute scaling.

11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_it_is: Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) is a Transformer efficiency technique that dynamically decides which tokens should pass through each Transformer layer's full computation (attention + FFN) and which tokens can skip layers entirely, using a learned routing mechanism to allocate compute only where needed.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.why_it_exists: Standard Transformers apply the same computation to every token at every layer — a fixed compute budget regardless of token importance. MoD recognizes that many tokens are redundant or simple and can skip expensive attention/FFN blocks, reducing total FLOPS while maintaining quality.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.how_it_works:
At each Transformer layer, a lightweight router scores each token for processing priority:
1. Router produces a scalar relevance score per token
2. Top-k tokens (by score) pass through the full attention + FFN block
3. Remaining tokens skip the layer (carried forward via residual stream unchanged)
4. k/sequence_length = capacity fraction C ∈ (0,1) — typically C=0.5 (50% of tokens processed per layer)

Key difference from Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): MoE routes tokens to different expert FFNs at the same layer; MoD routes tokens to SKIP or PROCESS at each layer.

Combined MoD + MoE: isoFLOP optimal — same FLOPS as a standard model but larger, using dynamic compute allocation.

Implemented in: Gemini 1.5, some internal Google Deepmind models.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.use_when:
- Long-context models where many tokens are padding or low-relevance background
- Inference efficiency when latency and cost are primary constraints
- isoFLOP experiments: same compute budget, but larger model capacity
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.avoid_when:
- Short-context tasks where all tokens are dense with information
- When routing overhead exceeds savings (very small models or sequences)
- Tasks requiring uniform attention across all tokens (e.g., DNA sequence analysis where every position matters)
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_goes_wrong:
- Routing instability: router scores can be inconsistent across training, causing some tokens to be systematically ignored
- Load imbalance: if most tokens route to the full path, no efficiency gain (auxiliary load-balancing loss needed)
- Evaluation gap: benchmarks may favor uniform processing; MoD models may underperform on tasks requiring attention to 'unimportant' tokens the router skips
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.real_example: Raposo et al. (2024) 'Mixture-of-Depths': isoFLOP MoD models trained at 6B parameters match or exceed standard Transformer quality on C4 perplexity while using 50% fewer FLOPS per forward pass by skipping 50% of token-layer computations. The model learns to route function words and punctuation to skip paths while routing content tokens to full computation.

11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_it_is: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is the automated process of searching over the space of possible neural network architectures to find designs that maximize a target metric (accuracy, latency, parameter efficiency) for a specific task and hardware target.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.why_it_exists: Manually designing architectures (ResNet, EfficientNet, Transformer) requires expert intuition and extensive trial-and-error. NAS automates this search, finding non-obvious architectures tailored to specific constraints that human designers might miss.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.how_it_works:
**Search spaces**: cell-based (find a reusable cell structure, stack it), chain-structured (select layer types/widths), hierarchical (coarse topology then fine-grained ops).

**Search strategies**:
- **Reinforcement learning** (Zoph & Le 2017): controller RNN generates architecture; accuracy is the reward. Extremely expensive (800 GPU-days for NASNet).
- **Evolutionary search**: population of architectures, mutation/crossover, fitness = accuracy. AmoebaNet.
- **Differentiable NAS (DARTS)**: relax discrete architecture choices to continuous weights via softmax; jointly optimize architecture weights and model weights via gradient descent. Efficient (4 GPU-days) but memory-heavy.
- **Weight sharing / one-shot NAS**: train a supernet once, sample sub-architectures and evaluate without retraining. Single path one-shot (SPOS), Once-for-All.
- **Hardware-aware NAS** (EfficientNet, MNasNet): optimize for latency on specific hardware (mobile CPU, GPU) alongside accuracy.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.use_when:
- Mobile/edge deployment: NAS for Pareto-optimal accuracy/latency tradeoffs
- New modality or task where optimal architecture is unknown
- Large-scale deployment where small efficiency gains multiply
- When you have a specific hardware target with known latency models
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.avoid_when:
- Standard tasks where known architectures (ResNet, Transformer) are well-established
- Limited compute budget: DARTS requires 4+ GPU-days minimum; RL-based NAS is prohibitive
- When the search space doesn't contain architectures better than existing hand-designed ones
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_goes_wrong:
- DARTS collapse: all architecture weights converge to skip-connections (performance collapses)
- Proxy task mismatch: NAS on CIFAR-10 proxies doesn't always generalize to ImageNet
- Weight sharing bias: sub-architectures in a supernet are coupled and don't reflect standalone performance accurately
- Hardware latency modeling errors: if the latency model of the target hardware is wrong, the found architecture is suboptimal
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.real_example: EfficientNet (Tan & Le 2019): NAS found the baseline EfficientNet-B0 by optimizing for accuracy + FLOPS on MobileNetV3 search space. Then compound scaling (width/depth/resolution multipliers) was applied. EfficientNet-B7 achieved ImageNet SOTA at 8.4× fewer parameters than GPT-2 era image models. NAS → 84.3% top-1 accuracy at 66M parameters vs ResNet-152's 77.8% at 60M.

11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_it_is: Model stitching is a technique that combines layers from different independently trained neural networks by inserting a 'stitching layer' (a small learned transformation) between them, enabling analysis of representation similarity across models and architectures.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.why_it_exists: Model stitching reveals whether different models learn similar representations by testing if early layers from model A can be connected to later layers from model B and still produce correct predictions. It is used for studying transfer learning, representation universality, and model merging.
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.how_it_works:
Standard model stitching (Lenc & Vedaldi 2015, Bansal et al. 2021):
1. Take model A (frozen) up to layer i: encoder Aᵢ
2. Take model B (frozen) from layer j onward: decoder Bⱼ
3. Insert a stitching layer S (typically a 1×1 conv or linear layer)
4. Train only S on a dataset: min_S L(B_j(S(Aᵢ(x))), y)
5. Measure stitching accuracy = how well the hybrid model A→S→B performs

If high stitching accuracy is achievable with a small S: representations at Aᵢ and Bⱼ are compatible (similar feature spaces).

Applications:
- **Representation similarity**: compare representations across architectures without CKA
- **Model merging**: merge parts of fine-tuned models (related to model souping, weight averaging)
- **Efficient transfer**: stitch a pre-trained encoder to a task-specific decoder
- **Pruning analysis**: stitch around pruned layers to assess representational impact
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.use_when:
- Research: studying whether different architectures converge to similar representations
- Model merging experiments: combining domain-specific heads with general-purpose encoders
- Debugging: identifying which layers of a model contribute most to task-specific features
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.avoid_when:
- Production deployment: stitched models have extra parameters (the stitching layer) and inference overhead
- When representations are known to be architecturally incompatible (CNN spatial feature maps vs Transformer sequence representations without reshaping)
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.what_goes_wrong:
- Stitching layer overfits: small stitching layers can memorize the training set without genuine representation alignment
- Architecture mismatch: spatial dimensions, sequence lengths, or feature dimensions between A and B may require complex stitching layers that obscure the alignment signal
- Layer index alignment: 'layer 5 of ResNet' ≠ 'layer 5 of ViT' semantically; must align by relative position or functional role
11|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Add.real_example: Bansal et al. (2021) 'Revisiting Model Similarity in Transfer Learning': stitched pairs of ResNet-50 models trained on different random seeds. High stitching accuracy across layers confirmed 'representational convergence' — independently trained models learn similar representations despite different weight initializations.
